SPRING. The Earth, awakened from her wintry sleep, Calls Nature forth her carnival to keep, 410 longer meanly clad, but now arrayed In tenderest greens, and richly varied shade.

The budding hedgerows ope their leaflets gay, ' The woodbines flaunt, the hawthorn spreads its spray, While violets cluster in the flowery dale, And birds new-mated warble in the vale. The twittering swallow and the babbling rill Re-eche to the speckled throstle's trill; Lambs, plaintive bleating, roam o'er lea and fell, or sportive strip the thickets in the dell. Fair blooms the daffodil, the fairy reed Begirts the sedgy rim of spring-decked mead, Laden with a king-cup gay and daisy white, Tipt with a rosy glow of halcyon light. The silvery dew yet kissed the opening flower, When thro' the balmy air from lowly bower A lark on flutt'ring wing rose, singing clear His gladsome welcome to the maiden year. London Society.

div.head: TIME'S FLIGHT.
div.p: TIME'S FLIGHT.

O'er the level plains, where mountains greet me as I go, O'er the desert waste, where fountains at my bidding flow, On the boundless beam by day, on the cloud by night, I am riding hence away; who will chain my flight? War his weary watch was keeping—l hace crushed his
spear ; Grief within her bower was weeping—l have tiried her

- - tear; Pleasure caught a minute's hold—then I hurried by', Leaving all her banquet cold and her goblet dry. Power had won a crown of glory; where is now his' fame? Genius said, "I live in story ;" who bath heard his name? Love beneath a myrtle bough whispered, "Why so fast ?" And the roses on his brow withered as I passed. I have heard the heifer lowing o'er the wild wave's bed; I have seen the billow flowing where the cattle fed. Where began my wanderings? Memory will say! Where will rest my weary wings? Science turns away.

WIN Groan.—A vain man-is motto is: "Win gold and wear it;" a. generous man's: "Win gold and share it;' a miser's: Win gold and spare it.;" a profligates : "Win gold and spend it ;" a broker's: "Win gold and lend it; a fool's: "Win gold and end it ;" a gambler's i' "Win gold and lose it ;" a wise man's: "Win gold, knd use it." Among other advantages which King Tawhiao has derived from his residence in England is a certain facility in the use of Parliamentary "rhetoric. Thus, when on his arrival at Auckland, New Zealand, some exclamations of surprise were excited by his declaration that in Eng- land "ho did not see a single drunkard," he immediately explained that what he meant was that "the drunken- ness was slight in comparison with the sobriety which prevailed." At a Fifeshire dinner last week the following was given, amid roars of laughter:— Jack and Jill went up the hill. To fetch a pail of water, • The tenant fell down and broke his crown,

And the landlord came tumbling at ten At anecdote is related, illustrative of the slyness of the Bohemians, c mpared with the simple honesty of the Germans, and the unscrupulousness of the Hungarians. In war times three soldiers, one of each of these three nations, met in the parlour of an in over the chimney- piece of which hung a watch. When they had gone, the German said, "That Was a good watch ; I wish I had bought it." "I am sorry I did not take it," said the Hungarian. "I have it in my pocket," said the Bohe- mian. ' _ _

MR MIGHT HATE WORN MOHANING.—" What is that you say? Harry married? Well, I'll never believe in men again." " Why ?" "The oaths of love that man swore to me r, " Well, but ycru threw him over. You've been married three months.". "I don't care. He was so devoted to me, and when Jack proposed to me and I accepted, Harry declared that he would be true to my memory and mourn me as one dead to him." "Well, it is of no consequence now to'you." "He might have been decent about it. Ile might have gone into mourn- ing for a year, anyhow."—Toledo Blade. WINE AND A DRY TONG 12.1.—Tw0 Polish co-roligionists were on a journey on a hbt summer day. "Have_you anything with you, Matthias?" "Yes, a bottle of Hun- garian wine. 'What have you got, Tiloif ?" "A dry tongue:" ",Good. Then we will divide our provisions." "Very good, begin." Matthias produced a bottle of wine from his wallet, and its contents were honourably divided. After this had been done Matthias, wiping his mouth, asked his fellow-ttaveller to bring out his pro- vision. "r?" answered Tiloff. "Why, yes, your dry tongue." "I haven't got one now I" was the reply.— Hebrew Journal. __ _ .

_ A witty old lecturer in a South Carolina college was surprised one morning to find his class assembled and loo'king wondrous grave. On advancing to his chair he found it occupied by a goat, which had been tied bolt upright. Instead of storming, as they expected, the doctor mildly .remarked, "Young gentlemen, quite re- -publican, I see, in your tendencies—fond of a representa- tive government. Elevated one of your own members to the chair. Well, well, it's all right, I dare say; the present incumbent can fill it as well as any of you. You may listen to his lecture to-day. Good-bye! Don't feel sheepish about it !" and he departed without leaving a -smile behindlim.-

TWO OF A KIND. A dude and a monkey met one day, And to the dude the monkey did say, "How do, Mr. Dude?" Then to the monkey the dude replied: Remember my high ancestral pride. 2 You're only a monkey, sir; beside, Please don't be so rude." Said the monkey : "Pardon my dudish friend, Sure. I did not really Mean to offend; You take a high shelf. If I'm a monkey. I own it is true, But I could not help it; and as for you. You're just my picture in all you do. And you made yourself !" MORAL. • Misfortune's uses are sweet as pie When they don't interfere with you and I. OPEN CONFESSION.—A gallant captain of a heavy 'cavalry regiment, who was more noted for his interest in racehorses than regimental duties, was in the habit of making most extraordinary remarks on parade as well as off. an one occasion, when inspecting his troop, he found that one of the men had neglected the washing of his neck and ears. When he was inspected in the" rear," the captain said to him. " You dirty fellow, sir, you have not washed your face behind, sir; turn round and look at yourself, sir." He also had a great dislike to one of his- "troopers," who certainly was not what is called " smart" He was always a marked" man on parade. One day he was absent on other duties. When the cap- tain came on parade. he at once called out, "You are not • dressing,' Jones." Turning to the sergeant-major, the captain said," Let Jones have three days confinement to barracks for inattention." The sergeant-major said, "Beg pardon, captain, Jones is not on parade." "Very well," said the captain, "let the next man to him have three days." When the captain was promoted to command the regiment, he assembled the troop officers and com- plained of the want of uniformity, saying," I am deter- mined to have everything uniform, and I shall commence witlithe men's boots ; let them all be made one!size, and to fit the stirrup-irons." The same gallant officer was noted for his style of writing, which 'was more like Chinese than English. He wrote an official letter to the authorities himself which was returned to him because it could not be read. Hahancled the letter to the orderly- room clerk, with the remark that they must all be fools. Can't you read it ?" After a long attempt to deciper it, the clerk said, "I can't read it, sir." "Why, then, you must be a fool too !" Then, snatching the letter from him he tried to make out what it meant, but, after some time, blurted out, "Why, I am the biggest fool of the lot, for I can't read it myself!" THE FIRST FCCHSIA. IN ENGLAND,—The foll Owing ac- count of the introduction of the first fuchsia, F. coccinert, which was written some forty years ago by Mr. Sheppard, of Dublin, is worth reproduction. Some sixty years ago, the late Mr. Lee, of Hammersmith, was showing some of his fine plants to a gentleman, when the latter remarked, Well, Mr. Lee, you have not a prettier flower in all your collection than one I saw in a window in the east end of London a few days ago." Mr. Lee inquired, "Pray, what is it like?" The, gentleman said the plant was most ele- gant, the flowers hanging in tassels from the pendant Branches, colour of the richest crimson, and in the centre a fold of deep purple ,and so forth. Mr. Lee having I sarnt where the plant was to be found, posted off di- rectly, and on his arrival perceived at once that the plant was new in this part of the world. The plant belonged to a sailor's wife, and she had it in a pot in the window. R 3 stood and admired it, then entering the house, he said, 'My good woman, this is a nice plant, I should like to bay it. " I could not sell it for money; it was brought to me from the West Indies by my husband, who has left again, and I must keep it for his sake," "But I must have it." said Mr. Lee." "But you shall not." said the tilor's wife." Here Mr, Lee emptied his pocket of gold, silver, and copper, the stock amounting to something over eight guineas' "Well-a-day," said the woman, "but that is a power of money; sure the plant is yours." Having got theplant 'safely deposited in his nursery, Mr. Lee's first work was to pull off everyprestige. of flower. Every effort was now made to multiply the plant, and by the next season, Mr. Lee was the delighted possessor of 300 plants. The two which opened first were removed to the show-house. A lady came. "Why, Mr. Lee, where did you'get this °harming plant." " H'm, this is a new thing, my lady; pretty, is it not?" "It's price ?" "One Buhl". Thank your ladyship," said Mr. Lee. Another and another went until un at tne end of the first season Mr. Lee had 300 golden guineas in his purse, the produce Of the single plant. Mr. Lee did not forget to gladden the sailor's wife py presenting her with a plant of his favourite flower. Have you any idea, old lalieg, of what the Hydrostatic Paradox, I with which comfort is thus associated, can possibly be? I The Hydrostatic Paradox, ladies, is a coffee-pot. What , hard names it is now the fashion to give to common I things—is it not? If a coffee-pot is styled the Hydro- static Paradox—what next? We shall probably have a roasting-jack denominated the Differential Calculus. Henry Ward Beecher tells this at his own expense:— "A regiment of lumbermen—big, tall fellows, six-foot- five; from Maine—were passing through Brooklyn in '62. There were about 1,000 in all, and I marched them up to Plymouth Church, invited them in, and gave every man of them a whole seat with a cushion in it. There they all sat with their knapsacks on, and I got on the platform and began to preach. My friends, it's the only time in my life I ever preached a whole congrega- tion to sleep." I THE FARMER AND THE BISHOP.—It is not generally I known, the Globe says, that the new Bishop of London was once taken for an Excise spy. The Bishop—who is a great walker—had lost his way on a Devonshire road, and was very fatigued. Being overtaken by a farmer's gig he asked for a lift, and offered to pay for it, adding that he was the new Bishop of Exeter. " Noa, nee," said the farmer, as he gave his horse an extra flip, "I know whom you be—you be an exciseman; I know 'ee by your gaiters." It ought to be explained that farmers' gigs pay no license when they are used for the owner's business. The Bishop, however, trudged on, and finished his walk of about seventeen miles late in I the evening. THE Potacsuares Penantsz.—The police system of Mexico is admirable. At every street corner there is a patrolman, night and day—not a patrolman, either, for he never moves. Be stands like a statue during the day, occasionally leaning against a lamp-post, and answers inquiries with the greatest urbanity. When- ever there is a row two or three policemen are instantly present, and if their clubs cannot suppress it they use 1-evolvers. At night the policeman brings a lantern and a blanket. He sets the lantern in the middle of the street,- and all carriages are compelled to keep to the right of the rew of lanterns, which can be seen glimmer- ing from one end of the street to the other. As long as people are passing he stands at the corner, but when things quiet-down he retires to a neighbOuring doorway, wraps his blanket around him, and liicZ'.!` down to pleasant dreams. OLD AND NEW SUNS.—D, is becoming generally recog- nised that in suns and planets, in all the orbs, in fact, which people space, there are stages of existence akin to the stages of life. There is a period of preparation, a period of youth, a period of mid-life, a period of detity, and finally there comes the end of life. The stages of an orb's life may be described as, in the main, stars of cooling. In suns we find evidence of such changes ai the different condition of (as shown by thespettroscope) of such orbs as Sirius, Vega, and Alleao on the one hand, and orbs like our own sun, mllct, smaller, and therefore much more advanced in orl-1 life on the other. But also we find much older Suns than ours in the orange-redand yellow stars, and older orbs still in the brood-red and garnet-tinted suns shown by the telescope in various parts of the star depths. Nor do 'astronomers doubt that there are older suns yet, suns which have passed on to the last stages of all (mayhap), the stage of darkness. Moreover, as it is a known law of cooling bodies that the larger a cooling mass of given temperature is the longer will be the stage of its cooling, we may safely assume that, apart from differences (which may, nevertheless, be enormous) in the beginning of orb life, the larger suns, having much longer periods of life, will have passed through leas of their longer lives than the smaller suns. —Richard Procter. According to a Washington correspondent, when General Spinner was Secretary of the Treasury he got hundreds of requests annually for his autograph, the oddest in America. For a time he answered each one in an autograph note, but the labour involved became so great that finally he had a printed form prepared, run- ning :—" Your request of such a date is hereby complied with." Then when an autograph request came in he simply signed this blank form and let it go at that. One day a tall, raw-boned countryman walked into his office. "Morning," said he. "Good morning," said Spinner, looking up. "I came for that place you promised me," said the countryman, after an awkward pause. "Place ?" said Spinner, crossly ; •" I promised you no place." "Yes, you did," insisted the countryman, stoutly. "I've got your promise in your own hand- I writing." With that lie hauled out one of Spinner's I autograph replies: "Your request of such a date, Sec." "But; man alive," said Spinner, "that was in response to a request from you for my autograph." • No, ,twasret," said the man; " I never asked no autograph. I want a place ; that's what I wrote for." Spinner had the man's letter hunted up. Sure enough it was a formal application for a place. "Here," said Spinner, -emptying into his big hand all the money he had in his pocket, "here's some money for you. I can't give you , a place. I haven't any to give." And with that the ' countryman had to be content. DISADVANTAGES OV A 'UNIVERSITY TRAINING.--,.BelNVeen ' the maa and the boy—the hobbyede-hoy age—there is a very critical period to be passed through. At this time, said a distinguished physiologist, the animal nature is developed, but the moral nature lags behind; man is supremely selfish apd wrong-headed. To get creditably through this crisis Is the difficulty, and so far Oxford served as a wider school to exercise some modicum of restraint and to give full liberty by degrees. A man if idle had better be idle in good company; the worst set he can join at Oxford would be an improvement on the rakes of a country-town. Only yesterday a friend asked me about a University education for his son. I replied, "For what profession or course of life do you intend to prepare him?" He said, "For the Bar." "But does he aspire to become an enlightened jurist, and like Lord Selborne to rise from college to the higher walks in poli- tical life? If so a college education will be a profitable investment for a man of property, but if you only expect him to earn a moderate income in ordinary business. I cannot say that the high road to legal success lies through Oxford." Oxford should be regarded simply as what it professes to be, a place of education. Ex- cept so far as it sharpens the faculties it has no bearing ' on professional life. Instead of being any aid or pre- paration for business, College is decidedly a hindrance; first, because it is a peculiar and almost to be called an artificial sphere, with a very partial view of life in general; and secondly because the Collegian forms habits of nicety and exclusiveness, studying human nature rather in books than in the wide world, which habits the man of business must at once proceed to correct. "I would back a young attorney's clerk," said an old barrister, "to pick up information by his eyes and ears, and there is no little for a lawyer which cannot be learnt otherwise, faster than the best scholar that ever came fresh from the University." After hearing this, my friend rejoined, "Then the same time spent first in a solicitor's and afterwards in a conveyancer's office would be so much time and experience gained in advancement for the Bar ?" "Undoubtedly as you say, for the Bar,' for Oxford has no more to do wifh a man's legal habits than with his agricultural habits, in case he were in- tended for a farmer. Oxford proposes neither to make the lawyer nor to make the farmer, but to make the man. It teaches man cloth not live by bread alone,' having heart, brain, and divers mysterious feelings and sensibilities, as important to a properly bred human being as his digestive organs; it prefers the wide views of a Newton to the L.S.D.-ism of a Cocker."--London Society. THE AUTHORSHIP OF "ADAM BEDE," &c.—The follow- ing has appeared in The Times, signed by the well-known initials, "S. G. 0." :—Sir,--The reviewer in your columns of the "Life of,George Eliot," in the concluding para- graph of the second review, alludes to the false claim made by one Joseph Liggins to the autliorship of George Eliot's works as one of the curiosities of literature." It certainly was one of the greatest of these. It may, perhaps, interest your readers to know how this man imposed upon the credulity of very many people. It fell to me to expose the fraud in your columns, and this by pure accident. A rather strange chance WI made me aware that Miss Evans was George Eliot, but I kept the information to myself. Some time after I saw a paper handed about at a friend's house, which my host told me was a subscription list in favour of one Joseph Liggins, whom the parties active in its promotion declared to be not only the author of George Eliot's i works, but that he was n deep poverty, and bad been paid in a most niggardly way by his publisher. I mildly suggested to a lady of rank who was active in the mat- ter, that she was altogether mistaken, and that I felt certain that this man had never written one word of the said works; and that I was equally certain the real author had no reason whatever to complain of the pay- ment for them. I was met by the most positive assur- ance that there was more than one person active in promoting the subscription who know from actual proof that this Liggins did write the "Scenes in Clerical Life" and other of the novels. I consulted my host, and told him that it was a deliberate fraud. Ile was a generous man, and said, "Do prove it to be one ; if you fail, I would rather myself pension such a writer than allow him to want." I assured him he might be quite at ease in the matter, for I would by that day's post send to your columns an exposure of what I knew to be a fraud. My letter was published at once, with a foot note from the editor confirming it. But now comes the most curious part of the affair. In the face of my own letter, corroborated by Messrs. Blackwood and George Eliot, I had several most severe attacks made upon me, upholding the fraud, and, if my memory serves me right, one was in the pages of the Athourum. One well-known public man wrote me a strong lecture, and said a lady was then in his house who knew Mr. Lig- gins, and had actually seen him at work on the manu- script of one of the works published as those of George Eliot. That Mr. Liggins was clearly an able fictionist there can be no doubt, -but it has always been to me an enigma asyet unsolved how he could have imposed upon those by whom he hoped to he subsidised in his author- ship, seeing that I knew some of the most active in the matter to be people wise above the average of folk. The Veterinarian of this current month states that up to the last day of January no fresh outbreak of foot- and-mouth disease had been reported to the Agricultural Department since that which occurred in November last near Newsteed Abbey in Nottinghamshire, and that "there is good reason for believing that this disease has now disappeared from this country." . The Board of Trade returns for January again show a great decrease in the imports of live stock, namely, 18,125 oxen and bulls, 3,873 cows, 1,962 calves, 27,202 sheep and lambs, and 128 pigs; against 22,326 oxen and bulls, 5,123 cows, 2,664 calves, 57,900 sheep and lambs, and 1,191 pigs in January, 1884. Fresh meat imports have increased. Tim UNPARDONABLE SIN.—At a dinner given by Lord Gerard to his tenants, at Ashton, last week, the Hon. W. Gerard, who is a master of foxhounds, told a good story, illustrative of "a fearful thing, which had led to the ruin of many farmers, both mentally, physically, and in every other way." A hunting clergyman went to see a farmer who was dying. The old farmer told him that he had fared very poorly in this world, but that he hoped to be much better off in the next, to which the hunting clergyman replied that there was not the slightest chance of it. Did they know why that was? It was because he had wire in his fences! We differ from the Hon. M.F.H. The Game Laws were not made in heaven. Moss ON GRASS Lawn.—Question: I find that three of my grass fields are very much overgrown with moss. I am now ploughing one field, but must leave the others for a season or two. I shall be much obliged if any of your correspondents will kindly suggest a means of de- stroying the moss. The fields are high and the soil thin. Also any suggestion for destroying grass on paths and a large back yard will oblige.—Answer: Grass on paths ca,n be killed by salt, but the best plan is to hoe it up by the roots. Mossy pastures are best ploughed up and re- sown, and afterwards well manured to stimulate the growth of grasses that will keep down the mess. EXTRAORDINARY TITRE.—The agitation against extra- ordinary tithes is not allayed by distress sales. At one recently announced in Kent, the auctioneer did not turn up, and the farmers present held an indignation meeting against the tithe. Mr. A. Bath, secretary of the society Nall is agitating against the tithe, said he thought the verse of a little song brought out about forty years ago was applicable neW t 9 the clergy in Kent and Sussex, viz.:—

Let the land of old England go barren, go bare Let the farmer be driven away, the red rust of sloth cover blade, plough, and share, sink into decay; Letln despair let him wriggle slid writhe, thed thlaeboh I'm the Man of the Mountain, fixed safe in the earth, rrere.gadiroin the land of his birth, I'm the ruthless collector of tithe. THE DUKE OF DEFONSIIIRE'S FAIWr',44 the Mont, reut akidit Qf. the Furness farms of the buke of Devon- shire, one of the tenants remarked that they had antici- pated a " fertiliser " in the shape of a 10 per cent. abatement of rent. Lord Edward Cavendish, who pre, sided, said that, "If, after a fine year, such aa was experienced last year, a reduction had bees given, it would then appear as if the rents sts.sig be revised. The farms on his father's estate nen so rented as to en- able tenants to meet g0c.4.9.ha bad wears. It could not be expected that a reduction would be made this year. If, however, there was a general feeling upon the sub- ject, his father would like it brought to his notice, and would discuss the matter, because he did not wish any of his tenants to have cause for fault finding. Though the weather of the past season had been good, prices had been low, especially for wheat. Meat, however, he thought, had realised fair prices. He would not like, to see land laid down to grass, to the interference of agri- cultural labour. If one landlord reduced his rents, 'other landlords must follow suit His father's farms were all low rented, and it would therefore be a hard- ship to other landlords." Commenting upon this latter remark, a farmer told me that he rented a farm adjoin- ing one belonging to the Duke of Devonshire, and that his land was 15s. an acre more than was paid by the Duke's tenant. But the great difficulty, he said, was to get hold/of one of the Duke's farms, it being a rare oc- currence that one was in the market., an exoellenttribute to the landlord.—R. EARL BEOTIVE'S Sitos.—Recently, Earl 13ective opened four silos, at which a number of farmers attended. No new thing. propounded in agriculture that is at all feasible is untried at Underley, and, guided by the prac- tical skill of Mr. Punchard, nothing is left to chance. The silo building at Underlay has been erected at the foot of a bank, the grotind at one side being level with the top for convenience of filling. It is 42 feekby 23 feet, and divided into four compartments. These have been filled respectively with (1) green oats, cut just as the ears had begun to appear; (2) meadow grass; (3) second cut of clover and seed grass; (4) coarse grass from river banks, hedgerows, and from under trees, and common turnip tops, mixed with layers of straw. The roof of the silo is a movable one, covered with Willesden four-ply, paper, and the total cost of the silo is placed at £lOO. It is so constructed that if not needed for a silo, it can be converted to other purposes. In one com- partment of the silo Seward's (Lancaster) Patent Levers are in use. In the other three the weightage was by boxes of stones. By the former mode a pressure of 1441b5. to the square foot was obtained; by the latter, for purposes of experiments, 941bs. and 65Ibs. It seemed to be the general opinion that these latter weights were insufficient where the grass had been put in uncut All the material, with the exception of that in No. 4 silo, had been cut before putting in, one of Bust's ensilage cutters being Used; and,opmions varied as to the advisability of cutting, more especially on the question of cost. No. 3 was pronbunced to be the best ensilage; the turnip tops were a failure. The others were good food, and were relished by the cattle. Wooden doors had been placed at the bottom of the silos, and around these there was a little waste, air having evi- dently been admitted. Experiments in feeding the en- silage to live stock will be commenced, and the results made known. • VANCOUVER ISLAND.-011 Vancouver Island are to be found splendid locations for hundreds of families, and the opening of the railway reserve will supply hundreds more. It is estimated that there are 389,000 acres of arable land on the island, of which 300,000 are well suited for agriculture, the greater portion, however, being densely timbered. This mammoth island and the numerous smaller ones along the coast will in a few years be settled upon by thousands. The New West- minster District, of which much has been said, is not exceeded in fertility by any tract of land on the coast. The productiveness of the delta land is marvellous. Statistics carefully prepared give the return, per acre, at 75 bushels of oats ; bay, 3A. tons; barley, 40 bushels; turnips, 40 to 50 tons; potatoes, 30 tons. Roots and vegetables attain an enormous size, and the yield to the acre is prolific. The growing and ripening seasons being slow, the farmer is given ample time to prepare the soil to receive the seed, and, after it has ripened, to harvest and house the result of his labour and toil. A ready market is found almost at his door for the products of his farm, is, very good prices, as the following list of ruling rates will demonstrate :—Hay. per ton, $l5 to $18; wheat and oats, $4O to $5O; barley, $35 to $4O; potatoes, $3O to $35; carrots, $lO to $l5 ; mangolds, $B. The dairy and poultry business can be rendered exceedingly remunerative. Fresh eggs are always in demand at figures ranging from 40 to 75 cents per dozen. A large quantity are imported annually. Chickens, by the dozen, realise $8 to $10; turkeys, 30 to 35 cents per pound; geese, from $2.50 to $3.50 each; ducks $1 per pair; dairy butter, 50 to 80 cents per pound; Cheese, 25 to 30 cents per pound. GRANDMAMMA'S VALENTINE. (From Cassell' Magazine.) A merry lot of girls we were—nearly a dozen of us—and we were shouting with laughter, the greater number of us; while an occasional quiet one was enjoying a keener, though more subdued pleasure, as we passed round our valentines among each other, and admired, or laughed at, or ridiculed each one, according as it deserved. Cousins and friends we were; and we were congregated in grandma's great front room, where we were always wel- come, and where we dearly loved to gather and listen to stories of nearly half a century ago. There the dear old lady sat now, in her favourite corner, knitting stockings for her youngest grandson, while the "click, click, click" of her busy needles made a pleasant music in the pauses of our Laughter. Now and then she would look at us over her spectacles and smile, and then we would smile too, and turn towards her some outrageous caricature as an explanation of a more than usually explosive burst 0 laughter. "Grandma is laughing at us. I'm sure she thinks we're a silly lot of geese,' said Cousin Fanny. "Nothing of the sort!" I protested In defence of myself, for I was behaving in a very uproarious manner. "I'm sure grandma was just as wild over her valentines as any of n.

Grandma beamed assent. "Tell us, grandma; we would feel encouraged," said Fanny. " ro carry on worse than you are doing now?" laughed grandma. "Not that I think you need the encouragement, teensy; but it's true I was just as glad of my valentines as toe gayest of you; and, to be quite frank, I can even enjoy that pleasure yet. Fgot a valentine to-day." "Oh, grandma! You dear, giddy, young thing !" cried Hefty (she was grandmother's pet, and privileged to do and say what she pleased). "I must be looking after you," and she slid down on the ottoman at grandma's feet, and flung her arms about her. "Now, dearest granny, tell us all about it. I know it must be quite a story. Be good, now, and I'll promise not to be a very strict duenna though I did catch you and Mr. Allison looking at each other last Sunday in church." Grandma laughed merrily, and it was pretty to see the pink colour flush up in her dear, faded cheek. After protesting that the story was a very old one, and that it could not interest any one save the actors in it, and that it wasn't much of a story any way, and other sueh weak and futile excusee, grandma, clicking her shining needlet more than ever, began "Once upon a time there were three people, two girls a handsome young man. One of the Off WA/ t black-eyed, black-haired, dark•browed creature, with skin alesest as dark as an Indian's; but, as all the young fellows in that part of the country thought, powerful good looking. And so she was, Mandy was a handsome girl, and hadn't she a temper! But when it was up it only helped to set off. ter good looks. I tell yOli it uy.4l to Make. those black eyes of hers flash like diamonds' and the colour would stream up in those sallow ambermoloured cheeks of hers till they glowed like the brightest hollyhocks. " Well, the other girl was Alicia, and her friends used to call her Alice, and Ally, for short. There were a few of the boys who reckoned she was kind o' pretty-looking too. She had blue eyes, and the stra!ghtest, tallest, slimmest figure in the village; and as to Tier complexion, she had a beau who used to say her skin was whiter than the first fresh skim- ming off the ; and fer her checks end lips, he eeed to be always singing an old Irish song that no pretended was wriaten on purpose to describe them; it was all nonsense, of ceurre, but it went this way: 'ln the town o' Kilkenny There lives a swate dame Her cheeks are like roses, Her lips much the same; Like a dish o' fresh strawberriert Smothered in crams." 4' Well, well! I often thought, myself, Alicia was a pretty girl, though she had red hairs und that worried her—oh! you can't think! You man look surprised, Hetty, dear—it was just like yours, bet it's nigh on to fifty years ago now, and red hair wasn't the fashion then. You've heard yours praised for outshining the sun, and likened to melted gold, andeall that sort of thing, Iletty, haven't you? I know it, dear, and you wouldn't exchange it for the fairest flaxen, or the glossiest black or brown in this room, and you're right It's as beautiful as a halo round your head this minute, and Ally's was jest the same, all shining and curly, and when she combed it out it would reach in glittering shiny waves half-way to her feet. But many a time I've known her cry herself to sleep because some one had called her that 'pretty red-headed gal,' and she'd have given the red hair, and her blue eyes, and her complexion of strawberries and creme,' for the black eyes, and smooth, shiny black braids of Mandy, all because she once heard John say there was nothing so handsome, as a dark, beautiful woman, with black hair and soft dark brawn eyes. "John was the young man—you wonder I've been oolong coming to him, I suppose? Well, it's because I kind of dread it, now I've started—you see these tsvo girls, Alicia and Mandy, were both in love with John; and as a matter of course he couldn't be in love with both, and somebody had to be miserable, however things went. And as they did go all three were miserable. Oh, my heart! how miserable, at least I can speak for one, and, as I know now, the other two suffered just as much, and it may be even more. " Alicia was the daughter of the richest man in the village, and being an only child she was a match for any one, how- ever grand, in that part of the country—in fact, she was reckoned the best match for a hundred miles around, and she had niany lovers, and might pick and choose till she suited herself. But the choice was made already. She loved John, and she tried, as well as she could without being forward, to let him know it; for he was very much below her in worldly position, being only a poor young car- penter. Sometimes she felt almost sure he loved her, bat, if he did, he lacked courage to tell her so, or perhaps be feared she might think it WAS her fortune he was after; and if she was too proud to be won because she had a fortune, he was a great deal too proud to have any one think him mean enough to marry for money. "Oh! many a time poor Al;y• wished her father might fail, and that she could earn her living knitting socks and mittens for the village boys, if it would only bring John nearer to her, and make him as easy and sociable as he was with Mandy. Poor little simpleton! if she could only have Iknown it, the very embarrassment and confusion he showed in her presence, compared with his easy good-nature when he was with Mandy, ought to have told her the state of his feelings. But she didn't know much on the subject, though she was in love herself; and then there were times, as I said, when she felt quite sure that John really loved her; if he would only pluck up courage to say so! It was leap-year, and she had wild ideas of telling. him straight out that he might speak, and net be afraid to get 'no' for an answer; but if it had been twenty leap-years all rolled lute one, she was far too modest a girl to do anything so bold and un- maidenly. But chance helped her, at least she thought so at the time. "It had been a hard winter, and there was considerable suffering among the poor of the village; and about the middle of February a sale had been organised, and all the proceeds were to go to the poor. It was a great success; and, after it was all over, every one who had helped was invited to finish off the day by taking supper at Alicia's home. It was a splendid supper, set out in the great, long dining-room; and everybody, gentle and simple, humble or grand, met there as equals. Of course John and Mandy were among the guests; and it really seemed to Alicia as if John tried to get away front Mandy that night, and get as near to herself at he could. You may be sure she did what was modest and ladylike id help him; and once or twice their glances met, and they couldn't help seeing thet each other's eyes said just as plain At itx.7 ceeld op:ak, li love you—l love you r All aorta ot things were spoken of, and all manner of eubjects discussed. And just as if it had been dens on pur- pose, somebody started a discussion on unequal marriages. Some were in favour and some were against them. One young man said any man was good enough for any girl if he loved her and sheer loved him; another declared that he wouldn't ask a girl richer than himself to marry him, not if he was dying for her, and knew that she would say 'yes.' A third answered be would be a great goose in that case, for hearts were worth more than money any day. A fourth asked bows bashful lover, who was too much in love to dare to say so, could be helped out, and at this there was a great deal of laughing, and in the first pause of silence Alicia suddenly said, 'He might send her a valentine !' Her cheeks coloured up scarlet as soon as the words passed her lips, for her gaze met that of John, and there was something in his eyes just then that she thought she could not mistake, and her heart beat and throbbed till she thought everybody all around must know it. "Then there was more laughing and talking, but ehe didn't hear much of it, or seem to care what it was about; yet.when the supper-party brought itself, somehow, to a close, and there was a general leave-taking, she was quite sure that John held her hand a long, long time in saying 'good-bye,' and let it go at last with such a lingering pres sure that her very finger-tips tingled with joy. She didn't shake hands with any ohs else that night after John said 'good-bye.' "Well, the next day but one was Saint Valentine's Day, and about noon, for she couldn't stand it any longer, she sent a messenger over to the post-office. It was at the far end of the village, in a grocery store, and Mandy's father was the post-mast.r. Alicia got a regular arm-full of valentines, all sorts; pretty ones, homely ones, gay ones, witty and stupid, sentimental and droll; but the one that made her fingers tremble so that she could scarcely take it out of the envelope, that was all covered over with hearts and arrows, and doves and flowers, was directed in John's beautiful clear copper-plate handwriting that she knew as well as she knew her own. It was sealed with wax, and she got a sci:sors and cut carefully round the seal, thin slowly took out the valentine, and unfolded it. It was a hideous caricature, with big goggle blue eyes cheeks red as paint could make them, and a mane of red itair, all loom and flowing round the shoulders and down the back! "What the words were, written underneath it, poor Ally never knew. With a scream of pain, for no stab from a knife could have hurt her as much, she dropped the horrid thing on the floor; then quickly passing from wounded feel inn to rage, she stamped on it, and tore it into a thou: sand pieces. ••J,ext day she met John face to face; he was the first person she met when she went into the street. He came towards her with a beaming face, and both hands out- stretched. " ' Oh, Ally!' he said, I've been waiting all morn- ing—" "' Good morning, sir,' she said, and her eyes pierced him like a gimlet. " Be turned pale, and his lips quivered, then he seemed to make a great effort, and said— " 'Mies Alicia, you got my valentine—'

PPLISH.

One of the handsomest of all varieties of domestic poultry is the Polish, and -for ornamental purposes we know of no breed which at once is so beautiful in colour, in shape, and in carriage as this. Others may have richer colour, or greater style, but for a combina- tion:thereof this breed undoubtedly holds the palm. This is equally true of the Gold Spangled, the Silver Spangled, the White-crested Blacks, the Balfor Chamois, and the other rarer varieties whin are now very seldom seen. And were it not for one special point, namely, the crest, which is so difficult to keep in order, and if al- lowed to get wet brings on colds and other diseases, there is little doubt but that the breed would be a popu- lar one, for apart from the handsome rich appearance of the fowls they are capital layers and good on the table, also standing confinement very well. There Can be no question that when a breed combines good looks with economic qualities it has a very great advantage over any other which possesses but one of these recommen- dations. A.-studylof the Polish fowl is interesting, as it has evidently been the progenitor of some very valuable races, such as the Crevecceur and the Houdan. The name would indicate that these fowls had their origin in Poland; but this is an error, and the name is , evidently a misnomer. It has been suggested that the title came from the crest, which in some districts is called a Poll, and, considering how many of our English words and names have undergone such changes, it is not improbable that at first they were called Polls, then PolPed fowls, and: afterwards Poland fowls. If this were so, it is not difficult to see how that a misconcep- tion of the last-named title has led to their being called Polish. A similar error accounts for the title of another race of poultry, the Hamburghs, which have no more to do with the 01(1 Free City of that name than have the , Polish with Poland or the Poles. Still, there is the name, and it does not make a great deal of matter now; to at- tempt to change it would be folly, however much we should have preferred a different designation at the first. All that is needed is to explain the origin of the name , as far as possible, and let alone that which we find. The Polish owe their origin to Holland, and on the Continent they are called "Hollandaise."

The great glory of the Polish fowls is the crest, which, in the finest specimens, is of a large globular shape, sometimes nearly nine inches in diameter. Shape is re- garded as the most important point, then colour, and lastly size. Any division or parting in the crest is re- garded as a fault, but it is very difficult to find any bird without some tendency fd a middle parting. The face is generally completely hidden, so much so that special drinking troughs and food trays have been devised. To support:sci large a crest the skull of Polish fowls is of a peculiar shape, and in tual:old poultry book we find it there recorded that "The chickens of this family aft) no sooner hatched' than peculiarities may be noticed by which they may be at once distinguished from those of any other fowls, viz., the elevated roof of the nostrils, the round and prominent appearance of the head, and, in the bearded varieties, the peculiar thick-looking neck." This is one of the truest tests of a Polish fowl, and un- til one is acquainted with it there is certainly a most un- natural of' uncanny" appearance about the head, when the crest is very small or removed. Below the beak is a beard, usually in size proportionate to the crest above. The head is thrown well back, which gives the breast a prominent appearance it wOuld not otherwise have. The neckhackle is full, the body plump and round, and the tail, which rises very high has long sickles, both the sickles and coverts being high, edged with dark i colour. The legs are clean and dark n colour, and the body itself is very much like that of the Hatnburgh, close, compact, and rotund. It is rather small in size, and does not usually weigh more than five or six pounds, but, as already stated, the meat is good on the table. Polish are good layers, and if they can be kept from wet they are fairly hardy, but it is always necessary to pro- vide a good, covered shed in which they can be kept during wet weather. They are non-sitters as a rule, though sometimes, as is the case with all non-sitting breeds, there are hens who like to be so far out of the common as to assume maternal duties.

•The Gold Spangled Polish is a very handsome bird. The ground colour is a golden brown or red, with nearly every feather edged, or laced, or tipped with black. This gives the fine spanged appearance, the spangles being half-moon or crescent markings all over. The Silver Spangled has a ground dolour of white or silver, with the same markings as in the richer hued variety, and tho effect is very fine in the best specimens, though scarcely go grand as in the Golds. The White-crested Blacks are perhaps the most striking of all the varieties of this breed. The body alt! tail 1/3 pure black, of that rich metallic black, which is ever the endeavour of a black fowl breeder, and the crest is white, or as nearly white as possible, for black feathers make tiiir appear- ance in spite of the most careful 'breeding. But so long as the large malbrity are white these are not objected to. At one time some Black-crested White Polish were known, but these have died out. We heard some time ago that a few had been seen in Holland, but the owner would not sell at any price. Chamois Polish are very pretty. In these the ground colour is buff or light gold, and the spangling white. Blacks, Cuckoos, Grey, and Blue Polish have all been seen, but these are not at all cultivated, and do not command any favour. To any- one who has a suitable place and wishes to lake up with a handsome fowl, there is none better than this. It will exercise the skill and knowledge of the most ardent fancier, and if he produces really good specimens he will be well rewarded, for these always sell at good prices. It is highly ornamental, and one or other of the varie- ties can be made to match with the surroundings of any poultry yard. Green food is very scarce 3ust now, and what there is of it is not very good. If cabbages are plentiful they may be used very freely or any other kinds of vegetables. But failing these the next best things are roots. Turnips may be given raw, just cut in too, and if suspended by twine they will not only satisfy the craving for green food, but also be a means of exercise for the birds. Some poultry keepers prefer to boil the roots and mix them with the soft food, and this is very good also. Potatoes and carrots may be used instead of or with the turnips. The manner in which they are given is of less actual consequence, than the fact that they are given.

In the town of Kilkenny—' "She turned like a lightning-flash, and took the arm of the singer; and the next Sunday their two names were called in church. John waited till the wedding was over. Alicia supposed he was waiting to marry Mandy on the same day. But be didn't. On the day after Alicia married the husband whom she afterwards learned to love very dearly, John left that part of the country, and they did not meet &stain till her red hair was like the mow, and he had very little left, ef any kind, and what there was matched hers in colour."
"Oh, grandma! and what became of Mandy ?" "She lived and died an old maid. When she sent for me yesterday it was to beg forgiveness, and to give me this valentine."

Grandma took from under the snowy folds of her necker- chief a worn and faded piece of paper; it had a border all flowers and doves, and other old-fashioned valentine signs, but in the centre just three lines :- 4" Alicia, I love you with all my heart. Will you marry me "And that was your valentine, grandma ?" netty asked, awestruck.

Grandma smiled. "It was Alicia's valentine," she said. "Mandy lad unsealed John's letter, taken out this valentine, and substituted the horrid red-haired caricature." "Oh, the wretch! But she's dead, only I conld never have forgiven her. It would have been a case of Queen Eliatheth and the wicked Countess of Nottingham." Grandma stooped and kissed Betty. "At your age Alicia might have felt the same, dear," she said. "But the things of this world pass away, and beyond we shall lose sight of all the wrongs and disappointments we leave here." She folded up her valentine and laid it, tenderly, just over her heart.

That evening, when old Mr. Allison called for his grand- daughter, my grandmother held his hand softly between hers, and looked into his eyes with a look he must have remembered, for he seemed to flash up and grow younger as he met it.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

SEED SOWING.—We are remiriNl by OUT friends the nurserymen who are kind enough to Send us their seed lists, that the time for seed sowing is drawing nigh. These lists increase in bulk annually as the natural Con- sequence of the introduction of new Vegetables and Flowers, so that the number of varieties catalogued at the present time make it puzzling to the inexperienced as to what is best to order. It IS disappointing to those with limited space and far more limited means to dis- cover, when too late, that the kinds they: have selected have proved unsuitable to the locality and soil. Experi- She 6 undoubtedly is the best teacher in these matters, but the observance of one or two rules will be a valuable auxiliary Note those varieties that do well in the locality on soil of similar description to your. own. Select old. established kinds if known to you by name, if not they may usually be recognised by their low price. The fact of their having been in cultivation :so much longer has enabled the seed growers to have ample stocks whilst recent introductions are comparatively scarce. On some- what heavy land we have found the following Peas— William I. and Sutton's Ringleader—as good;as any for early, and for second early advancer Laxton s Supreme and Harrison's Glory whilst for the latest Omega, Veitch's Perfection Telegraph, and Telephone. The two last being about the besf. for exhibition,tut for ordinary purposes we would select Ne Plus Ultra, Emperor of the Marr ' ows and Lord Raglan. Of Beans: For the earliest we select Early Mazagan or Early Long Pod, and for general crop the old Broad Windsor. Seville Long Pod and Leviathan are excellent for exhibition. Amongst the dwarf French Beans Canadian Wonder should have a place in every garden; it has proved itself as hardy and as-prolific as any, as well as producing pods of im- mense length., Negro Long Pod is another good all round dwarf Bean. Of the tall growing runner Beans we have grown Scarlet Champion and Painted Lady. Beetroot have been represented by Cattell's Blood Red, Nutting's Selected, and Dell's Crimson. Of Onions Blood Red is the best keeper, and James's Keeping comes next; as this quality is the Chief importance it is a matter of little moment which are sown for early use. Mr. Troughton, of Church-street, Preston, has a representa- tion of his "Lancashire Prize-taker" in his seed cata- logue, which has been most successful in taking prizes at various exhibitions in the district. Six of them have averaged 16-i ounces. Parsnips should include the Student and Hollow-Crowned. TEE FRONT OARDEN.—Any Spireas that may have been planted out here with the view of potting may be attended to now. They will have made a considerable amount of root, which may be reduced so as to.get them into a conveniently sized pot; or the clump may be di- vided, as they do not resent this somewhat severe treat- /tent. In potting, care should .be taken that the spaces round the roots are well filled with soil. To make sure, apply a heavy watering, and give the bottom of the pots a slight tap on the ground. They may then be either covered over with ashes, or, after the water has drained away, taken indoors and placed in any warm position. At all times they must be well supplied with water. Tug Wrwoow.—Deutzia gracilis is a hardy plant, easily propagated by dividing the roots. When introduced into heat or a warmer position than out of doors, it soon commences to grow, and for this reason it will make a valuable window plant to flower in April. We intend giving it a trial. Those not acquainted with the plant, but who have visited the spring show a the Preston and Fulwood Horticultural Society, will recollect some splendid examples of a shrubby plant smothered with innocent-looking white flowers; they were Deutzia gracilis.

A CorrikoE GARDEN IN EssEx.—A correspondent in the Gardening World gives a sketch of a cottage garden in that county Being an agricultural county, the cottager is, a course, a labourer, his working hours being from 5 o'clock a.m. to 5 30 p.m., and his average wage 15s. per week. No sooner is the day's work finished, and tea over, than he is busy in his garderi; and ' besides what is termed the 'home garden,' he has 20 rods of allotment, for which he pays 7s. 6. per year— the home garden being about half .the size of the allot- ment. Potatoes is the predominating crop, but various other vegetables receive their share of attention. But the flower garden is one of the chief objects of interest, being a strip on the left hand side leading to the front door, about 151 t. long and sft. broad, with a rustic edg- ing of large stones, inside of which is a row of red and white daisies while the border itself is planted with stocks, wallflowers, pansies, &c. In spring, a row of crocuses may be seen peeping through, inside the row of daisies, and later on a few tulips join in welcoming the coming of summer. During the summer it is gene- rally gay with annuals, candytuft, dwarf nasturtium, mignonette, dahlias, &c."

PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR. A sale of work was opened on Monday by Mr. Thomas Morris, in Legh-street Primitive Methodist Schoolroom. Warrington, which was continued on Tuesday, and was held in aid of the chapel and circuit funds. The roorn was tastefully decorated and the stalls were plentifully provi- ded with the usual miscellaneous articles. Amongst those present at the opening proceedings were the Revs J Calvert (pastor), and J 111cTurk, Mr Hall, Mr and Miss Horton, Mr Crampton, Mr and Mrs Throsall, Mrand Mrs Titchett, Mrs Venn, Mrs Bailey, dee. Mr Morris, in declaring the bazaar open, said that the pro- ceeds of that sale were to be devoted to the chapel and cir- cuit funds. Whoever, whatever, they were, whatever their business, professional calling, or religions convictions, they could not in this life very well get OA without money. There were some who would say that whilst it was impose eible to carry on business without either money or barter, It was possible to do without places of worship or preachers to preach in them. Same :nen high up in the scientific -world claimed that we could do without religion. It pleased them to use such arguments ; but let those argu- ments stimulate others to find stronger and better ones in favour of religious work. (Hear, hear.) He thought that without places of worship, and learned and pions men to preach and pray in them, England would indeed cut a sorry figure. He believed that many se-called unbelievers adopted that line of thought simply on the score of econo- my, thinking religion an expensive piece of machinery, which might always be r,qoiring their share of the needful lubricant to keep its various bearings in good working order. (Applause.) If there were such people they were suffering from a delusion. Who had ever heard a man say that he was the worse off for attending a place of worship Cr Sunday school if he went in sincerity, or who had heard anyone say that they were the poorer because they had en- dowed or built a place of worship ? So long as there were willing workers for such causes; so long should we have in our midst cur time-honoured places of worship and our devout men to conduct the services. Mr. Morris then refer- red to the voluntary work undertaken by those wise had provided articles for the sale, and in conclusion said that to show his appreciation he should give a prize to the maker of the greatest novelty' combined with neat workmanship. (Applause.).-.A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Merris, on the motion of the Rev. J. Calvert, seconded by the Rey. J. hlcTurk.—The sale was then proceeded with the varioul stal's being under the management of Mesdames Calvet t, Swale, Dodds, Williams, Hall. R Jones, Cotton, Biese;l, Wakefield, Silt, Podmore, Titchett, J P Jones, Throsall, and Littlewood ; Misses Jones, Calvert, Cramp. ton, Littlewood, and Morris ; Messrs Bissell (senior and junior), and Wakefield.

GENERAL GORDON ' (Reported killed at Khartoum, Jan. 26, 1885.)
SKETCH OF GENERAL GORDON'S LIFE
_ Our readers will see from the detail we give in another column of the fall of Khartoum, that an Arab arrived on Sunday at Korti, who states that General Gordon met his

death in a volley which was fired whilst he was making his way to the house of the Austrian Consul. There would seem therefore no room for hope that the gallant English- man survived the fall of the city he defended so long and so well. Below we give a sketch of his adventurous career. _ _

He deemed it the height of philosophy to think of it only as a release. "I, value my life as naught," he said, writing from Khartoum on May 4, 1877, "and should only leave much weariness for perfect peace." Upon retiring from the Governorship of the Soudan Gordon was, in May, 1880, appointed private secretary to the Marquis of Ripon, Governor-General of India, but resigned the post as soon as he landed at Bombay. Gor- don wrote— In a moment of weakness I took the ap- pointment of private secretary to Lord Ripon. No sooner had I landed in Bombay than I saw that, in my irresponsible position, I could not hope to do anything to the purpose, in the face of the vested interests out there. seeing this, and seeing, moreover, that my views were so diametrically opposed to those of the official classes, I resi.aned. Lord Ripon and I parted perfect friends." _A flying visit to China, intervening between. the abortive Indian appointment and his acceptance of the command of Royal Engineers at the Mauritius, pre- ceded Gordon's attainment of the military rank of Major. General.. He was then appointed to an important post at the Cape of Good. Hope, but relinquished it in conse- quence of a disagreement with the Colonial Ministry about Basutoland. _ _ .

Soon after his return to England from South Africa Gordon went to Palestine and lived outside Jerusalem fora year in retirement. Events in the Soudan mean- time developed, and Hicks Pasha's expedition after in- flicting a severe defeat on a section of the Mandi's troops was itself annihilated in another encounter. Gordon, as will be remembered, had accepted service under tbe King of the Belgians, and was just preparing to start for the Congo when he was recalled by telegram from Brussels, and on Jan. 18th, 1884, he left London for the Soudan. "General Gordon went," said the Premier, "not for the purpose of reconquering the Soudan, or to persuade the chiefs of the Soudan—the Sultans at the head of their ' troops—to submit themselves to the Egyptian Govern- ment. He went for no such purpose as that. He went for the double purpose of evacuating the country, by extricating the Egyptian garrisons, and reconstituting it, by giving back to these Sultans their ancestral powers, withdrawn or suspended during the period of Egyptian occupation. General Gordon has in view the with- drawal from the country of no less than 29,000 persons under military service in Egypt, and the House will see how vast was the trust which was placed in the hands of this remarkable person. We cannet exaggerate the importance we attach to his inission. We are unwilling —I may say we were resolved to do nothing which should interfere with the pacific scheme, a scheme, be it remembered, absolutely the only scheme, which pro- mised a satisfactory solution of the Soudanese difficulty by at once extricating the garrisons and reconstituting the country upon its old basis of local privileges." Gordon reached Cairo on Jan. 26th last year; entered Berber on Feb. 9th, and, after spending several days there, was at Khartoum on Feb. 18th. On Feb. 28th he telegraphed, "If Egypt is to be quiet, the Mandi must be smashed up." This view was repeated on subsequent occasions. The Gordon relief expedition was finally sanctioned on August 22nd, but early in May the pur- chase of 12,000 camels had been ordered. Lord Weise- ley arrived at Cairo on Sept. 10th. Gordon's deep and constant thoughts on religious sub- sects are again and again expressed in his letters, and also in the little book, Reflections in Palestine," nominally written by Gordon himself, but really compiled from his notes by friends. His mind was often engaged with speculations upon the future state, and for him certainly death had no terrors. On Sept. 11th, 1877, when on his anti-slavery expedition near Khartoum, he wrote, "God knows what my anxiety was. Not for my life' for I died years ago in this world, and to all its comforts, honours, and glories." Writing to some friends he said, " God has given you ties and anchors to the earth; you have wives and families. I, thank God, have none, and am free. • . . You are only called on at intervals to rely on your God; lam obliged continually to do so. I mean by this that you have only great trials, such as the ill- ness of a child, when you feel yourself utterly weak now and then. lam constantly in anxiety." Bored with the complaints of the Soudanese, he wrote, "I must not complain if they have no thought of what I have gone through. There is only one issue of it, and that is death, and I often feel I wish ft would come and relieve me." In every reference to death it was with him the great "release." Gordon once said that "inaction was terrible," and he wrote, "The future world must be much more amusing, more enticing, more to be desired than this world—put- ting aside its absence of sorrow and pain. The future world has been somehow painted to our mind as a place of continuous praise, and though we may not say it, yet one cannot help feeling that thus it would prove monotonous. It cannot be thus. It must be a life of activity, for happiness is dependent on activity; death is cessation of movement; life is all movement." On the road from Suakim to Berber in January, 1878, Gordon wrote:—" You ask me what my ideas are of a future life. I think that this life is only one of a series of lives which our incarnated part has lived. I have little doubt of our having pre-existed, and that also in the tinte of our pre-existence we were actively employed. So, therefore, I believe in our active employment in a future life, and like the thought. We shall, I think, be far more perfect in a future life, and indeed go on towards perfection, but never attain to it." When in December, 1877, Gordon sus in the camp of Waled el Michael—" in the „lion's den"—and absolutely at the mercy of this brigand chief, he wrote :—" I do try and think and try to put in practice that God is the Supreme' Power in the world, and that He is Almighty; and though "use-your-judgment" people may say, You tempt God in putting yourself in positions like the pre- sent," yet Ido not care. Ido it because I wish to trust in His promises, and, however trying it may be, I gain strength and faith by it. If He wills mote fail, so be it." In complete accordance with these views is the follow- ing statement as to the burden of Gordon's prayer writ- ten at Lardo (far away to the south of Khartoum), June 25, 1875:—" I ask God for the following things: (1) Not to be disturbed if the Khedive sent me away to-morey ; ' (2) • Not to be disturbed if he keeps me; (3) Not to have anything of the world come between Him and me, and I not to fear death or feel regret if it came before I com- pleted what I think my programme." At a subsequent meeting he remarks:—" I like the Muissulman ; he is not ashamed of his God; his life is a fairly pure one. Cer- tainly, he gives himself a good margin in the wife-line, ' but at any rate he never poaches on others. Can our f Christian people say the same?'

"Well, to tell the truth, papa, I did not think much Of the close of the sermon," said a fashionable young lady. "probably you were thinking more of the clothes of the congregation," replied her father. When a young man lays siege to a young lady, and insists upon her consenting to become his wife, she can- not but confess that he is a man after her own heart," however heartless she may appear. snocrruso AN Eresins DnivEß.—At Leigh on Monday, a publican named Jones was committed for trial charged with anlawfully wounding Robert Gorton, an engine driver on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. The prisoner went out shooting near Atherton, and for some reason or other fired his gun at the prosecutor's engine, which was just starting. Gorton received several pel- lets in his face, and one entered his .left ear, causing partial deafness. It was Stated in Jones' behalf that the driver held up a can, and, that he then, very imprudently but without any intention of causing harm, fired at the impromptu target.
