div.head: 801JD.A.N CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE 801JD.A.N CAMPAIGN.
DETAIL'S OF GORDON'S DEATH AND THE BE. TR AYAL OF KEIAETOUSI.-THE SITUATION AT META MMELL .

IfEAD QUARTER'S, Komi, SUNDAY.—The Arab who made his way across the desert from Khartoum to Debbeis hap just arrived here. He says that he was a cavil's em- ployed in the town, and that he saw General Gordon killed. He gives the following account of the events at Khartoum :—At early morning aan the 27th of January, Faraz Pasha treacherously opened the gate in the southern wall. The bulk of the Mandi's fighting men were close at hand. These at once rushed into the town* General Gor- don, hearing the confusion in the town, went out armed with a sword ked axe. He was accompanied by Ibrahim Bey, the chief clerk, and twenty men. He went towards the house of the Austrian Consul. On his way he met a party of the Mandi's men, who fired a volley. General Gordon was shot dead. The Arabs then rushed on with their spears and killed the chief clerk and nine of the men; the rest escaped. The Consul Nicola is alive, and a pri- mer. All the redo( the Europeans were killed, also most of the notables The rest of the inhabitants fraternised wits the Mandi's men. With the exception of firing upon General Gordon's party, there was no fighting whatever. No women or children were killed, and all who surrendered and gave op their valuables were allowed to go away with- out harm. The Mandi is reported to have hanged the traitor Farag. His troops were, when the men left Khartoum, still too much occupied by the plunder of the town to think of moving forward against -Gubat. Indeed, a great many of the Mandi's best troops were killed at Metamtneh. The people employed in the arsenal, for the most part Greeks, were killed by the Mandi's men. The only person besides Consul Nicola spared and kept as prisoner was the doctor. All the rest were kept prisoners for three days and then allowed to go free. The Mandi did not enter the town until three days after its capture, and then only remained there for a short time. Farag Pasha was a black slave. He was given his freedom and advanced by General Gordon, who trusted him impli- citly. The Matadi has with him at Khartoum 4,000 gsod fighting men but these have been mach scared by the disaster which betel their comrades who went to Metammeh, and by the reports of the terrible destructios dealt by the white soldiers there and at Abu Klea. A messenger who has arrived from Gubat to•day reports that General Buller has arrived here, and has assumed the command. All the wounded have left Gubat, and should before this time have reached Galrdul. A large body of the enemy from Berber marched on to assist those at Metammeh, but were recalled by the Emir of Berber upon the latter hearing of the boat column coming up the Nile towards Berber. Some deserters from Khartoum who have arrived at Gubat assert that the Mandi will shortly advance against us there. Others deny this. Some of the enemy have been leaving Metammeh, and we hope to hear of the capture of that place by General Buller in a few days. A sheikh of the Kabbabish tribe re- ports that men who have arrived from Khartoum say that there is muck sickness and disaffection among the Mandi's troops, and that many are leaving him and making off to their homes, and that many more are only anxious for peace and English protection. The Mandi has cent out a procla- mation demanding fresh levies from the tribes, saying that the English are but few, but have much wealth with them, and that the gates of Paradise are now open to all true be- lievers. There is very little response to the proclamation, as the tribes object to conscription,and are heartily sick of the war, and most anxious for peace and quiet again. Chief Paymaster Olivey has arrived here. General Dormer is expected to-morrow or next day.—&tanclard. A correspondent of the Daily News writes :—" The way in which Press messages from the seat of war have been ' edited' by the authorities on the spot tends possibly to the fact, widely rumoured in well-informed quarters at the pre- sent moment, that the whole text of General Gordon's last message was not officially made public in England. The message as published was : ' Khartoum all right. Can hold on for years.' It is now said that these words were preceded by ' What are you coming for ? I have not asked for you: "

div.head: ADVANCE ON THE NILE.
div.p: THE ADVANCE ON THE NILE.

OPPOSITE DIILEA ISLAND (VIA MERAWI), SATURDAY.— Corporal Harrison and Privates Newham and Riley died of their wounds yesterday. The Staffords and Cornwalls are DOW three miles ahead. They will proceed farther to-day. The Gordon Highlanders arrived yesterday. They have lost three boats since leaving Hamdab. They proceed to- day. The Royal Highlanders and the transport leave to- morrow. Colonel Butler found the Sbukook Pass clear Yesterday. Only one battalion a day has been able to get up this cataract. The Gordon Highlanders were fired upon on the 10th from the right bank. The wounded were car- ried forward in boats comfortably, stretchers being placed athwartships, just fitting between the gunwales and the stern sheets. The enemy state that their numbers in the last action were 2,000. Many ran away on our appearing in the rear. Among them it is said was Suleiman Amr. A good many got across the river. ON THE RED SSA.

Stream, SATIIIIDAY.—Spies report a considerable concen• tratien at Tamai of tribes from the south. Stramm, SUIsiIAY.—A new sand-bag battery has been thrown up to cover the extension of the railway, which has now been carried forward into the plain towards flassem, to a point 1,300 yards beyond the camp. This will protect the Working parties from any sudden attack by the enemy. The redoubt was only begun at daybreak, and was finished before nightfall. It has been garrisoned by a detachment of Marines. Native spies report that there is great activity In Osman Digma's camp. A number of his followers are employed in digging trenches, throwing up breastworks, ex- cavating rifle pits, and forming shelters along the sides of the nullahs. Even the women are being armed and drilled, and every possible preparation is being made for an obstinate resistance to our advance. The news of the capture of Khartoum has been received at Osman Digma's camp, and raised the enthusiasm of his followers to the highest point. RAILWAY FROM SUAKIM TO BERBER,

The Government having approved the contract with Messrs Lucas and Aird for the construction of a railway from Solara in the direction of Berber, as stated on Mon- day, no time is being lost in making the necessary prepara- tions, the contractors being instructed to carry out the work with the least possible delay. The Admiralty have been instructed to find tonnage for the conveyance of all the stock, locomotives, gear, rails, and sleepers, besides the staff of men, and Mr. Banghan, of the Transport Depart- ment of the Admiralty, has been bully engaged In hiring transports for that service. The Turin has been engaged, and will be despatched from the East India Docks with plant. his believed that a large number of native la- bourers can be engaged at Suakim for the rougher and un- skilled work. The route having been already surveyed the actual construction of the line can be commenced without delay. The gauge is to be 4 feet 8,4 inches, the rails being good flat-bottomed iron, laid upon wooden sleepers, and this is thought to indicate that the railway is intended to be of a permanent character, although the primary object of its construction is to bring stores from the base of General Graham's operations at Suakica to the nearest convenient spot at which his troops may be. The work is to be done in sections, as thee. Government may direct. Carriages are likewise to be provided, and several small alx•wheel locomo- tives of an improved pattern. On Monday, the Admiralty hiebd the transport Zuric for the cenveyance of some of the plant fof the Bnakim-Berber railway from the East India Docks this week. Admiralty officials are also negotiating for another ship that will load a similar freight at Hull. Over a thousand applications were made at Messrs. Lucas and Aird's on Wednesday morning for employment in con- structing the new Bnakim•Berber railway. None of the applications, however, were successful, as the firm have decided to send out only a hundred of their, own employes at present, and to supplement them by engaging natives accustomed to work in the climate. The line will be completed in about 12 months, and steel rails will be used.
GENERAL EARLE (gala at the Battle of Irerbekan, Feb. 10.
MEMORIAL TO GENERAL ia-LE.

Last week we gave a brief sketch of the career of General Earle, whose family was formerly connected with Warring- ton. We are glad to see that a movement is on foot amongst foreigners to honour his memory. A telegram from Egypt, dated Mr.ndav, says r—A committee, consisting of Greeks, French, and other nationalities except England, has been formed, and is collecting subscriptions to raise a memorial to General Earle in Alexandria. THE INDIAN AND COLONIAL CONTINGENTS. CAIRO, SUNDAY—The 9th Bengal Lancers, the 15th Sikhs, the 17th Bengal Infantry, and a Bombay Native In- fantry Regiment will arrive at Suakim about March 51b, and the British Regiments some three days later. The 2nd Battalion Royal Dublin Fusiliers will leave Gibraltar for Alexandria on the 26th inst. Lord Wolseley having ex- pressed a wish that Hassan Pasha, brother of the Khedive. should be appointed to the command of a troop in connec- tion with the Soudan campaign, negotiations on the subject have been proceeding between the Khedive, Sir Evelyn Baring, and Hassan Pasha. The latter first made his accep- .t ince ef the appointment conditional upon 4,000 Turks being recruited, but it is believed that he will finally accept the command of the Egypt,on troops, under the title of Goveraor-General of the Soudan. This measure is expected to have a great moral effect on the Soudan population, as showing that England is not desirous of the conquest of the country for herself.—LArEß —Haesan Pestle bas accepted the command of a troop of Egyption cavalry in the Soudan I expedition. r SYDNEY, MONDAY.—Ex:raordinary enthusiasm has been ! excited here by the news that the British Government has accepted the oiler of troops from New South Wales for ser- vice in the Soudan. A Patriotic Fend has been established,l to which liberal donations are kleinK contributed. The em- barkation of troops is fixed for March 3rd. CAIRO, MONDAY —The contingent from New South Wales for servic.: in the &tidal], consisting of a battrliun of infan- try 500 stro .g and a battery of artillery, is expected to ar- rive here about March 18 h.

Orrawa, MONDAY.—Col.Williams has received a telegram from Lord Wolseley, staing that he will be glad to see a Canadian contingent in Egypt. Sir Arthur Blythe, Agent General for South Australi -has received the following telegram from the Government at Adelaide, dated yester- day :—"Please intimate to Imperial Government that South Australia offers at her own expense to supply 250 infantry, with officers, for service in the Soudan." The Agent General for Victo Ia ha i received from the Hon. James Service, Premier of the Colony, the following tele- graphic despatch :—" If England values assistance of colo- nies in Egyptian campaign, assure Imperial aovernment that Victoria is ready to do her part as integral portion of the empire." Lord Lorne has written to the Times bicking the request of Col.-Williams, a member of the Canadian Parliament and commander ef a Canadian militia regiment, that the services of a Canadian corps be accepted by Her Majesty's Government at the present crisis.

The following telegram has been received by the Agent- General for New South Wa;es from the acting Colonial Secretary, dated Sydney, February 17 :—" Munificent con- tributions from colonists in favour of patriotic fund daily being made. Numbers of wealthy colonists off:r £l,OOO a year while the colonial contingent is engaged. Contingent leaves March 3rd. consisting of 212 artillerymen,2oo horses, and 522 infantry." The clony of Victoria has intimated its readiness to send 600 or 700 men, consisting of ntral brigade and mounted 'infantry, fully equipped, to the Soudan.

div.head: REIN'FORCEMENTS FROM ENGLAND.
div.p: THE REIN'FORCEMENTS FROM ENGLAND.

The Duke of Cambridge inspected on Saturday the troops at Aldershot who are under orderers to depart for the Soudan within the nest few days. At the conclusion of the manoeuvres, the Duke said he had come down to see them on the eve of their proceeding to the far East, and he was glad to say that he had found them very efficient, both as to men and hersto.

I - A council of Ministers sat at the War Officio until late on Saturday afternoon. Lord Kimberley joined Lord Darting- ton, Lord Northbrook, and Mr. Childers shortly after noon. It was decided to accept the offer of military assistance made by the colony of New South Wake. The steamship Orient will convey the contingent to Suakim. The transport Queen on Monday left tke Royal Albe,t Docks for Suakin', with the balloon and telegraph corns and field detachments of the Royal Engineers. Three bal- loons are taken. Compressed hydrogen for lading is car- ried-in strong iron cylinders. Captive accents only will be made, the balloons being tethered by rope or wire. Tele- phonic communication between the groundland the car will be established, the object being to discover the enemy's position and movements. The hired transport Cameo left Woolwich on Monday with nearly 1,000 tons of commissariat stores and camp equipment. The Admiralty have issued orders that a large number of steam launches and cutters are to be got ready immediately, and sent without delay to Suakim. They are to be employed in Landing troops and stores on their arrival at places where the water is shallow.

According to a detailed statement of the transport ar- rangement received at Portsmouth, the total number to he embarked in respect of the new expedition is 338 officers, 56 warrant officers, 11,604 men, and 723 horses, with 18 wag- gons and 4 guns. But a proportion of these will not go beyond the Mediterranean. Attempts are being made to recover a portion of the vain. able cargo of the British India steamer Et Dorado, wrecked on the Birlings, off Lisbon. She had on board, in addition to 600 tons of war stores for Egypt, £BO,OOO in gold and a large quantity of military clothing. The services of the 4th Battalion Prince of Wales's Own Yorkshire Regiment have been placed at the disposal of the Government for service at home or abroad. Orders re- ceived at Chathatn announce that volunteers from the First Class Army Reserve will be ttken from the following regi- ments :—Cheshire, South Yorkshire, Dorsetsbire, South Staffordshire, Cameron Highlanders, Dublin Fusiliers, and Yorkshire.

On Monday night, the Newcastle and Jarrow wings of the Ist Newcastle and Durham Engineer Volunteers were par- aded, and those who were willing to go upon active service in the Soudan were asked to step forward. At Newcastle 92 men responded, and at Jarrow 37. The same corps sent a number of men to General Graham in his last campaign. The Duke of Cambridge held a levee on Wednesday after- noon, at the Horse Guards. General Sir Gerald Graham and nearly all the officers who have received staff appoint- ments in the Suakim expedition at'ended. Forty-fiveofficers and 751 men of various corps, medical and fighting, sailed from Southampton on Wednesday in the Union steamship Arab, en route for Suakin]. The corps were heartily cheered. Colonel H. Brackenbury, who took command after the death of General Earle at Dulka, has been raised to the posi- tion of Brigadier-General. The Government have, it is understood, prepared a reso- lution proposing a further vote on account of military ex- penditure in Egypt, amounting, it is rumoured, to about £2,000,000, which., it is believed, will be submitted for the approval of the House of Commons. Mr. Chamberlain, through his secretary, has sent the fol- lowing acknowledgment of resolutions passed at a meeting of the Friends of Peace, and forwarded to bine by the Rev. Arthur O'Neill, Birmingham —"I: am directed by Mr. Chamberlain to acknowledge the receipt of resolutions under date of February 13, Mr. Chamberlain agrees with you in deploring the war in the Soudan, but he fears that the policy of running away from the fanatical leader who now OCCI:t. pies Khartoum would not further the cause of peace or pre- vent the effusion of blood." Sir Henry Gordon Is said to have come to the resolution, if the tidings of his btother's death should be unfortunately confirmed, to prepare for immediate publication the letters and other scattered writings of the hero of Khartoum, a considerable number of which are in Ms hands. It is the more desirable that publicity should be given to this di— position because the flood of cheap "lives of our modern Bayard has already set in." The Coldstream and Scots Guards, under orders for Sna- kim, were inspected on Wednesday at Wellington Barracks by the Duke of Cambridge, in the presence of the Princess of Wales and her daughters, the Marquis of Hartington, Sir B. Northcote, and a large namber of distinguished visitors. His Royal Highness after the inspection a,!cli essed the men, urging them to do everythin in their power to preqeme the honour of the British arms. He dewed them above all things to take care of their discipline. Daring the day there were further departures of troops from Aldershot en route to the Soudan. The Queen will inspect the Grena- dier Guards at Windsor Castle, prior to their departure for Egypt. The embarkation of some portions of the force be- gan on Wednesday at London and Portsmouth. ITALY AND THE RED SEA.

ROME, SATllRDAY.—Despaches received here from Sualthn state that the military situation at Massowah continues to improve. Before the arrival of the Italian troops bands of marauders infested the surrounding country, asserting that they bad been sent by the Mandi. Colonel Saletta has orders to rid the country of these bands, and to establish order and confidence everywhere. A third expedition of

1,4n0 men will leave for the Red Sea next week, probably tke 10th. It is said that a General will be despatched to Massowah. l'oar SAID, TIIESDAY.—The transports conveying the troops forming the second Italian expedition to the Red Sea, which left Naples Hat Thursday, arrived here to- day. FIGHTING NEAR GUBAT.—ATTACK ON A CONVOY. The War Office has issued the following telegram from Lord Wolseley, which was despatched from Kerti at mid- night on Tuesday All remaining sick and wounded, 75 of all ranks, left Gubat early morning of 13th insr, and reached Abu Klett safely. When some eight or nine miles distant from Gubat halted for breakfast, and when about to resume march had a long skirmish with a convoy of men, guns, and ammuni- tion on the way from Khartoum to Metererneh. The skir- mish lasted about one hour and a half, WilEl) the enemy re- treated. The Light Camel Regiment, on its way from Abu Klee to Gubat, arrived towards close of skit flush. Colonel Talbot commanded our convoy, and speaks in high terms of 4he men's conduct, and especially reports upon the excellent work done by Surgeon Major Conolly. Ail the sick and 1 . wounded doing well, and have not suffered from journey. He gives a fair account of Sir IL Steweree condition, his wound doing well, but be is suffering somewhat from fever. . Convoy should be at Galidul to-morrow. List 0 casualties: —K.lled, one private ; wounded dangerously, one non- cernmissioned officer ; wounded, four men The Morning Post says ;--:-Nouran Ja, who is at present commanding the rebels who now occupy Aletirnmeh, has, it is reported, applied to the lelandi fur fturher reinforce- ments to enable him to hold the place acd light our troops. He is also stated to bare urgently asked the Alabdi to send him ammunition, saying that he could not in he any fight with the English while his men were. arupd only with swords and spears. The Mandi is reported to have sent the following reply :—"Do not fight at present. God willing. I will come soon and eat up the infidels.' RETREAT .OF THE ENGLISH FROM GUBAT. KORTI, WEDNESDAY, 11-40 P. 31 -'r Redvers Buller hse juat successfully executed a difficult inilitary operation. lets the fail of Khartoum had dsstroyed what hid been (be main ohject of sending forward the dreert column in ad- vance, its remaining at Matamn”h hod become in fact use- less. He, therefore, after carefully consid...ring the whole situation, catne to the conclusion that it waa best to remain no longer exposed to the risk of b-ing surrotmdtd by the troops of the Mehdi. Sir &doers then started from Gubat en the morning of the 14th inst. with the ewire fo:ce. Lord Charles Beresford before starting took cite to render the steamers useless. The men tuarcle.d on foot, and the camels were employed in carrying water arid seepriea. The whole force reached Abu Klea without having encountered any opposition whatever. They arrived at that place on the 15 h ißst ,the rapidity with which the movement hid been executed having completely taken the enemy by surprise. It was reported that the Mandi had left Khartoum and was marching on Metammeb, haying with him a very large force, as well as gune.-11forhing Post. The following communication has been sent from the War Office :

I Lord Vi'otselay reports from Korti flirt a despatch has I been received from Major-General Buller that he evacuated I Gubat on the morning of the 14th inst., and reached Alm r Klee, the next day without any attempt by the enemy to interfere with his movements, and that be now awlits in- structions at Abu Klea. Major-Geuetal Bohr also teportr that the health and spirits of his men are excellent, and the sick and wounded are doing well. But t..or 'lseley regrets to add that Sir Herbert Stewart's case was less hopeful, as his fever has increased. The Daily Teegraph war correspondent says :—I learn that the Mandi left Khartoum with 40,000 to 60,000 men and inat..y guns for Metemmeh, travelling in great state. He detached several thousand men, with four cannon and one Krupp, who arrived within seven miles of Abu Kru. On the morning we left, the Mandi and his army were 20 miles off. The Daily News says that the expected attack on Me- tammeir was merely a ruse to deceive the enemy into in- activity while General Buller commenced the withdrawal of his forces from Gubat.thtit pmition having become worse than useless after the fall of Khartoum. The manoeuvre has been executed with great skill and dexterity. INDISPOSITION OF GENERA.L. FREEMANTLE. CAIRO, Tnnusaay.-7-Major-General Davis will leave for Suakirn tomorrow in order to relieve Brigadier-General Freemantle, who is slightly indisposed. GORDON'S BLACK TROOPS AND HIS PAPERS. CAIRO, THllRSDAY.—lntelligence received here states that after the fail of Khartoum the black troops, who had served under General Gordon, piled their arms and joined the Mandi.

A Daily Chronicle telegram says the Mandi when Khar- toum fell secured the whole of General Gordon's papers, together with a large number of bank notes issued by the gallant defender of Khartoum. These, we are informed, he is now taking steps to negotiate and obtain much-needed ready cash by discounting them. As General Gordon pledged England's word to redeem them it will require some ingenuity to defeat the Mabdi's objects. THE ADVANCE OF GENERAL BR ACKENBIJRY. Lord Wolseley sent the following despatch from Korti on Thursday afternoon:— Messages have been received from General Bracken- bury, dated MAI Island, 15th inst. His cavalry entered 1 Salamat and found it deserted. The leading infantry are I within five miles of Salamat. The horses and camels are I safely through the Shukook Pass, which had been prepared 1 for defence, but was abandoned by the enemy. Brackenbury hopes to be at Abu Ahmed by the 15th inst., but doubts if he can concentrate there before the 29th, owing to the , nceseity of crossing the mounted troops over to the other 1 r side of the river. He adds that any estimate of time must be very uncertain, owing to the difficulties of the river. DEPARTURE OF THE COLDS EttEAM GUARDS. The Ist battalion of the Coldstream Guards, 800 strong, left London on Thursday for Suakim to take part in the forthcoming operations in the Soudan. There was a great display of popular enthusiasm between the Wellington Barracks, where the battalion paraded, and Westminster Pier, where the men were taken on board river steamers for con- veyance to the transport Manora. The men of the 20th Hussars ordered on service left Aldershot on Thursday, and proceeded to Portsmouth, embarking there on board the transport Italy. From Portsmouth also sailed the steamer 1 Queen, with the telegraph and balloon detachments of the ' Royal Engineers and the Commissariat and Transport Corps. Large quantities of stores, cJothing, and ammuni- tion were shipped from Sheerness and Gravesend by the transports Tyne and Duke of Devonshire. On Thursday afternoon the Queen reviewed at Windsor the 3rd battalion of the Grenadier Guards, who will leave on Sunday for Suakim. In an address to the troops, read by Colonel Home, Her Majesty expressed an earnest hope for their success in the coming struggle, and asked the Divine pro- tection for them in time of danger. The Queen was as- sured that the Grenadiers would equal the glorious deeds of those who had lately fought in the distant land to which they were proceeding. Her Majesty's message was received with ringing cheers.

MR. TROM4SSON, M.P., ON DIRECT TAXATION.—OR MOE. day night Mr. J. P. Thomasson, M.P., delivered an address to the voters in Church Ward, Bolton. He said he was very much atruck with a remark made the other night by Mr. Arnold, M.P.. for Salford, to the effect that nobody up to now had paid anything towards the expenses of the Sou- -1 dan expedition except those who paid income tax. If a nation bad to pay some £10,000,000 or £20,000,000 for war, and a share of that were put upon the house tax, the oc- cupier would then know exactly what share he had in the payment of the tax, and he would be very careful not to support any war unless he felt that that was absolutely necer.sary for the safety of part of her Majesty's dominion. Such a tax would also facilitate registration and voting, for if a receipt card were given to the voter and this were presented to the returning officer at the polling booth, it would do away with tbe necessity of revision courts.

last week 'furnished a sketch of the life of General EARLE, who was killed whilst gal- lantly leading his troops at the battle of Kerbekan. The news to hand this week Places it beyond doubt that General GoaDoN was killed in a volley which was fired as soon as the rebels had, by treachery, got within the walla of Khartoum. He anticipated such an end, well knowing that some of the men about him might at any moment prove unfaithful. He could have preserved his own life by leaving Khartoum with the soo men that he sent in his steamers to meet the British, but he scorned to think of saving himself and leaving others in danger. He had lived the life of a hero, and he died at what he be- lieved to be the post of duty—heroic to the last. The ttoops of the MADHI are still in possession of Kbartaum ; and it is reported that the False Prophet is marching at the head of his elated followers to the .relief of Metemmeh. Sir REDVERS BULLER, acting on instructions from General WOLSELEY, has retired from Gulrat on the Nile to the safer position at Abu Klea, and for a time at any rate it would seem that our soldiers will have as much as they can do to hold their own. It is hardly likely, however, that they will be attacked at Abu Klea, for the Soudanese are still suffering from the terrible beating they got there a few weeks ago. Yesterday, we regret to add, news was received of the death of General STEWART, who was woun- ded at Abu Klea on January 19th. It is sad to think that already three of our bravest and most skilful commanders have lost their lives in this unhappy strife in the Soudan. "Thus bad begins," and we fear we must " but worse remains behind."

THE SUNDAY LIQUOR TRAFFIC.—The annual conference of the Central Association for Preventing the Sale of In- toxicating Liquors on Sunday was held on Monday after- noon in the Mayor'e Parlour at Manchester. There was a very large attendance ; amongst others, the Mayor of Man- chester, who presided, the Rev. Canon Davenport Kelly, Mr. E. Whitwell (Kendal), Colonel Shaw (United States Consul in Manchester), and delegates from various parts of the country. The report was read by the secretary (Mr. W. H. Perkins).—Mr. T. Linton (Public Prosecutor of Edinburgh) read a paper on the results of Sunday closing in that city. He was satisfied that the closing of public-houses on Sunday had not only been approved of by the citizens generally, but that there were few, if any, publicans who desired a change. The result was also satisfactory in Glasgow ; in fact, the results of Sunday clesing throughout Scotland were, with very few exceptions, recognised and appreciated by magistrates, police officials, and the general community. (Applause.)— Various officers were thanked and the com- mittee and officers elected.—ln the evening a public meet- ing was held, at which Mr. Houldsworth, M.P., moved a resolution pledging the meeting to support the bill for stop- ping the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday throughout England, TRADES UNION ADDRESS.—The Trades Union Congress Parliamentary Committee, of which Mr. J. S. Murchie is chairman, and Mr Broadhurst, M.P., secretary, have issued an address to the officers of trades societies and trades councils. The committee review the work that has been done by trades unions since 1.887, and print a list of over 20 measures that had been introduced and passed between the years 1871 and 1884 at the instance of the Trades Union Congress, or amended by the influence of the Con- gress. They point out that from 1871 to 1884 the total income to Congress was £9,010 Os 8101. With this com- paratively small BUM much has been accomplished. For instance down to December, 1883, the total compensation obtained' in the law courts under the Employers' Liability Act was £23,224, and the committee 'have no doubt that the Bums obtained by mutual settlement amount to £20,000 more. With regard to the future, the committee urge that the number of workmen in Parliament must be increased, that greater numbers must be placed upon municipal and other bodies of local governing authoritits, that representa- tive workmen should be placed upon the magisterial bench, unless stipendiary magistrates are substituted for justices, and they hcpe the electorate "will insist that all wealth I which truly belongs to the nation shall be used for national purposes, and that natural sources of wealth and accommo- dation shall no longer be so used that fields are lying fallow while men are idle and starving." WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS: WIDNES BRANCH.— The annual meeting was held in Victoria-road VVeslevan Chapel lon Monday evening. Mr. S. Robinson presided, and there was a good attendance. The Rev. R. Harper read the annual report, which stated that during the year ending Conference 1884 the Widnes circuit contributed £22 3s tid towards the expenses of the parent Society. He made an appeal for increased assistance in the good work.—The Rev. 1 Mr. Binns, of Southport, the deputation, delivered a short address, in which he remarked that whilst paying so much I attention to the heathen abroad they had neglected the heathen at home, but through the efforts of the Home Mis- sionary Society much spiritual consolation had been given ' on English ground, and at the present time there were mariv I Godly men in bothqbe army and navy, amongst the mern• lbare of which forces the missionaries laboured with un- abated zeal. He advocated the erection of missien rooms in every town even if they were in close proximity to chapels or churches, because, he argued, the lower orders of society would enter a mission room when they would not enter a place of worship. He wave credit to the Church of England for the exertions they had made during recent years in the cause of Christianity, and observed that he was ready to welcome labourers for the spread of religions tra'h no matter in what section of the community they were connected.— Mr. John Glover also made a humourous speech.—On the motion of the Rey, .1. Hattlioreall, secon- ded by Mr. T. S. Swale, the usual votes of thanks were ac- corded.

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART LIBRARY.—To this library Mr J fl Bolton has recently presented a number of wOrks on free trade and fair trade, and the fiscal pcllcy of the nation generally. Rev CANON .BLECLA.Y.—Our readers will be glad to learn that the Bev Canon Barclay, vicar of Runcorn, is now con- valescent. Be is not yet, however, able to resume his parochial duties. SuNDAY SCIIOaL IA PARTY AT WIDNEI3.—AbOut 300 of the senior scholars of Ltceratreet Wesleyan Sunday school were entertained to tea on Tuesday evening, ond afterwards amused themselves by a variety of games Havrow• :Armes. IMPROVEMENT boom-ma—At the weekly meeting of this society, held on Monday night, Mr F J Norman, of Runcorn, read a paper on "international Arbitration." faitaisrsJ Hancock, 8 Barrow, and R Hughes joined in the discussion which followed. Rev S Alters occu- pied the chair. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.--Etbel May, the infant daughter of John William Tudor Lucas, of Percaval'e-lane, Runcorn was found lying dead in bed besides its mother on Wednesday morning. The child was in the beat of health on the previous evening, but its dead body-bore all Los out- ward marks of having died in convulsion. The Coroner Was warned bat thought an inquest was not necessary. LEcor.mg ON COAL AT lietreems.—Un Thursday evening a tea meeting was held in the Baptist Chapel, Wiriness, in aid of the chapel funds. Subsequeutly Mr E Carey delivered a lecture on coal to a good audience, the Rev kt Yeatman presiding. The lecture, which was illustrated with diagrams. and the performance of several ch meal experiments, was listened to with great Interest, and at the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr Carey, on the motion of Mr It Yeatmae, seconded by Mr Pass,y. THE PROPOSED NEW BOARD SCHOOL AT RUNCORN.— Ala special meeting of the Runcorn School Board on Wed- nesday, Mr. J. Pritchard presiding, the members discussed the desirability of appointing a clerk of works during the building of the proposed new school in G reen way-road. It was stated that the person appointed would have to devote the whole of his time, and although &slows of appointing a local builder, there was not one in the town who could fulfil this condition, and Mr. Brimelow, of Liverpool, was appointed to the position at a salary of £2 10s per week. It is estimatel that the appointment will absorb £B5 of the £lOO provided in the loan for this situation. "BACHELORS' TEA PARTY" LT WIDNES.—At the Primi- tive Methodist School Chapel, Simm'a Cross, Widnes, on Tuesday evening, a tea party of a rather novel description took place, and no less than 200 persons were present. Al. though entitled a bachelors' tea party me.nbers of the" fair sex" were admitted, but the duties usually perfur used by them were on this occasion performed by the " lords of creation." Dressed in suits of black, and adorned with white tie and " mob caps," the bachelors prepared the tea and I waited at the tables, the whole affair exciting the heartiest merriment. Sabsequently an entertainment was given under the presidency of Mr. D, Weight, music, yecal and instrumental, recitations, and hOmourous speeches appro- priate to the Oecasioreforming the programme. It is need- less to state that the preeeedinge throughout were highly enjoyed. 'fug CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—. FORMATION OF A BRANCH AT RUNCORN.—In the schools room attached to Holy Trinity Church, on Thursday even- ing, a meeting was held for the purpose of forming a branch I of the C.E.T.S. in connection with Holy Trinity Parish.l The attendance was very limited, only about 30 persons be- , ing present, including several lediee, het there was ea &ode dent determination to go forward with earnestness and energy. The Rev W Preston, MA, presided, and in a brief opening address advised those present not to despise the day , of small things. Ile stated that this effort was now being made in Trinity parish chiefly at the instigation of his goed ' friend, Mr Cunningham, not with any selfish motive, but simply iu order that they might "rescue the perishing."— Mr T Miller, organising secretary of the Cheshire C.E.T.S., then delivered an address upon the temperance question, in which he referred to the origin of teetotalism and the C El S., speaking words of encouragement and hope to those present. CONCERT AT HALTON.—In aid of the choir of Halton Parish Church, a concert was given in the Girls' Scheol- room on Tuesday evening, the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar, presiding. There Was ft large and appreciative audience. A long and attractive programme had epee nrovicl d, the I choir contributing several part songs. Miss Wright gave a pleasing rendering of the songs " Home" and t• Daddy," and she was loudly applauded, whilst Miss Clarke for her capital interpretation of " Cartier John " was recalled. She was also very successful in the song "Let rue dream again." " Exiles dream " and "A summer shower" were placed opposite to the name of Miss Poole, who, in the letter song, elicited the applause of the audience by her capital vocalisation, and had to repeat the list verse in res- ponse to a recall. Mies Tudor fewoured the audience with a tasteful rendering of " The New Kingdom " and " The , distant shore." Mr. S. Acton contributed " Mignonette." The song "Madonna " and " Tom Bowling" were done. full justice by Lieutenant Timmins, and Mr. R. Fryer sang the old favourate "I fear no foe" and "The yarn of the Nancy Bell" in good style. A violin solo by Mr. Kay and a cornet sol. by Mr. J. Wards were highly appreciated fee. torso in the programme. The comic element was supplied by Mr. Chrimes, and Mr. J. Leach, who were each encued. The eieging of the National Anthem brought the concert to a close. ' ATTEMP TED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.—MT James Craig (L anion University Intermediate BA. Examination), head master of the Runcorn Collegiate School, made a most de- mined attempt upon his life early on Monday morning. For several weeks Mr Craig has been in a weak state of health, and owing to the severe mental trial to which he constantly subjected himself, and his unsuccessful efforts to commence a school at Frodsham,his mind had given sigos of slight mental aberration. During a few nights preceding his rash act, the unfortunate gentleman had been unable to sleep, and between five and six o'clock on Mondry morning, he asked Mrs Craig to allow him to sit in a chair by the fire in the bedroem, hoping by this means to induce slumber. Whilst ; Mr Craig was sitting upon the chair, Mrs Craig lay dozing upon the bed, but awaking in a few minutes she discovered that her husband had left the room. She went in search of I him, and in the dressing-room her husband, lying on the! bed in a pool of blood, and with a blood-stained ranr in his band, met her horrified gaze. Blood was gushing from a fearful gash in the throat, the wound no doubt having been inflicted by the razor. Dr. Robinson was immediately sent for, and that gentleman has done everything that skill and medical science can suggest for his patient. Last even- ing Mr. Craig was in a very critical condition, although conscious, his mind is evidently disordered to some extent, and throughout the town the greatest sympathy is expressed for the unfortunate gentleman. ATLAS CHEMICAL COMPANY, LIMITED, Wings.—The tenth annual meeting of the !shareholders of this company WAS held at the Central Hotel on Tuesday; Alderman T Cook, Mayor of St. Helens, in the chair. The directors in their report stated that the advanced prices which were realised for salt cake and bleichint powder early in 1884 , were not fully maintained throughout the year ; neverthe- less they were such as to enable a fair amount of profit to be realised. The net balance of profit for the year was £14,215 Is Os •, surplus from previous year, £514 18s ; total, £14,729 19a 6d. The directors recommended that this sum be appropriated as follows :—let, A dividend of 15s Per share, free of income tax, £l3OOO ; 20d, a bonus of 10a pr share he credited to each shareholder on account of un- called capital, £4 000 ; 3rd, to depreciation fund, £4,000; 4th, balance due to next year's account, £729 193 61. The directors very much regret the loss, by death, of Alderman Joseph Cook, who for so many years held the position of chairman, and had rendered efficient service to the cornleelve since its formation.—The Chairman, in moving the adop- tion of the report, said he looked forward to the coming year without apprehension, and in spite of the continued depression of trade, which had been brought about by the , competition of rival processes, he ventured to hope that I brighter times were in store for the company in the future. I —The motion was seconded, and Mr • Robinson observed' that the company was in an incomparably better poittion than it ever had been. The report and statement of ac- counts were adopted. The retiring directors, Mr Thomas Cook, Mr B Brown, and Mr H Brunner, were unanimously re-elected. Messrs Stead, Taylor and Stead were re-appoin- ted auditors to the company. LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INQUIRY AT FRODSHAM.— An inquiry was held on Thursday at the Town Hall, Frod- sham, by Major-General John C Phipps Carey, Royal Engineers, respecting an application of 'the Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary Authority to borrow the sum of £756 for works of sewerage for the township and lordship of Frodsham. There were present—Mr A Thomas, J.P , Lieutenant-Colonel A sbton, Messrs Thomas Lewis, W H Linaker, Thomas Riley Thomas Davies, C E Linaker. James Rigby, Robert And rews, H Linaker, H Bancroft, J Cannel], J Farrington, and E Aaron.—Mr Linaker, clerk to the Sanitary Authority. explained the scheme, and said of the sum asked for £463 was for the sewering of Flubs-lane in the township of Frodsham, of which £347 5s had been apportioned to the township of Frodsham and £ll5 15s to Frodsham Lordship--Mr Bancroft having explained the details of the scheme, Mr Challoner argued that a special draining districi should have been formed, as there were certain parts of Frodsham Lordship which would not benefit by the scheme in the least. The ratepayers in Frodshem Lordship had no objection to the particular scheme before them, but they preferred that it should be deferred for a few years on account of the present depres- sion in trade and agriculture.—Mr. Linaker said that as a matter of fact fully three-fourths of the area of Frodsham Lordship would not be benefited by the scheme.— The fault was really in the law, which put the capitalising of the works upon the occupiers instead of upon the land- owners.—Mr Challener said the occupiers had to pay the cost for the landlords' bemefit.—Mr Thomas Davies, as the overseer for the township of Frodsbam, said that he thought a larger sum should be apportioned to the lordship, and less to the township for the sewering of Flmin-lane.—The In- spec'or replied that Mr DaviPS'S objection had not been made within the prescribed time, and the subject then dropped.—Mr Linaker stated that the present estimated an- nual rate for sanitary purposes was 10d in the pound on houses, and 211 on land. The aggregite amourst of all rates in Frodsham, including lighting, for the past three years had been as follows t-1882, 2e 3(1 ; 18'3, ffs Oil; 1884, So id. The balance on outstanding loans were r—Frod• shim, £3,375; and Frodsham lordship, £1,242 lie. The rateable value of Frodsham was £11,102, of Frodsbam 10-dship. £9,260; and the united population in 1681 was 3,si3S.—The Inspector then proceeded, vr:th Mes<rs E Aaron, C E Linaker, and J Farrington, to Weston Point, where he inspected the district of the proposed new sewer, and took evidence on the application of the Authority to borrow £OOO to defray the cost of the works. •

DUSKY MUCTREL ENTERTAINMENT AT WIDNES —The A minstrel trottpe in connection with the Widnes C.E.T.S. on Tuesday gave an excellent entertainment in waterloo-road school, to a large audience. Wright Williams delivered one of his popular "gossiping " lectures the subject being " Egypt." Mr. J. Ferrant occupied the chair, and there was a capital attendance. I LECTURE AT ‘VLDNES.—In aid of the Oakland-street Methodist Free Church, Widnes, the Rev J. W. Chrisholm' of Liverpool, delivered an interesting lecture to a good audience. The subject was "It can't be done at the price," and the lecturer was frequently applauded ; Mr. John Bray presided. CAMDEN WESLEYAN SAND OF HOPE RUNCORN.-1 meet- ing of the members took place on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr J W Shore. An interesting programme of songs, recitations, etc, was goue through, and the choir, under the leadership of Mr Tickle, sung several glees. Mr T Holt presided at the harmonium. Mr Woodland delivered a abort address: A HORsE KILLED AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday night a horse belonging to Mr Randle, con.rector, was drawing several waggons at et est Bask, when it became affrighted at the noise of an engine whittle, and plunging violently, broke the chain, and dashed off along the docks. On rata.. ing the dock side the terrified animal leaped to the bed of the river. aud was killed almost instantly. HAND-BELL RINGERS AT RUNCORN —With the object of aiding the funds of the Runcorn Y.M.C.A.' the Royal Poland-street Hand.bell Ringers gave an entertainment in Runcorn Public Hall on Wednesday evening. Their skil- ful performances with the bells, and the manifestations of the wonderful Speaking machine, were highly enj ryed by a large audience, bet we regret to state that tioancially the entertainment woe not a success. WIDNES Pouce. Couar.—Yesterdey, before Mr. F. H. Gossage, William White woe sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging in ledwu-ro ad, Hale, on the previous day. —Eliza McDermott. WAS tined 10s and costa, and Gilbert Blundell 5s and costs for being drunk—Robert Gaul, 15 years of age, was charged with stealing two pigeons, value 21 (Petite propetty of Thomas McManus, of IValmsley-street. —The prisoner was remanded. ROBBERY FROM A VESSEL AT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, James Prior, a. seaman, was charged with steal- ing 601bs of rope, the property of Edward Byrne, master cf the barque Crystalline. The prisoner was engaged as an extra band upon the vessel on Friday and Sa'urday. and on his departure the rope was mimed. It was afterwards found to have been sold for 4e 22 to a marine store dealer named Finegan, and the prisoner was apprehendec by P.C. Bryan. —The prisoner was fined 203, or 14 days' hard labour. CATHOLIC BALL AT Wiatees.—The sixteenth annual Catholic b sli leek plsee in Widnes Volunteer Hall on Mon- day evening, when there were upwards of 300 persons Present. The room bad been beautified for the occasion, and the stewards and cOmiulttee ei enenasernent had made every arrangement for the comfort of the gitere., Itl JChn Talloo, junr, officietel as MC., and the deities of secretary were performed by Mr S Quinn. Mr Owen Tansey had charge of the refreshment-room. Dancing was Indulged in Until about tire o'clock on Tuesday morning, to the strains of Mr Powell's string tend. ASSAULT AT Bus cons —1" ester day , at Runcorn Police Court, Alfred Haddock was apprehended under a warrant for not appearing to a summons on Monday, charging him with assaulting Margaret Bramwell.—The prisoner stated that he did not appear on Monday because the complain- ant had given him money to leave the town.—The com- plainant alleged that on the 12th inst the prisoner, who had lived with her for the past four months, gave her a "good thrashing" and blacked her eve. She was drunk. He had previously ill used her when she was drunk.— l'he prisoner wee fleet 10e and coets, Sc 6e. Rtoecertel SOROOL BokllD AT Woett.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the following persons were each fined 5s for neglecting to fiend their children regularly to school : —Mary Burke, Brunswick-Street; Eliza Maddock, Egerton- I street; Richard Seymour, Gilbert-street ; John Sho van, Mersey-street ; John Antrobue. Spring Garden; John An. trobas, Wilson'e-row ; Mary Lamb, Cooper-street ; John Wo-thineton, Gilbert-street; Edward Spencer, boatman ; John Higgins, Pereival'alene ; Jeseph Marshall, Gilbert- street; Walter Forster, boatman; John Lawson, Nelson- street; Job Neil& Loch-street ; and John McDonald, King- , etreet.—The Cases were proved by Mr. Bowyer, school attendaec? offictr. THEFT OF LINEN AT RUNCORN.—At Rencorn Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr JAMSS Handley, Thomas Parker and Elizabeth Ma-y Ann Parker, man and wife, of IBridgewater-street, were charged with stealing and receiving '5O yards of linen towelling, the property of Elizabeth Burton, Devonshire Place, Rune ,rn. About eleven o'clock 01 Saturday the prOSeetittix locked, as she thought, the door of her shop, bat after retiring into the sitting room she beard a noise, ard feud l the shop door open. She also discovered the ma'e prisoner on the premises, and after his departure she missed' the linen. Information was piven to the police, and P.S. McMieheel apprehended the prisoners, and also recovered about 40 yards of the stolen property I from the house of the prisoners. The Bench sentenced each I prisoner to 21 days' hard labour. WIDNES FARMERS IN THE COUNTY COURT.—Before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson. judge. at the St. Helens County Court, or Wednesday, Win. Grace, farmer, Upton Rock Farm, near Whines, brought an action to recover £22 12s 9.1 from S. J. Francis, greengrocer, Widnes, for cabbages sold to the defendant. The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Ilueband, and Mr. J. O. Swift appetred for the defenders. It ap- peared that In May last Mr. Grace had a field of cabbages, and the defendant offered to buy them as they were grow- ing, and the Enna of £4O was agreei upon as the price. He paid sums amounting to £2O ss, and fetched the cabbages as he required them. During the time the defendant's horse was pastured with the plaintiff, and for this the sun of 16s was charged. The defeed ant lead, however, put in a coun- ter claim of £33 12s 91 in consequence of the plaintiff not carrying out a contract t 3 loeeen the soil and manure it. The counter claim was repudiated and denied. Before the plaintiff's case had been concluded the court rose, and the case stood adjourned until next Tuesday. JEWELLERY ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.—Before Captain Haziehurst at Runcorn Poi ce Court on Thursday, Annie Price, a young woman, was charged with having on Tuesday last stolen a glass case containing 24 silver finger rings, 12 smrf rings, and one silver glove stud, value £4 Is, the pro- perty of James Sutton, watch.naker and jeweller, Church- street, Runcorn. The evidence showed that on Wednesday afternoon Mrs. Sutton, wife of the prosecator, missed the case and contents from the counter of the, shop. In tills evening the prisoner was in the Barleymow public-house where she "treated " Margaret Bramwell, a woman living in Back Cooper-street, to several glasses of gin, and in ex- change for a common red ring gave her a silver ring Of a pattern similar to those stolen. The prisoner at the time was wearing four or five silver rings on her fingers, and she had also given away several to persons in the neighbour- hood of Cooper-street. P.S. McMichael baying ascertained these facts apprehended the prisoner, who explained that the rings had been given to her by a man he did not know. She was remanded until Saturday. SAD BURNING FATALITY AT WIDNES.—Mr. S. Brig- I, house, the county coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at 1 the Arch Hotel, Widnes, tonching the death ot Emily Gray- I son, 11 years of age, daughter of William Gray- son, a chemical labourer, residing la Irwell-street. It ap- peared that On the lint. Mrs. Grayson was ill in bed.. having been confined three days previously, and In Order that she might have her five children "under her eye" she had them in the tedroom. There was a fire in the grate, and the deceased commenced to toast a piece of bread. In a few minutes the mother noticed that her child's dress was in flames, and in a state of great alarm she jumped from the bed and attempted to extinguish the fire. She did not succeed, however, and the girl ran scramming into the street, where a man named George Lowndes went to her succour. Although she had had ths benefit of Dr. Mac- Donnell' skill, her injuries were of so severe a nature that she gradually sunk, and died late on Sunday night. The Coroner said this was a very hard case, and much sympathy was expressed for the bereaved mother by the jurymen. A verdict of accidental death was returned. CANTATA AY BETHESDA SCHOOL, Roncoaß,.—The tarred cantata entitled " Daniel, or the captivity and restoration," was performed in Bethesda Congregational School-room en Tuesday everaing. The room was comfortably filled with an audience prepared to listen and enjoy, but the music was rendered in a manner that would have pleased a more critical company, and must be considered.a further testimony to the ability and skill of Mr. W. Handley as a conductor. The conceited music was sung by a well-balanced chortle consisting of the Bethesda chapel choir and a numbsr of friends, and evi- dence of very careful training was very conspicuous throughout. A small band of instrumentalists greatly added to the effect of several of the choruses, which were loudly applauded. The principal characters were repre- sented ley the following ladies and gentlemen :—Queen, Miss Horton ; Sister of Az ariah, Miss N Handley ; Azariah, Mr R Morris ; Daniel, Mr F Fairhurst; King, Mr Littler, Herald, Mr It Moore ; while Miss Littler, Mrs Moore, and Mr A Fox ably assisted in several quartettes aud tries admirably. Mr Ravenscroft skilfully accompanied at the harmonium, and Miss F Handley at the piano. The proceeds of the performance will be devoted to reducing the debt on the minister's manse.

FEARFUL FATALITY AT WIDNES. A GALLANT ACT. A most deplorable accident occurred at the works of Messrs. Mathieson and Ca.. Widnes, on Saturday morning. Within the past four months plant hes been erected for carrying on a process for the recovery of sulphur from chemical wastes. About 11 o'clock on Saturday it wss desired to drain one of the settling tanks in connection with the process, and George Roberts, 40 years of age, a labourer, who resided at 51, Bridge-street, attempted to draw from the outside a stone plug. The plug, which is eight inches long, projected about two inches from the tank, but Roberts was unable to affect his object. Re therefore by means of a ladder, his feet being encesed in large boots im- pervious to acid, descended into the tank. At this time there was a sediment of sulpbur, and About 7 inches of

mariatic acid in the tank, but Roberts easily knocked out the plug, and had ascended te the third step of the ladder on his way out when be was either overcome by sulphur- etted hydrogen ot the ladder tilted brckwards, for be suddenly fell to the bottom of the tank. A labourer named Henry Dillon, who was on a platform about 15 feet above the tank, saw what had occurred, and he raised an alarm.' His cries brought Mr. T. Matkieeon, son of the proprietor 'of the works, quickly upon the scene. Comprehending the position of affairs in a [nutrient, Mr. Mathieson leaped into the tank. raised Roberts out of the corrossive liquid, and succeeded with the help of Dillon and other men in getting him bodily from the tank. He was unconscious, and medical aid was at once procured. Mr. Mathieson almost fell a victim through his own gallant conduct. The in- idiome and poisonous gas bad penetratedanto his system to a great extent during his exertions in the tank, and he also tecarne unconscious; but the remedies applied by Dr. MacLennan revived him, and he was at once conveyed home. aloberts WAS also token to his home, where notwith- standing the skill of the doc,or he died (roan his injuries on Sunday morning. Mr. alathieson'e heroic conduct has ex- cited the greatest admiration in the town. At the Arch Hotel, on Tueaday, an inquest was held upon the body of Roberts, before Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner. Mr. H. S. Richmona, Her Mtjesty's inspector of workshops and factories, was present, and the arm was re- presented by Mr. Dougias Mathleson, Mr. E. Marston, and Mr. L. Kilcroas.—Williarn Jones, of 10, Gossage-street, brother-in-law of the deceased, gave evidence of identifica- tion, and Henry Dillon, of 30. West Houk-street, gave evi- dence confirming the narrative given above —ln answer to Mr. Richmond, witness said the ladder was very upright , It was placed in the teak by the deceased. He had never , seen a stone plug pulled out, but be had seen one knocked out of a similar tank with a long piece of wood.—Mr. D Mathieson stated that the tanks were pat up more as an exwriment than as a working affair. The stone plugs , tapered from the outside to the inside in order that they could be drawn from the outside. When the plots were put in a little red led sac placed round the joint, but be was of opinion that when this lead was removed the plug conld , bs taken out from the outside. 'This was the hrst time the tank had been emptied. It was a new tank just put up. In reply to the Coraner, witness said he did not see any necessity for the deceased to enter the tank.—Mr. Richmond suggested that the plugs should be lengthened, so that there would be more leverage from the outside, and further that the ladder when uszd should have clamps affixed to the top. —Mr. Mathi son promised to carry out Mr. Richmond's suggestions, and the jury returned a y.-rdict of accidental death.—The Foreman of the jury (Mr. Farrant) said the jury could not leave the room without expreasing their ad- miration of the courageous conduct of Mr. I'. Mathieson in risking his own life in rescuing tee wo-km on from the tank. His gallantry was very crediteble, and the feelings of the jury tawarde him were those of the highest resaect —Toe Coroner concurred in these remarks—Mr. D. Mathieson thank,cl the jury for the cernplitnent they had paid to his brother. In reply to Mr. Kann% be said his trother was gating on very well, but he was still confined to his bd. I

Fl,Valt OLTalattsS AT ileieveuterit—A report woe received from Dr. Ademe, medical officer of health, feeling that an extensive ouhreak of measles bad occurred in the tewsship of Badworth. He had made almest a house to house visi- tation of the township, and had' discovered at least 22 eases of measles, which he enumerated. He also found tneny cases of children who presented indications of convales- cence from measles, which led him to suppose that the out- break had been more than that which his report embraced. In regard to the origin of the outbreak the general impres. sion he gained from the occupiers of infected premises was thAt the infection was originally conveyed by members of infected families attending the Budworth Schools, lie had been informed that measles had for some time been pre- valent at Wincham (in another union), and that many chil- dren from that parish attended the Bud worth Schools, and J that seemed the most probable explanation. He had ofteu been met with the avowed opinion that measles was a dis- ease" better had and over," which opinion, strongly held, was a principal reason for the lack of isolation which was au constantly encountered in smell districts. At the time of his visit he insisted on whatever means of isolation that, were possible being curied out, and called the attention of occupiers to the provisions of section 126 of the Public Health Act. He had also notified the names of all infec:ed families to the proprietors of the schools in the village, and j requested them to refuse admission to their children to I school until the period of infection had passed. All other usual preventative and disinfectant measures would in due j course be carried out. Up to the present only one death I had occurred. He had also to report thtt he had inspected 1 Ia ditch or open sewer, on premises in Halton-roAd, Helton, which he condemned as a euisance dangetoue to health. He . hoped that the Authority would take effectual meAsures for its suppression.—The Inspector was instructed to report at ' the next meeting regarding the nuisance complained of. Tate PROP,ThEn 11RAINAGE WORKs AT STRErrote.—A I letter was read stating that the ratepayers of Stretton had held a public meeting at which the following resolutions were passed :—(1) " That this meeting of the ratepayers of the toveuship of Stretton protests against the excessive cost of the new drainage works proposed to be carried out in the village, and rtquests the Rencorn Union Rural Sanitary Authority to receive a deputation of the ratepayers of the above-named township to be head on the matter," and (2), "That the Rev. The proposal now made was on the recommendation of a committee appointed for the considera- tion of the matter.—Finally, it was agreed that the matter should ho adjourned to allow the deputation to meet the Surveyor on the ground of the proposed works to see if any Iplan more satisfactory to the ratepayers could be decided maom—Tbis was all the business of public interest, RAI -Ei.a.YERS' MEETING Al RUNCORN LAST NIGIIT.

, Last evening, a meeting of the inhabitants Of Runcorn, called together by placard to consider the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme, was held in Bethesda Congregational Schoolroom. Dr. MacDougall made no secret of the fact that be was the promoter of the meeting. Three members I of the Board of Commissioners were present—Mr Taylor, IMr LighOurn, and Mr Speakman. Mr H. Colehurn was voted to the chair, and he at once called upon Dr Mac- Dougall. The doctor prefaced his remarks by saying that they appeared in more free air than they did when last they were in that room. Public indignation, he said had been simmering in Runcorn in silent disgust for a long time. The Commissioners had failed undoubtedly in attend- ing to the town's interests. Although the Beard received the plausand specifications on the 29th November, dee 'Commissioners did not consult the law clerk until the Ilith I December. He went on to describe the course the proposed canal would take, mentioning its capacity to beer much larger vessels up to Runcorn Docks than could now enter those docks. He argued and gave legal opinion iu support of his statement, I that the Board of Commissioners would have no locus standi before a committee of the Rouse of Commons except as a sewer authority. Ile contended that there would be no difficulty in settling the question of sew ege disposed (Applause.) The traders were also directly effected by the canal, and the sooner they took the onestion into consideration awl the better. (Applause.) Speaking of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, he pointed out that the rates charged on the Bridgewater Cereal were regulated by a railway ring, and that the Ship Canal promoters expected to reduce these rates by 50 per cent. It had been stated at a meeting 4f the Commissioners that access to the present system of docks would be through a very narrow lock into the canal and toll would have to be paid. This statement he denied, end contended that the action taken by the Board of Corn- missioners on Monday was a proof that the course taken by rthe ratepayers on a previous oecasion WAS right. He con- eluded by arguing that the canal would ad Ito the prosperity wad importance of the town. (Applause) Mr. Worthington put a question to Dr. Mc Dangall as to the Commissioners preserving the interests of the town; and Mt' J N. Zella commented adversely on the remarks of Mr Lightburn at the last meting of Comissioners. Mr Lightburn afterwards proceeded to address the meeting amid some disorder, and interruption from Mr. Z 211 s. He went on to show that the Commissioners had not delayed in the matter, and said the reason they had not called in the law clerk earlier was to prevent scaring up a large bill for the ratepayers. Mr. B. Kniveton warned them not to place themselves unreservedly in the hands of the Snip Canal Committee nor put trust in unofficial letters. The meeting bad not concluded when our parcel was des- patched.

div.head: RE-OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: RE-OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIMRSDAY. Parliament re-astembled after the winter recess. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack soon after four o'clock. There was an unusually largs attend- ance of members, and the galleries were well filled with ladies and other visitors.

THE SOUDAN CANPAIGN.—There was no Queeb's Speech, and immediately on the House of Lords assembling Earl GRANVILLE proceeded to make the Ministerial explanation ef the position of aff tire in the Soudan. In the course of his statement, his lordship paid a high tribute to the memory of General Gordon, of whom he said that genius and virtue and disinterestedness were combined in him to an extraor- dinary degree, and his struggles and his death had excited an enthusiastic sympathy and a unanimous regret. The Marquis of SALlsßurry said General Gordon had been sacri- ficed to the squabbles of the Cabinet and the necessities of party tactics. Al to the expedition which was being sent out, he asked for an assurance that it would not be rutile, and that ws should not retire fro.n E4ypt leaving behind no record of our presence except the mischief and cantusion we had wrought and the bones of the unhappy troldiers which would remain there. 'rne House ad j mrned shor.ly after five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMNlONS.—Tuurtsimv. The Speaker took the chair in the House (If Ci,lll none at four o'clock. Thire was a numerous attendance of mernbsts at prayers. THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN=P4raPOSEO vorE

OF CENSUBB. Notices followed on a variety of subject.—Sir S. NORTH. COTE gave notice that he ebonld on an early day—on Mon- day next if possible—.nove "that a humble eddrrss be pre- *anted to the Queen humbly representing to hot hi.jesty that the course pursued be her Maktety a Government in respect of the affairs of Egypt and the Soudan has involved a great sicrifice of valuable lives, and a heavy expenditure, Witbout any beneficial results—(cheers)—and has rendered It imperatively necessary in the interests of the British Empire and the Egyptian people that her Majesty's Gov- ernment should distinctly recognise and take decided measures to fulfil the sp cial responsibility now in- cumbent upon them to ensure a good and stable government to Egypt and all those portions of the Soudan which are necessary to its security." The al erqu's of Hee rrso ros, refe•ring to the eats of affairs in the Soudan, confirmed the telegram of yeeterd ,y that General Bull-r had retired to Aba Klea, and added that it would probably be found that the retirement of the forces would be continued to Galtdul, and event, Korti.—ln refer- ence to the appoimment ef Prince Hessian to a command, Lord E FrrstlaCHlCE said the office of High Chenmissioner had been codferred upon the Prince by the Khedive and no- body else, and the appointment di I not iodic tte an intention to establish the do ninion of the Khedive or any member of Iris family in the &leaden. The Prince would have authority over Esyptian Madirs, and civil authority generaly. Lord E Fiterneurice informed Mr Forster that the Geverement was not in possession of tke disries of General (leaden. Tux ORDER OF BUSISESS.—Ia the coarse of a statemeut with regard to sessional business, Mr. GLADyTONE remarked that ene large and sorneweet complex tell was already in the hands of the House. The Gevernment e'er ph d ged go forward with it, and they dashed to ask the House to ex- pedite it even by means involving a departure from the usual arrangements of business. The time available for Important legislation would depend noon the rate of pro- gress made by the Seats Bill. . The Government intended under any circumstanc .8 to introduce and, as they hoped, pass a hill relating to the crehers in the Highlands. Bil's would be introduced to enable the Australian colonies to associele for certain purposes, to amend the Lemacy Laws, and there would be an Extradition Bill and the Secretary for Scotland Bile—Sir C. Deese laid on tha table the re- ports of the Boundary Cominieeiontre, with the exception of the one dealing with Englisli caunties —Mr. J K. Cnoss if rand ir Li. Campbell tut the extra expeuditure in- volved by the deepatch of Indian troops to the Soadan would be charged on the revenues of this country. THE EGYPTIAN ?OLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT. Mr GLADSTONE mesented pipers on the affairs of Egypt, and made a statement on the policy of the Government. It had, he said, always been the evacuation of the Soudan, it had undergone no change, and up to the 3,d of January cir- cumstances appeared to justify the saoguine hope that the military problem was near its solution. The news of February 4—that of the fall of Khartoum—entailed new duties, and led to new and strictly military decisions. The Government had instructed Lord Wolseley to frame his military measures upon the expectation and upon the ; policy of proceeding to overthrow the power of the Mandi at Khartoum. With regard to the time at which effeCt must be given to thet intentien, that was a matter for the Ijudgment of Lord Wolseley. The impression of the Govern- ment was that Lord Wolseley would postpone the operra- 1 tion.s until after the hot season. The Government did not think that the present situation allowed of their making any overture to the Mandi ; and their belief was that any such overture, however benevolently and philanthropically in- tended, would tend to defeat its own object and make more remote :he prospect of that very settlement which was aimed at. An instruction had been conveyed to Sir E. Bar- ing that any communication which might proceed from the Matadi should be referred home for the consideration of the Government. Sir S. Noe:marts expressed the loss the whole cluntry felt at the death of General Gordon; the sense they felt of the valour, conduct, and discipline of our troops •, and their deep sympathy towards the relatives of those who had fallen. He reeognised the ready and spirited overtures which had been made on the part of many British dependencies.—Mr. Medina gave notice that he ! should move a resolution declaring that the House deplored ' the betrayal of Gordon and the purposeless destruction of human life in the Soudan, but w ,uld disapprove of con- continued military operations if undertaken for no other ob. eta than those mentioned by the Prime Minister. 3 BE SEATS BILL.—On the motion of Sir C. Daum, the ' Seats Bill was put into Committee pro forma, for the Inser- tion of amendments relating chiefly to the echedules.—Sir S. DthICE stated that the principal boundary alterations re- lated to Preston and IVektfield.—The Panne MINISTER said he should ask the House to assent to the princiale that Iprecedence should be given te the measure, at any rate for Committee and report stages, on those days on which it was at down, and the bill passed through Committee pro i forma. A London Water Rating Bill was reads second time, and the House adjourned shortly before eight o'clock. LAST. NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN—EarI MORLEY stated that there was no additional news rerr'ardMg Colonel Buller 's force. He reed a telegram from Lerd Wolseley announcing Sir H. Stewart'a deatti.—The LORD CHANCELLOR presented messages from the Queen to the effect that persons in the army entitled to be transferred to the reserves should con- tinue in army service, and the MURIA should toz embodied. —Earl DERBY intimated that the Government had accepted the offer of New South Wales troops for the Souean.—The House shortly afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at fear o'clock. Sir if. Tyler gave notice to move addition to Vote of Censure to the effect that it is incumbent on the Government to take and hold Khartoum, and to open up and develop the trade rotate between Suakim and Berber. A further telegram bad hen received , from Lord Wolseley that day which stated that he \ had yet only one of the six volumes from General Gordon. GLADSTONE Stated the offers of assistance that had been made from the colonies of troops for Egypt, and expressed high appreciatiop of the various loyal offers.
