THU Simms. —ln reply to Colonel S s tanley 'Lord Ilimmerrose said it was not intended to embody gits whole ' ef the militia, but two batteries of the militia artillery and ; eix regiments of infantry. THE SEATS BILL—Mr. GLADSTONE moved that when the R-.dietribution of Seata Bill was put down by the tia. vernment, that the order shauld have precedence of all others.—A discussion ensued, in which Sir C. DILEE stated that the motion would extend to Wednesdays and FridAys, it being understood that there was a general desire to get the Seats Bill through as rapidly as possible. On a division there voted for the motion 223 ; against, 15. SIIPPLY.—On the motion for going into Supply, Mr. Sencrox called attention to the manner in which the forms of the Crown bad been recently ranployed in Derry in sup- pressing lawful Nationalist manifestations and encouraging Orange riotimg. Mr Sex•on's amendment, after much dis- cussion, was rejected by 59 to 15. The House adjourned at 12-55.

THE PEABODY Tats.r.—An abstract of the report of the Pe body Trustees for the year 1884 is just published. The total expenditure up to the end of last year was £1,170,787, and the number of separate dwellings provided was nearly 5,000, containing between 10.000 and 11,000 roams. The . birth rate as regards these dwellings was nearly 11 per thousand above that of all London, and the death rate 1.2.1 per thousand less. REDUCTION IN THE NUMBER OF TRIM JUDGES —The Soliciter-General, on Saturday, at Dublin, brought before a full meeting of the Irish judges, presided over by the Lard Chancellor, the Government proposal for reducing the num- ber of judges. The intention is stated to be to have one Common Law Division, as in England, and thereby dispense] with the Chief Juice of the Common Pleas and the Chief Baron, and to reduce the number of Common Law judges to eight by taking one frost the Queen's Bench. DIGNITARIES PROSECUTED IN TEE ISLE OF MAN.— At Douglas, Isle of Man, on 13 iturday, Demeter Gill, recently appointed second judge, the Speaker of the House of Keys, the Governor's secretary, the High Bailiff of Peel, and four members of the bar were, at tbe petty sessions, Sued dl, without cost', for being in the Castle Mont Hotel after eleven at night on Dec,mber 19th. Deemster Gill was en- tertaining officials and advocates to celebrree his elevation ' to the Bench. The prosecution has caused muc excite- ment.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, ThuRSDAY.

Public interest in the opening of Parliament was teeffied to both within and without the building. From an early hour a crowd began to congregate by Palace-yard- Al members passed in they were eagerly scrutinised, and in the case of known individuals were discussed with charming frankness. The police were conspicuously on the Wert. No one was permitted to enter Palace-yard. except members. and perms provided with special tickets. La'er in the afternoon there was seen the strange spectacle of boys and men hurrying to and fro across the yard, everyone with a badge on his arm. This new Parliamentary institution is. modelled exactly upon the form of the cabman'a bodge. The wearers, however, were net dismounted cabmen, but autho. Heed messengers of the various newspapers hunting np I copy." All the new restrictions with respect to the general public were rigidly observed, with the result that there was a delightful absence of crowding in and about the lobby. how long it will last is quite another thing. The 'absurd and wholly impracticAble regulations respecting the press shrivelled up in twenty•feur hours under the blast of indignation with which they were received. Already mem- bers are beginning to kick against the diflicalties which surround the admission of friends to the Strangers Galleries, and it is probable that before very long the new roles will have to be modified.

Inside, both Houses presented evidence of exceptional in- terest. The Prince of Wales, travelling day and night from Cannes, arrived in time to take his seat on the Cross Benches in the Lords, a part of the Boum otherwise distinguished by , the presence of Lord Brat:mune. All the priacipal Minis- ; lets and ex-Mini era were present, and the throng of ladies I in the Galleries added to the attractiveness and animation lof the scene. In the Commons Mr. Glacletont was early in ! hie place, lookinl grave, but strong and well. The meeting I WAS happily memorable for the absence of the debate on the address. We had that in October, and the pteeent being a renewal of the sittings after adjournment, not prorogation, ' this unnecessary and time-wasting pert umance was dis- pensed with. The first basiness on the peptic was the motion to go into committee on the Redistribution Bill. But matter of fact business like this is still afar eff. The Conservative leeders have been pusbled and hectored into screwing up their courage to the point of moving a vote of censure on the Government. This will lead to a long debate, and a division interesting only as showing how scme half-a-dozen so-called Liberals will vote. But the time occupied will be gratefully conceded by the Governments who welcome an opportunity once for all of disposMg of the nonseeseep trtly that of wilful misrepresentatiou and partly of sheer ignorance, that has been talked and written I daring the past three months. It is characteristic of the Effiontery of " Alexander Chat- fete, gent." that he should not shrink from reminding the 1 world of his existence. His application to the Qneen's !Bench to replace him on the roll of solicitors recalls the in- cidents of the famous Twiss case. I had bu-iness in the I court during the unfolding of that domestic drama, and ! have a vivid recollection of the shabby man in the dock, I plying with merciless cross-examination the quietly-dressed Ilady in the witness box, who gallantly attempted to hide ; the emotion which the blanched cheek and auivering lip I betrayed. It will be remembered that Chaffers had for years levied blackmail upon Lady Twiss and her husband, i threatening painful dieclosures if money were not forth- ,co eing. At lastthe hunted hare turned at bay. Lady LOSS I defied her persecutor to do his worst, and he did it, OH- ileasly. Arrested on a charge of attempting to extort money ' he in the form of crose-exemination tore aside the veil that (as he ass.rted) hid a life hitherto regarded as spotless. The sympathy of the court and the public was strongly with the persecuted woman. Even if she hid sinned, this spect:cie 1 of her betrayer holding her up to infamy made men's blood boil. If the crowd in court or the other tint bun,: about the entrance, could have got hold of Chaffer he would not have lived till to-lay to make hie unh'ushing apptic alert :to the Court of Queen's Bench. For two d tys Lady Twies had gone through the ordeal of ex tm'netioif and cross-ex- amination. Everything was settled, and Chaffer's emeic- , tion WAS assured when he claimed the right to rcc ill her. I She was to appear on the next day, a Thursday. The court Imet at the usual hour. But it som beceine deer that s reme- ! thing had gone wrong. Half are hour after the time ap- pointed the magistrate teok Lis seat upon the bench, and 1 the truth was made known. The unforbenate woman, unable Ito stand any mere torture in the witness box, had fled, and . all that remained to be done was to discharge Chaffers. I never forget his smile as he left the dock. Oilier people also remembered the occasion, and when ' Alexender Chaffers, gene" applied to ehe Master of the Runs to be re- placed on the Roll of Solicitors, the Incorporated Law Society merely put in a newspaper report of the Twiss case and the application was refused, a refusal yesterday contir- I need by the High Court of Justice. The London Omnibus Company are at last beginning to act with spirit and wisdom. The inca'culable good of op- position is at last shown in a practical advance. The ecm- posy are opening new lines, and are making wonderful im- provements in their rolling stock. It is a most singular 1 thing that wherever there is competition there is not only improvement but support. Now that the underground rail- ways are working pretty peinctu illy over the Circular Line, one can see that the chief change has been materially to develep the traffic with Hammersmith sod West Kensing- ton. There are about three times as many trains as there were this time twelve months. One would say that would tell heavily on the omnibus traffic. On the contrary, the company have increased the number of their whicles, and I have put on this line the Lest carriages they have. At laet they seem to be considering public cemfort in minor matters of detail. For instance, arms divide off some of the seats, \ as in the Paris 'bus, so that selfish people may not take mere than their own room. The lighting is greatly improved, and a placard is exhibited when the vehicle is full. London is getting nearly as civilised as Paris or Milan. Travellers through the streets of London will very soon again have an opportunity of judging of the electric light as an illuminator of thoroughfares. It will in April be four years since the first systematic attempt was made thus to light tbe main streets of the city, and only one of the three companies which then undertook the task continues it to tleis day. Now it is intended there shall be another and a larger Hee and, believers in " the new illuminant " are sanguine 1 that it will have good results.

GROSS CRUELTY TO A CiILD.—At the SIOUX Assizes, held at Lewes, on Saturday, before Lord Chief Justice Cole- ridge, William Carr, 32, and Jane Carr, his wife, were charged with the manslaughter of their child, aged five years, by starvation and systematic ill-treatment. The pri- soners resided at Ore, near Hastings. The deceased child be- longed to the male prisoner by a former wife. Prisoners went to lodge with some persons named King' in June, 1883. At that time the deceased ehild was strong and healthy. They lived there about nine months, and at the end of that time the child had become very pale and thin. The female prisoner used to beat it with a thick stick and his tather'w shoes, drag the child about by its hair, strip it naked, and lock it up in a cupboard for hours together. While the other children of the family were well treated, this one was made to eat dry crusts, and OR one occasion its food was rammed down its throat with a stick. It only weighed 25:b. at death, when it Should have weighed 451b.—The jury, without leav- ing the box, found both priaoners guiltv.—The Lord Chief Justice sentenced the man to he imprisoned with bard labour for eighteen months, and the woman to ten years' penal servitude. THE EXPECTED LITIGATION. The CLERK said, with respect to the expected litigation be- tween that Board and the Newton Commissimeers, that Mr. Jeans (solicitor of the Guardians) had consented to an appli-i cation by, Mr. Woreley (the solicitor of the Newton Com- missioners) to defer the hearing of the case pending between the two authorities until the decision of the Local Govern- ment Board on the matter in dispute had been given.—Mr. HARRISON asked if that decision had net yet been given.— The CLERK: No, not yet.—Mr. HARRISON said he should be very sorry indeed if the Warrington Board of Guardians were to figure in an equivocal position in any court of Illa- tive. His object in rising was to tell them that in his opinion, which went for what le was worth, they ought not to fight that action. Mr. Worsley had shown him a letter by their (the Guardians') clerk to him twe or three years ago, and he (Mr. Harrison) did not find any fault with the clerk for writing that letter, as: he was no doubt morally justified in everything he had said, though perhaps tech- nicelly wrong, but in this letter the clerk intimated that uses similar to the one now in question would be- treated by the Guardians as pauper cases. When the Board was arguing and discussing tha question they were in ignorance of that fact, at least he did not remember that anything about the writing of such a letter transpired. He did not think, therefore, that it would be just to themselves or to their clerk, knowing that he had written bona fide, to go on with the case. He thought that if they appeared as defen- dants at any court and Mr. Worsley produced that letter they would feel themselves placed in a position they ought not to be in. He did not think they should ignore what the clerk had done, but they should haVe to do so if they were to commit themselves to the defence Mr. Jeans had set up.—The CHAIRMAN asked if the letter re- ferred to had relation te the present case.—Mr. lieleatsoer, said it had not but it dealt with such cases, and the Com- missioners said they relied upon the Lana fides of that letter in dealing with the present case. He (Mr. Harris,) said ' that Board would stand in an equivocal position if they ignored what their clerk bad done.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said Ihe believed the feeling of the Newton ratepayers was in favour of the Guardians. He, ' as a heavy rate- payer in the township of Newton believed that the persons had been sent to the 'hospital on sanitary grounds, and he could not conceive how the Board of Guardians could be justified in paying the amount in dispute. The Newton Commissioners were far too high-handed, and could not stoop to anybody else. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)— Mr. HARRISON bad no doubt the Guardians would win the case if they thought proper to go on with it.—The CRAtE- MAN thought it would be better to ask the Clerk his opinion about the letter.--Mr. HARRISON (to the Clerk) : Am I not right on the whole P—The CLERK thought Mr. Harrison had scarcely put the proper construction on the letter. When the subject was previously before the Board he took a strong view, and he had never varied from the opinion he first expressed: With reference to pauper cases, people who were without homes and without the means of provid- ing what may be necessary,if such a person became afflicted with disease, whether of an infectious character or not was utterly immaterial, it was for the Board of Guardians to deal with that case. If it was for the advantage of the inhabitants of a district that a person, being seized with an infectious compleint, should bo isolated, that became the duty of the Sanitary Authority for the district in the be- half and for the protectien of the health of the inhabitants generally. He hi tried to draw that distinction all the way through, and he did not depart from it now. He agreed with Mr. Ratcliffe that it was for the advantage of the people of Newton, bee:use if the inhabitants ha a to be charged in cases that were not pauper cases they would pay a very much larger sum of money than they were required to pay in dealing with cases under the direction of the Sanitary Commietieners, With regard to the letter referreg to, he might tell them that Mr. Worsley read it one way and Mr. Jeans read it another.—Mr. HARRISON: You assent to our defending the case P—The CLERK thought they were quite right in defending it.—Mr. Ileunisoer said he had been misled by Mr. Worsley. (Laughter.)—The CLERK said the point of law that Mr. Jeans would put was that the husband,who was not in the hespitalat:all, was not liable to pay according to the statute, and if he was not liable to pay it was not for the Guardians to allow W him any sum of money which he was not liable to pay. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. APPLETON thought it would be better to or: on with the case.—The CHAIRMAN said the case would pro- bably not come before the courts before the next Board meeting.—Mr. BLACIIHURST was of opinion that it would be better to let the case go on if it were only to settle the liability in such cases.—Mi. JEANS said with reference to the letter alluded to by Mr. Harrison that it did not refer to the present case, and was in no way binding on the Guar- dians either legally or morally.—Mr. HARRISON said the question was whether they were not morally bound by any- thing the Clerk had written.—Mr. JEANS said that as a corporation they lead no morals to, guide them. (Laughter.) A corporation could only be bound in certain legal ways, and anything which occur- red in a louse letter written by the Clerk did not bind them is any way. He said that the Newton Commis- sioners in the exercise of their legal powers removed this family, and they were bound to bear the expenses.—Mr. HARRISON said that from the construction Mr. Worsley put upon the letter in question he led hint to believe that they could not defend the else, without ignoring the clerk's ac- tion. Mr. Worsley led him to think that the clerk or Mr. Jeans rather admitted that it was an improper letter to be written. Mr. Je.etts said he admitted nothing.— The CLERK said he guile agreed with Mr. Jeans that there was nothing in that letter to bind the Board of Guardians; it did not even morally bind the Guardians.— Mr.DARBVIIIIRE said he was rather surprised to hear Mr. Harrison advising the Guardians to withdraw, from their position. He hoped the Guardians would not withdraw from that position, but stick to what they had commenced. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN was quite of opinion that they might to go on with the case.—The subject then dropped. THE PENKETH VACCINATION STATION.—POLITITS AND VACCINATION.

ST. BARNABAS. T. BANE QUAY STAR.—A match between the above clubs was played on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and resulted in a victory for the home team. Score : One try and six minor points to three minor points. The try was obtained by Knowles. WARRINGTON V. RUNCORN.—The return encounter be- tween these clubs was played at Warrington on Saturday, when about 2',900 persons were in the fi dd. The game was opened by Lewie. For a short time play travelled up and down the field, and eventually resulted in a minor for War- rington e then, by good forward play, Runcorn menaced the Warrington line, where Wright dribbled very finely and compelled Walsh to save. Manfully was the game fought, and the little advantage the visitors had forward was nen- tralieed by the speed of the home team in the open. Gil- bert restarted after half time, and Warren was on to W Hughes before he could return. Play raged in the visitors' half, until by united efforts Runcorn reached the opposite end, where Barnes was promiremt by some splendid tacking. Mauls were new very frequent, when an opening presented Gilbert with an opportunity of breaking away, which re- moved hostilities to the half flag. Play afterwards remeined in the visitors' territory for the rest of the afternoon, and a good drop on the part of Barnes hit the uprights, Woods savirge Robinson hereabouts get in, but tho leather was ruled back. The scare at the cell of " No side " was four minor points to Warrington and one minor pointto Runcorn. On behalf of Warrington Barnes played a sterling game, and Massey. Gilbert, Jolley, Rigby, and Povey were very prominent. Runcorn was best represented by Hughes (cap- tain), Wainwright, Wright, and Clarke. Teams :—War- rington: T Walsh, back; J T Massey, T Barnes, and W Speakm in, three-quarter backs; E Gilbert and J E War- ren, half backs ; H Ashton (captain), F Turner, T Davies, J Rigby, W Peavey, W Hayes, J Jolley, J Robinson, and W Dillon, forwards. Runcorn : E Wouds, back; W Hughes, H Speakman, and G Wainwright, three-quarter backs ; H Hughes (captain) aud M Andrew, half backs; and W Wright, Clarke, Cox, Dean, Lewis, Hotil and, Gatley, Joule, and Clitle, forwards. ST. HELENS V. WAVERTREE.—These teams met at St. Helens on Saturday, and a pleasant game was witnessed by a fair number of spectators. Wavertree kicked off, and the bill being well returned, a scrimmage was formed, when the Saints, going with a rush, were only credited with a touch down. Wavertree dropped out, when 11 ;melt] on, getting hold, made a grand run, when he was cleverly c Alared by Hoyle, a number of scrimmages following, when the ball got near the 25 flag, where, the ball getting loose, Borthwick picked up, and dropped a splendid goal. Minor points only folio eed when half time was called. Borthwick kicked off, and the ball being followed up well by Halton, the visitors' lines were again in danger, when a line out was formed. Finney passed to Haseldon,who dropped a goal. Thisbeing thesecond, it seemed to liven up the visitors, who coon after added a try (Peters), which was not improved upon. The Saints were now playing up well when Edwards got hold and scored a try for St. Helens, which was not improved upon. Waver- tree dropping out, the ball was soon on the home line, where a second try was scored for Wavertree. This, hewever, was not improved upon. Borthwick dropped out, and Finney, following up well, secured another try for St. Helens, from which Borth wick added the major point. No side being called soon, the game ended in a victory for St. Helens by three goals, one try, and three minor points to two tries and one minor point. St Helens were only moderately repre- sented, being minus Gregson and Tickle behind, and Anders forward,but the Saints played well ,to a man. Teams : St. Helens; Rose, back ; Balton, liaeiltion, end Deanien, three-quarter backs; Finney (captain) and Edwards, half backs; Borthwick, James, Twist, Pennington, Harwood, Basnett, TJnsworth, Rogers, and Arnold, forwards. Waver- tree : Spedding, back; Scott, Hoyle, and Singleton, three- quarter backs ; Anderson and Peters, half backs: Sutton (captain), Goodman, Bez int, Edwards, Gavrne, Newman, Gandy, Wakefield, and Sanderson, forwards. LIVERPOOL DISTRICT CHALLENGE CCP SEMI-FINAL TIE: EARLESTOWN V. ST. Mane's.— Aceompanied hy a large number of their supporters, the first team of the Earle-- town club journeyed to Liverpool on Saturday afternoon to conteet with the St. Mary's Club one of the semi-final ties in the competition for the Liverpool and District Association Challenge Cup. The match took place on the ground of the Everton Club, at Anfield, and many persons assembled in the hope of witnessing a good game. The Liverpool Club has lately shown capital form, and it was expected they would prove a good match for last season's silver medallists. The latter, however, stepped into the arena full of confichnce, and attired in new white jerseys with a red Maltese Cross on both the back and front, appeared in fine condition. With the exception of the first few minutes the Earlestonians playing in rare form, beat their opponents at almost every point of the game. This was especially noticeable in the second half when they scored no less than six goals, and the result was that St. Mary's had to submit to a most decisive beating. The teams were as follows : Earlestown : James Appleton, goal ; J Green and R ' Green, backs; J Whalley, R Bowker, and Danbury, half- backs; W Rich and J Ellison, right wing ; J Sims and J Ogden, left wing; A W Dagnal, centre. St. Mary's : F Roberts, goal ; Dunbar and O'Donoghue, backs; Kehoe, R Gorrie, and E Borne, half-backs; W George and Schuma- cher right wing; W Gorrie and Miles, left wino ; Baker, centre. Earlestown won the toss, and decided to play up bill, Baker giving motion to the ball shortly after three. Earlestown replied by obtaining a corner, but the ball was sent behind by Sims. From the kick out George and Shumacher made some headway, but the backs repelled the attack, and Sims raced up the left. Dunbar interposed, and some long ex- changes were indulged in, until Baker rrished down the centre. The leather was soon back in the home end, where, after a sharp scum.. Sims defeated Roberts for the first time amid loud applause. Dagnall repeated the performance a few minutes afterwards, and again, before half-time, from a neat pass by Sims, the same player registered a third goal. With the change of ends, Earlestown having the advantage of the incline, kept the game almost entirely at the St. Mary's end. Dagnall restarted the ball, and George imme- diately after had a shot which very nearly came off. Green cleared, and Ellison soon notched the fourth point. From a well-placed centre by Rich, Sims scored the fifth, and Dagnall beaded a sixth from a corner kick. The Saints'left wing pair now gave a temporary relief, but Dagnall was again to the fore, finishing a good dribble by again lowering the St. Mary's colours. Two minutes later Sims did like- wise by a capital screw shot. Schumacher and George here put ma good dribble, and from a pass to Gorrie that player headed the ball over the bar. Meeting the kick out, the Saints assailed the Earlestown uprights, and Miles was suc- ceseful in scoring the only point for his side. The right wins pair were again instrumental in obtaining a corner, which, however, was barren. From the kick out Sims got on the ball, and by a grand screw reduced the Sainta'strong- hold for the ninth and last time, Earlestown thus winning by nine goals to one. The victory of Earlestown created a jubilant feeling among the footballers of the district on Saturday evening. Golborne and Everton meet at Bootle to-day, to decide who shall meet Earlestown in the final tie. 1

CATTLE FAIL—The first of the fortnightly cattle fairs was held on Tuesday, and, although the weather was very la-ad, a goodly number of cattle were in the market, and a fair business was done. These fairs of late years, owing to the prevalence of rinderpest, etc., have not been well at- tended, but this year the fast fair promises a renewal of large fairs. A SON'S MAINTENANCE IN A REFORHATORY.—JaMe9 Doddy, a labourer, living in Prescot, was summoned at the Petty Sessions on Tuesday for the recovery of arrears owing by him under an order of the magistrates.—Saperin- tendent Barker stated that some time ago an order was made by the Bench for the defendant to pay is 6d per week towards the maintenance of his son in a reformatory school. He had, however, fallen into arrears since the lath July last, and the amount now owing was £2 2s.—The Bench made an order for immediate payment. STEALING THE EARL OF DECRY'S FLownits.--Before Messrs. H. Bright and Willis, at the Prescot Police Gelid; on Tuesday, Joseph Burke, a middle-aged man, hailing from Liverpool, was charged with stealing a quantity of shrubs, value 2s, the property of the Earl of Derby. The prieoner pleaded guilty.—lt appeared that about le% o'clock on the previous day Isaac Owen, gardener, saw the prisoner near a plantation. He suspected him and watched his movements. He afterwards eavr him pluck several rho- dodendrons, which he made into a bundle with the intention of taking them away, bat Owen, caught him and gave him into custody.---He was committed to prison for 14'days with hard labour.

A ST. HELENS BILLPOSTER Frr TROUBLE—.--At the Present Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr. H. Bright and Cap- tain Willis, William Howe, formerly a billposter, residing at St. Helens was charged under a warrant with, deserting his child, whereby it became chargeable to the PreNcot Union. —Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk 70 the Guardians, stated tha'2 the prisoner's child was five yours old. For a considerable time the prisoner bad not lived with his wife and was not aware that the child had become chargeable to the union. He was willing to repay to the union 63 per week notil the total cost of the child's maintenance had been refunded, and he (Mr. Hartley) was instructed to withdrew the case on that understanding-.—The Bench stated that the prisoner would be discharged.

Ihe monthly return of attendances and fees was as follows :—Boys' School: Number on roll 212, Corres- ponding month latst year 250 ; attendances 3.820, last year 10 922 ; attendances lost 1,780, last year 1,578 ; average 176, last year 218 ; fees £ll 12s 9d, last year £l5 173 61.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Saturday the county match at Wakefield, between Yorkshire and Cheshire was the most important Rugby item in the north. The Yorkshire team were victorious by one goal and three tries to two tries. Yorkshire has won three games, lost one, and drawn one. Cheshire Las played two matches in addition to that of Saturday, one of which, that against Lancashire, was lost by one goal and three tries to one goal and one try, whilst tlie other, against Northumberland, was won by one goal and one try to nil. The Cheshire Associ- ation team at Northwfoh were more fortunate on Saturday, and by a victory of five goals to three over Denbighshire placed a set-off to the Yorkshire defeat.

The Old Carthusians journeyed to Church on Saturday and played off their tie against the local club in the sixth round of the Football Association Cup competition. The result was the defeat of Church by one goal to nil. The Blackburn Rovers at the same time defeated sßawtenstall in the fifth round of the Lancashire Challenge Cup competition. The clubs remaining to contest in the semi-final ties are the Blackburn Rovers,. the Blackburn Olympic, Church, and the Bolton Wanderers.

The great international Rugby Union contest between Scotland and Ireland is arranged to take place on Saturday at Belfast. Seven matches have taken place between Scot- land and Ireland, of which the former country has won six and the latter one. The total winning points gained in the seven matches have been 14 goals and 11 tries by Scotland to one goal and one try by Ireland.

SUDDEN DEATHS AT A WEDDING PARTT.—On Saturday night a large party of guests assembled at the residence of a farmer near Clonmel to celebrate the marriage of his daughter. A most enjoyable evening was spent until dinner was announced. Scarce bad no repast com- menced when a young man fell from his chair and was taken up a corpse. The body was immediately removed, and shortly after the party returned to the room, when another young farmer, unmarried, gave a violent scream, and immediately expired.

Two WOMEN CHARGED WITH MURDER. -At Chester, on Thursday, Elizabeth Davies and Jane Lloyd, were charged with the murder of William Morris, an employe at the Chester Lead Works. Evidence was given to show that on §aturday night James Rogers, a labourer, saw the prisoners, one of whom lodged with him, in company with the deceased on the canal bank. They crossed a footbridge over the canal, and shortly afterwards he heard a splash as of a man falling into the canal. The young women came running back across the bridge laughing. Witness asked them who had fallen into the canal, and the girls said soMe- one was throwing stones. Witness believed deceased was In the canal, and tried, unsuccessfully, to find him. On Monday morning both prisoners were at his house, and one accused the other of murdering Morris by throwing Win into the canal.—The magistrates granted a remand for al week.

UNWMCOME VISITOI29 AT HALE.—At the Preseat Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, three young men named John Old- ham, Thomas Oldham, and Robert Garrity (all of Liver- pool), were charged with stealing on the 2nd inst. a desk, value £5, the property of Mary Case, of the Wellington Hotel, Habe. The prosecutrix stated that on the date named the three prisoners and another man drove to her house in a conveyance and had some refreshments in the breakfast room. Shortly after they had left she missed- the desk produced from the table Of the breakfast room. The desk had been given to her by her late husband, and she would not sell it for £2a.--John Bostock, assistant to the prosecutrix, said that after hearing of the robbery he and another man proceeded in a trap after the prisoners, who had gm+ in the direction of Liverpool. Near the George Hotel, Garston, they came up to the prisoners and another man in &conveyance. The desk was in the conveyarce. and witness then gave information to the police, and the prisoners were afterwards apprehended.—Mr. J. 0. Swift Helens) appeared for the prisonere, and stated that he was insucted the prisoners had nothing at all to do with taking the desk. They were not aware that the desk was in the trap until the other man not in custody had told them and produced h.—They were each fined £5 and costs, or in defauleof payment one month's imprisonment. HOARD OF GIIARDIANS.—The fortnightly meethw of the Prescot Beard of Guardians was held at the Work: °use, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, under the presidency of Mr ZeT Hall. An estimate of the probable amount of ex- penditure in.the relief of the poor and other charges by the Guardiens on behalf of the Union for the half ending the 29th September, 1885, waa submitted by the Clerk. It amounted to £22,330. It was stated that the items had been very carefully gone into, and had been decreased as low as possible. The Clerk remarked that the estimate was the lowest that had been for many years, and the estimate was adopted. On the recommendalon of the Visiting Com- mitteee, Edward Wood was appointed bookkeeper at the Workhouse at a salary of £3O per annum with rations and apartments. The Clerk asked the Authority to pay the sum of £ll Os 61, charges incurred by the removal of a lunatic from Widnes to Raiehill Asylum. In the charge was included the doctor's fee of one guinea. The Rev. Father Finegan demurred to the payment of so large a sum as one guinea; and the Rev T Chambers observed that all the doctor had to do was to append his signature to the official document. After some discussion the matter woe referred to the Finance Committee.

div.head: ST. ANNE'S TEA PARTY AND ENTERTAINMENT.
div.p: ST. ANNE'S TEA PARTY AND ENTERTAINMENT.

-• On Monday evening, the annual parochial tea party and entertainment in connection with St. Anne's Church took place in the Schoolroom, Dannett-street. The tea was largely attended, there being about 300 persons present, and it passed off most successfully. Trays had been gifen by the Mayor (Aldermen Harrison), Lord Winmerl tier, Sir Gilbert Greenall, cart., Mr. J. G. Meal innies, M.P., Mrs. Beaumont, the Rev. J. G Richards (vicar), Colonel Black. burns, M.P., and Messrs. Peter Stubbs, John White, W. Sharp, James Marson, Dr. Mackie, H. Stanton, Robert Davies, P. Calvert, Eddowes, H. N. Houghton, E. W. Woods, Tins- ley, J. Baird, E. Rose, John Biker, T. CaVeley, Arthur W. Baker, W. Gill, W. Brooke, J. P. Leigh, W. Owen, J. R. Young, G. Gleave' J. Shillcock, Looker Williams. Mrs. J. Wood, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Bunch, Mrs. W. Woods, Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Fisher, and Miss Lythgoe,.Mr. R. Shackleton, Mrs. Ash- brooke, Mrs. Hemment, and Miss E. J. Bailey. The entertain- ment was held in another room ot the same building, which had been prettily decorated with banners, Sm. The Mayor presided, and there were also present the Mayoress, the Vicar (the Rev. J. G. Rlcharda), the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Mr. H. B. White, and others. The Mayor, in the course of a few preliminary remarks, congratul ited the Vicar and the con- , vegation of St. Anne's upon the success ef that getherinp at was very g.tooying, he thought, that notwi,hsrauding tne drawbacks St. Anne's Church bad had to contend with, they could still raise a tea party such as the ono they had jest 11 had. He thought it would be very gratifying to Mr. Richarde, or if it was not it oueht to be, (Applause. St. Anne's Church had once been very well attended indeed. , though it had suffered through many ef the most substan- , tial people who had lived in that locality removing to other neighbourhoods. He hoped, however, that the church would regain the position it once held. (Applause )—The Rev. J. G Richards, who apoloeised for reading his re- marks, said he would commence his observations by mak- ing use of that time-honoured and well-worn way of I expressing one's feelings, "I AM very glad to see you." He was indeed extremely glad to see them all, for he could assure them with all sincerity that nothing had given him greater pleasure than to behold before him so large an audience as was then gathered together. As far as he was concerned, now that things appeared so promising, as indicated by that gathering, no effort should be spare.' to accomplish the ends they desired in connection with a building not far from the one they were in. He believed that all that was needed was the concentration of their forces and the forces they had at command, and a combined agreement to effect their object, or, to use a common phrase, to do the business. (Hear, hear.) Of course, he need scarcely say that in the execution of this work there must be no little bicketicgs or private whimsies or animosities, to disturb their unity. (Hear, heat) He was persuaded that there were many there resent who would agree with him in believing that such meetings as they were having there were per st possessed of uncommon attractions, and were attended with uncommon advantages not otherwise to, be secured. But he was very doubtful whether those advantages were of a really permanent character. The people who gathered together on these occasions were in many respects like a conglomerated mass of atoms that had come together somehow from infinite space, and having kept merry jubilee in company for a time have gone off into infinite space again till the next time, the general result being onlyea pleasant recollection. But in a place like that, and' under present circumetances they wanted something more substan- tial than a recollection, and something more lasting than the ephemeral joys of tea parties. They wanted that that real practical good should acme to the Church of God, and to the cause of religion, which they had a right to expect from such gatherings as those. (Hear, hear.) He regretted to say that there were several hindrances and drawbacks to. be contended with in that parish, and some of them were rather formidable. The worst was the undeniable existence of enemies. It had been with profound grief that he had,. during the past two years particularly, observed these enemies becoming troublesome to them. He had observed them gradually coming into existence in and about St. Anne's. He was bound to say this, for these things were in- juring and hampering the church and himself in a manner very far from christian-like. They could not, he said, call the people he referred to men and women; they cofild only call them creatures. (Laughter.) He would tell them, if they liked, what they appeared to him to be like. They looked like dim, ungainly, ugly forms, without substance and without any appreciable shape except their hideousness, and one might imagine they were bred in the atmosphere about the church and in the pariah. He associated them with the , church because whatever their forms might be, they had voices, and his ears told him that he knew these voices in ' many places. The names of the forms he referred to were ' envy, hatred, malice, slander, detraction, false-speaking, hypocrisy, self-righteousness, and every other form of un- charitableness. These, he said, were the worst drawbacks they had to deal with, and he had felt it absolutely neces- sary to mention this, that people might know there were such enemies knocking about. He then referred to the poverty of the church, and to its intolerable coldness, and said that it ought to be heated in the same manner as St. Paul's or the Parish Church. In conclusion he asked that twenty or thirty men and women should make up their minds to attend the church regularly on Sunday mornings, and said that he- did not see why he should preach sermons when they did not appreciate them and come and listen to them. • -

The musical pregramme was then proceeded with, being introduced by an excellent overture by a string band. A- song, "Liquid gem," was so well sung by Miss Newell as tc. win an encore. A comic song, "The little scrub," by Air. F. Taylor, was els) so well liked as to secure an encore. Mr. Goodwin sung "Sailing," and Mr. Reddish "Surely," in an equally admirable manner; and Miss Biker was very successful with her song, " The valley of dreams." The, second part of the programme was very admirably rendered by the same artistes. An excellent harp solo was also. given by Mr. Mather. Mr. Percy Randall very efficiently performed the duties of accompanist.

DEPARTURE OF TEE QUEEN FROM OSBORNE. --The Queen, who has recovered from her indisposition, crossed from Osborne at 11 30 on Thursday morning and landed at Clarence Yard, Gosport. The vessels in harbour hoisted mast-head flags when the Alberta steamed in, and on. the Queen alighting she was received by General Sir Geerge Willie, Admiral Sir Geof:tey Hornby, an 2 tteir staffs,. A train was in waiting, and,the Police strictly guarded all the approaches to the platfozro, only oflicials.boing admitted to the station.

FIRE AT BLACKBURN..., 7 LIVES LOSTd,—Zarly on Thurs- day morning a fire occurred at Blackburn, which caused the loss of property valued: at £25,000, and also, it isleared, the death of seven persons. The fire originated in. an upper floor of the Knuzden.Mill. and spread with grent rapidity. When the brigade arrived the bading was. practicadly burnt out, and efforts were then made to saw adjoining property. A nnmber of firemen, police constables, and mill operatives were inside one of tha doorwaya when a large portion of th.a.gable end of the sft/raters tall inwards and buried them under a vast pile of atone anl brickwoik. Three hours elapaed before any of Uri= could, be reached, mad then Police.constable Dawson, was found in a dying state. fie expired ten minutes after being rescued. Another Can- stable, named Clayton, is known to have been in company with Dawson, and it is also supposed that five persona em- ployed in or about the mial.,,and who are missing, ar3 buried under the fallen material. It is well kn win that the Indians were formerly far more successful in the 1.-set- meat of Inflammatory disease than the znxst skilful and learned white men. It has been thus used for more than half a century, healing the most inveterate diseases, and giving joy and health to vast numbers. The power of the Green Mountain Vegetable Oint- ment Is asbonishiegly great. There is no rued nine known that can surpass it in prompt and energetic action. div.p: the same way, but was stopped by one of the railway offi- cials. On the 4th inst I made a statement to the police and laat Monday I was in the court, and immediately Ire- Cognised the prisoner Cunningham as the man wham I saw on the 2nd. lam positive he is the man. I have seen Burton frequently in Edgware-road before Christmas. I saw him talking to a gentleman with whom I had previ- ously done basiness.—Cross-examined : I could not fix how long before Christmas it was. Joseph Hammond, a guard on the Metropolitan Railway, said he was guard on the Hammersmith train on the night of the 2nd of January. They started from Aldgate at 8-57. His brake was at the end of the train. A man named Tay- lor was acting as under guard, and was in the carriage next the engine in the brake compartment. The next carriage was also a third class, the first compartment of which WaS a spare brake. Passengers carrying luggage were allowed to travel in this brake. The explosion took place in the tunnel between King's Cross and Gower-street at 9-14. The train had stopped a minute at ()batten-street signal before the explosion. The explosion took place in the fore part of the train. The passengers all got out at Gower- street. John Seward, one of the Hyde Park constablee, deposed that on the 2nd of January he was in the front part of the train when the explosion took place. Before getting into the train he saw Cunningham with his arms on the window sill of the brake, bolting out. He asked witness either for a match or a light, and the witness replied that he had none. He saw in the brake what he took to be a basket of tools. He could notsay whether any other person was in the brake. He entered another carriage. Henry Taylor, the under-guard of the train injured by the explosion, said he noticed two persons in the spare brake, and he c'euld swear Is Cunningham being one of the men. Police-sergeant Crawford deposed that on the night of Friday, the 2nd of J tnuary, he was on duty outside Gower- street Station at about a quarter peat nine o'clock. He heard the explosioa and ran into the station, and reached the platform on the aouth side about two minutes before the train arrived. When the train came to a standstill the spare brake was oppasite to the ticket collector's box He looked into the brake and saw three men standing. When they came out they stood for a few seconds outside the brake door. A lady who had been injured and others claimed his attention at the time, and when he again looked at the brake the three men had gone. To the beat of his belief two of the men were the prisoners. He had singled Out both men from a number of others. Annie Nunn, living at 138, Upper North-street, Poplar, deposed that on Saturday, the 24th of Janeary, she went to the Tower of London with a friend. When they were go- , lug from the chapel to the armoury she saw smoke rising from the floor, and then there was a terrible noise, after which she and her friend found themselves lying on the ground eomewhot injured. div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

RUNCORN COMMISSIONER AND THE CANAL. A. special meeting of the Board of Commissioners, con- -veneel by requisition, to consider the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, was bald at the Town Hall on Monday evening. Mr. i•T Norman was voted to the chair, and there were also present 'Messrs Speakman, Pritchard, White, Lake, Lightburn, Whit- taker, Taylor, Harris, Dobson, Meadowcroft, W H Linaker (law clerk), W Brooks (secretary), and M Barker (sur- veyor). Mr. D.:Also:4 said there had appeared in The Examiner a •paragraph that the Board had on Thursday passed a resolu- tion to oppose the Runcorn Gas Works Bill, and defray the • cost out of the public funds. As the ratepayers seven days pre- viously ha l decided that the Bill should not be opposed, there was considerable feeling in the town.—The Law Clerk and Mr Lake explained that the resolu ion passed by the .Board was simply a matter of form in accordance with the . advertisements.
Vie mectla; then proceeded to discuss the Manchester iShip Canal scheme.

The Cumutest expressed surprise at the result of the ratepayers' meeting, and pointed out that the Commissicners did not object te the Ship Canal bat r quire(' that if the Mersey was cut up as intended. Runcorn should have the same advantage they at present enjoyed. In reply to Mr. Lake, the Secretary produced a letter dated February 10th, from the promoters of the Ship Canal, asking that the clauses proposed by the Commissioners might be sent at once. Mr. LAKE thought the Board entitled to ask the chairman of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee for an explana- tion of the object ot the meetiog. Mr. PRITCFIARD replied that the committee had not given any inst.' uctions for the calling of the meeting, and he had no explanation to offer. He thought the members who had been instrumental in calling the meeting shoald now be prepared with some information. Mr. SPEAKHAN said he would give an explanation why he signed the requisition. The scheme of the Manchester Ship Canal had not assumed a very serious shape. The Par- liamentary Committee had been working for a long time, and had given .a great amount of attention te the work brought before them in the preparation of clauscs for the protection of elle town. The interests of Runcorn were bound up in those clauses or otherwise, and his impression was that after the report which had appeared in the news- papers, that the Saip Cane' Company invited all bodies requiring clauses to get such clauses in the bill before going To London, they should have them sent in immediately. their clauses ha I not been submitted, ant he maintained that it was the duty of the Board to send the clauses which they had already accepted. One or two members of the Board thought it wise that the clauses should not go up until they had the decision of the ratepayers at the poll. It might be too late then, and he, for one, thought if they could get the clauses settled before the poll was taken, they had 3 perfect right to do so, and that they ought to do so in the ivereres of the community. (Hear, hear.) He held that at the recant public meeting they did noe get tbe voice of the ratepayers, and they ought to be above any petty thing such as took place on that occasion, because they knew it was only just one individual who turned the-whole thing. His impression was that Dr. McDougall now felt sorry for the action he had taken. He thought the follow- ing resolution would commend itself to their judgment:— ' That the drafted clause, prepared by the Parliamentary and Legal Committee for insertion in the Manchester Ship Canal Bill be forwarded at once to the promoters of the bill, d that the committee be instructed to negotiate with the promoters to obtain the slid clauses." (Hear, hear.) Mr. H. WHITE seconded the motion. Mr. LIGHTBURN, after giving his reason for signing the requisition, sail be sympathised very heartily with the members of the Board who had hurled at them in a sense- less and brainless manner—(hear, hear,)—accusations which arose from an entire ignorance of the question under discus- aloe, and which he was sorry to say were applauded by people who were no wiser than the people who uttered those statements. It was not only for the Commissioners that he sympathised, but he felt sorry for those people who ap- plauded the sentiments, and he hoped by that time they were thoroughly ashamed of themselves. (Hear, hear.) R ather than deal with recriminations of that kind he would direct attention to some of the argumenls that had been used—if they might dignify them by that name. It was urged at the ratepayers' meeting, in entire ignorance, that the Commissioners had done nothing at all in connection with the matter. He might tell them that on October 10th they went to Manchester and saw an incomplete plan of the Ship Canal scheme, on the IB,h Oct. they asked for a copy of the clauses which the promoters intended to insert in the Bill for the protection of the port and trade of Runcorn. They did not get the promise that the old clauses should be inserted in the Bill until the sth December. On the 29th Nevember they had a plan of the canal deposited with them, and on the 18:h December they had the clauses Now, on the Ist December, they met Mr- Collier by appointment to try to ascertain as far as possible what might be the action which the Bridgewater Navigation Company were taking. On the 10:h. they had an interview with Mr. E. Leader Williams. Now, at the ratepayers' meeting, the people were entirely ignorant of these measures and there present were given to understand that the Commissioners had sat with their arms folded entirely oblivious to anything th it was passing before them. They spoke to the hest of their knowledge, but their knowledge was very pitiable —(laughter)—and he really felt that it was a reflection upon his fellow townsmen that people who were professedly ignorant of what they were talking about should receive applause from them. Up to withia a very late period, they had been receiving information w.bich had induced the committee to recom- mend clanses which they never would have thought of on the 18th December, when the clauses were submitted to them. There was no other town between Liverpool and Manchester in exactly the same position as Runcorn. They were told they would have a wall built right between the town and the river with a narrow entrance, and a toll at the gate. He would like to know what trader would like to Carry On his business under circumstances like those. It was incumbent upon the people who passed the resolution against them to say one of two things. They mast either say they did not want clauses, or they should say that the clauses they needed should be drafted by themselves. (Hear, hear.) In the bill it was proposed to make the charge on cotton from Eastham to Runcorn 2s St per ton. from East- tam to Warrington, several miles further, 21 7d per ton. At the rate they proposed to charge to Runcorn the rate to 'Warrington ought to be 4s 21. They then proposed to -charge a rate to Manchester of de 3L - When reckoning on the rate to Runcorn it ought to be at least 71 61. (Hear, hear.) He could read them a list of rates on china clay and other goods which were equally unfair ; and did they mean to say that the ratepayers who voted against the resolution the other evening were willing to allow Runcorn to be handicapped in that way without making an effort ; (Mr. Dobson : No.) If be thought the public meeting held on the sth instant re- . presented the feelings of the majority of the ratepayers, he would not remain a Commissioner another hour. (Mr. LAKE: Hear, hear). Mr. Donsole said during the last forty years the trade of Runcorn had been greatly developing. The Bridgewater Navigation Company, at an enormous ex- penditure, had made every accommodation for building up ' the trade. (Hear, bear.) They had constructed commo- dious docks. They had provided spacious wharves, built large warehouses, and erected steam cranes for the quick despetch of the trade of the port, and there was no port in the world where there were such facilities and privileges for the expedition of traffic, as there was at Runcorn. (Hear, heer.) They bad built up this Enormous trade at enormous expense. Were they going to have it bartered away at the bidding of an individual ? What effect the Ship Canal would have upon Runcorn no signs declared and no voice uttered. They could not tell whether the future was light or dark, but it behoved them to take such measures as would place them on their present substantial basis. Many people had an impression that the Commis- sioners were Opposed to the construction of the canal. That was not so. What they wanted was to protect any inter- ference with their trade. At the present time he under- stood that the Bridgewater Navigation Company were pay- ing upwards et £lOO,OOO a year in wages, all of which pas- sed through Runcorn. The interests of all classes were identical, and he hoped the Commissioners would do their utmost to get the clauses Inserted in the bill for the due protection of the interests of Runcorn. Mr. PRITCHARD conteuded that if the Board forwarded the chums to the promoters they would be placing them- selves in direct opposition to the wish of the ratepayers. The SECRETARY, at the instance of Mr. Meadowcroft, read a long list of the meetings held by the Parliamen- tary and Legal Committee to consider the Ship Canal question. Mr. LIGETBI7IIN said the minutes did not record one- !mirth of the metiegs held upon the subject. There were Often as many as three meetings a week. Mr. PRITCKARD observed that the clauses were placed in the hands of the law clerk on the 21th December, and they were received back properly framed on the 19th January. Their construction involved considerable labour, and, Iron his own personal experience he could assure the Board that not a moment of time had been lost by Mr. Line- ker or the committee in the preparation of the clauses, Which involved a vast amount of shyly. Mr. LIGHTMURN observed that it was impossible for the clauses to be prepared with greater expedition, as up to the 19th January they were not receiving such information which neceseitated alterations in their construction. So recently as the sth Februar y tion by which they received a communica- clause. they had necessarily to alter the fifth Mr. LAKE said there was now nothing more important than to disabuse the minds of the ratepayers as to the con- duct of the Board in the past, and of their intentions in the future. There could be very little doubt the vote of the ratepayers the other evening was given against the Com- missiouers on two main reasons. There was a strong feel- ing amongst the working classes that they were opposing the bill as a whole, and they saw naturally that such a coterie was a mistaken one, for while the canal was being made they were of opinion that it would mean plenty of Work for them. It had now been made clear that the Com- missioners were not op)ned to the construction of the canal, and that the word "opposition " was merely a tech- nical description. With all due respect to the statement of Mr. Pritchard, be must say that he did not think that the public meeting represented the ratepayers at large. (Hear, hear.) He thought the only logical position which Mr. Pritchard could take if be felt bound by the decision of that meeting was that there was nothing else for him to do but to resign his position as a member of that Board, and more especially as a member of the Parliamentary Corn-

mittee. He should not continue a member of the Board if he looked upon it as the feeling of the town. It was by all means a packed meeting. He did not mean that in an oan- sive sense, but persons interested in another object had come to look after their own interests and forgot the it. terests of the town. Thoir duty was clearly to guard the present and future welfare of the town, and if they Neese satisfied it was fer the good of the town that these clau.see should ba inserted in the bill, he took it that whether the ratepayers chose to bully them or not their duty was not done while there was a single stoma left unturned. _ Mr. LIGHTBURN objected to any money being spent upon the matter until the poll had been taken, and Mr. &posit- MaN agreed to confine his resolution to simply that the clauses should be forwarded to the promoters of the hill. Nine mombers voted for the resolution, Messrs Pritchard and Meadowcroft voting against.

The preparations for ascertaining the views of the rate- payers upon the action that the Board of C.mimis3ioners should take with regard to the Ship Canal Bill an nearly completed. The voting papers, which number upwards of 3,000, will he delivered on Tuesday, collected on Saturday, and counted on the following Monday. RUNCORN SHIPPING OWNr.B.S AND THE CANAL.

- On Tuesday morning a meeting of shipowners was held in the office of Mr It B Tuft, Perciyal's.lane, Runcorn, under the presidency of Mr J Brundrit, J.P. There were present—Messrs R B Tuft, 0 Thomas, R Clark, W J Shores, S Rovenscroft, Nirrn Knowles, I Bowyer, J Pritchard, T Cooper, Richard Abel, T Rayner. and John Beckett.—Mr Toft, in opening the meeting, said that the Ship Canal scheme would prove a great detriment to the interest of the port of Runcorn unless substantial clause° were inserted in the bill to protect the outlet and inlet of the present docks, and it was provided that the rates now in force should not be exceeded. The canal might improve the channel and it might not, and if the company were going to make charges for all vessels coming into the canal, Runcorn would suffer under great disadvantages. They had now a free river, and if they hod an impediment in the shape of a will right in front of the docks, all their vessels would be taken from them, and the town would suffer.—Mr Pritchard said he thought they ought to insist upon the freedom of the river for all traffic.—The Chairman said be thought the Board of Commissioners were asked too much they required that all crafts and barges of every description should use the canal free of toll.—Mr Pritchard said the clause to which the chairman referred meant that the vessels that could enter the docks at the present time should enter after the canal WM constructed free from tol!.—Mr Toft said at the present time Runcorn enjoyed the privilege of free tonnage, and he wished to know how the shipowners would be affected in that respect by the bill.—Mr Pritchard said the Canal Corn. pany were applying for pewers to let steam tugs, and they sought to infimt a penalty upon all steamers coming into the canal without a licence from them. No one would be allowed

to use a tug boat on the canal without a licence from the company. Ile pointed out thst no traffic could be taken from Runcorn Docks to the Old Quay along the canal without the imposition of 4l per ton, and that whatever distance they moved along the canal the charge would not be for less than three miles. He further stated that if a vessel *me up the canal, say from the south of England, it would he subject to a charge of 6.1 per ton on the - registered tonnage, and after remaining in the canal for a certain period an extra charge , would be mate. The vessel•would be subject to a similar . . _

_ charge on going down the canal. The Cani'l Company also sought to impose dues on china clay and china stoneovhich were Runcorn's principal trade. They sought to impose a wharfage rate of 51 per ton, a canal toll of Is 63 per ton, and there were also towage Tates. Ile pointed out that the dues upon chint clay to Runcorn would be is Od per ton for twelve miles, to Warrington, witch was distant 20 niiies 2s 3d, awl to Manchester 33 9d. The true proportion ought to be Warrington 23 &l and Manchester 4s 61. He showed that the same anomaly existed sith regard to grain, slates, and cotton, and he contended that the Canal Company in- tended to handlcap Runcorn in every shape and form. for what was the meaning of these charges but to drive the trade pest Runcorn to Warrington and Manchester. The more he looked at the matter the greater reason why they should mtke a stand. He would not agree to any terms unless; they could have the free use of the canal. After a lengthy discussion the meeting decided to adjourn for a fortnight, when the shipowners would agree upon some course of action. The general feeling was that they ought to wait until they saw the outcome of the Board of Com- mis:donors' negotittions with the promoters of the bill. OPPOSITION AT BIRKENHEAD.

On Wednesday night a meeting of ratepayers was held at Birkenhead to authorise the Corporation of that town to take action in Parliament against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. It was explained that opposition to the bill was for protecting the interests of the ratepayers, securing a locus standi, and not altogether with the view of defeating it. Mr T Shaw and Mr Little held that the canal would benefit Birkenhead, whilst the Mayor said the best thing that could happen Bilkenhead would be for the canal to be brouht to Tranmere Pool. Eventually, Mr Little and Mr Shaw, on being informed that the cost of a poll of the rate- payers would be about £BOO, withdrew their opposition en being assured that no more would be spent than was abso- lutely necessary in the interests of the town. There were only four hands held op in opposition to lodging a petition against the bill. COMMITITE MEETING YESTERDAY.

The weekly meeting of the Provisional Committee was held in the Board-room, 70t, Market-street, Manchester, yesterday afternoon, Mr. Daniel Adamson presiding. Con- siderable additional support to the fund for Parliamentaay expenses was announced, amongst other subscriptions being a substantial contribution by the employes of Messrs Henry Boddington and Co, Limited, of Strangeways. The Chair- man reported that acting on the advice of the Parliamentary Sub-Committee, he had addressed a letter to Sir William Forworad in reference to certain remarks made by him at the last meeting of the Liverpool City Council, a copy of which has already appeared In the papers. The committee hoped the letter would be the means of satisfying the representatives Of Liverpool and other interests in the es- ' tuary affected by the works proposed to be carried out by the Bill. It was reported that several important owners of land and property on the route of the canal bad been settled with and that other bodies with whom negotiations were proceeding would probably be arranged with on an early day. The committee made final arrangements as to the counsel to be retained in support of their case before the Parliamentary Committees and also as to a large number of witnesses, engineering and otherwise, to be celled on behalf of the scheme. The preparations necessary for the presentation of the evidence is fast approaching completion, and a very strong Case will be presented.

NEW BOOKS, Sce. a Under the Meteor Flag" (Messrs Sampson, Low, and Co., London) is a stirring story by Mr. Harry Collingwood„ author of "The Secret of the Sands," &a. It is presented in the form el the log of a midshipman during the French Revolutionary War, and it is lively reading from beginning to end. The hero, Ralph Chester, has a hundred " hair- breadth 'napes." and comes in oceasionally for some hard knocks. He is here, there, and everywhere as duty calls, and the story in this respect silently enforces a moral which young and old would do well to lay to heart. There is, of course, a great deal of fighting in the book, but fighting is just now the order of the day, and it will therefore be in fashion. It is due to the author to say that he has shown much fertility of resource in varying the incidents, and that, while he is open and natural in minner, he is faith- ful and graphic in his description. The book will hold the attention of those a% ho dip into its pages. It should be added that it is handsomely bound, and ifairly well illustrated.

" Charmouth Grange, a tale of the Seventeenth Cen- tury" (Sampson, Low, and Co.), is from the pen of Mr. J. Percy Groves, late of the 27th Inniskillings, and author of" From Cadet to Captain." The story deals with the troublous times of the Civil War in England, and will be read with interest as giving a picture of the post which will be generally acknowledged to be in its main featuraa historically correct. But it has to do with love as well as war, "Ronald Cathcart," whc figures sn prominently on the side of the King, having left his lady•love in his an- cestral home whilst he goes forth to do battle for Charles I. There is no lack of adventure, but the author, like Jove, sometimes naps. He rather neglects "Alice "; indeed the reader sees so little of her as to scarcely get interested in her. The story in this respect cannot be said to be success- ful. The illustrations are numerous, and they are all good. For frontispiece there is a very striking portrait of Charles I. " Billiards Simplified, or How to Make Easy Breaks " (Biarroughes and Watts, Soho-square, London), will be wel- comed by a large and ever .increasing section of the commu- nity. It is a most elaborate work, no pains having been spare.l to make i really useful. The cover is quite artistic as a representation of a billiard table, and there are photo- graphs of Messrs Cook, Roberts, Bennett, Peal], and Mit- chell as they are seen at play. But what is of more impor- tance, there are no lees than 00 di 'grams of their modes of gettiug breaks, and the text which accompanies them is so clear and intelligible that "he who runs may read." We anticipate that this opportone work will have a good run amongst billiard players. "With a Show Throbgh Sou.hern Afric t " (Messrs Dean and Son, Loudon), is a lively volume giving the personal reminiscences of Mr. Charles Du Val, who was amongst those who were tied in during the investment of Pretoria. His work, siopretentions as it is, is really a valuable contribu- tion to the history of the Transvaal War, and as it is full of anecdote racily written, and amply illustrated, it is ;tore to have a anecdote, sale. "Cassell's Fine-art Edition of Longfellow" reaches part 6 this month, and embraces the beautiful story of "Even. geline," which is appropriately illustrated, the heroine being in each scene charmingly depictcd. The" Encyclof Dictionary," part 13, gets well into "C," and, what with illustration and dissertation, it is of growing interest. The tenth part of the "Book of health " continues the import- , ant section on education and the nervous system, and passes oa to an interesting chapter on physical education. •• Cassell's Popular Gardening" (part 10) leaves nothing to be desired either in the way of illustration or text. Amongst the subjects treated on are florists' flowers, ferns, decorative use of flowers, the life history of plants, glass structures and appliances, kitchen and fruit gardens. ' Cassell's Mapzine" for February is a more than usually good number. There is a useful article on the County Court by a barrister, and another by _Mr. C. Ray Woods on" Humours of the sun," with most instructive lustrations. The "Family Doctor "gives us valuable ad-

div.p: rHE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 211, 1885

vice, while the stories, continued and finished, are in no wise lacking in interest. "The Quiver," too, is up to the mark with its bright illustrations and thoughtful papers ; wile "Little Folks" is fultriling the promise of good things made in the new year issue. Messrs. Cassell and Company have made arrangements to include an illustrated descriptive account of the cam- paign now proceeding in the Soudan in " Recent British Battles," by Mr. James Grant, the issue of which has just been commenced in monthly parts. The numbers to, band are very attractive. Nearly every page is illustrated ; there are maps and portraits in abundance ; and it need hardly be said that the text is admirably written. " The Book of Lords" (Modern Press, Paternoster-row), is a sequel to the "New Book of Kings" by Mr. J. Mer- rison Davidson, which made a stir some time ago. Like its- predecessor, it is exceedingly outspoken ; but backs ap its startling statements with facts of history too commonly. overlooked. It will serve a good purpose in helping on the. agitation against the Rouse of Lords, for its price (sixpence), brings it within generalirsaah. The "English Illustrated Magazine" (Macmillan and Co.) continues the articles on "Shakespere's Country,'"and, "The Dramatic Outlook,' both well illustrated. Mr. Hugh Conway's story makes headway, whilst "The Girl at the Gate," by Mr. Wilki&Collins, is brought to a close. Ward and Lock's "'Technical Educator " (part 3) inolndes a sheet of drawinga to scale of the details of salaam en- gines, which is in itself worth tne price at which the whole

jarn'al is published. The correspondence column, shows that the work is. regarded as most acceptable. "The Season," in its pueely English form, seems to. have got good hold as a high-class fashion journal ; and Le Moni- teur de la Mode " ineps its place as a standard authority on dress and fashion. We have also to hand" Myra's Journal" (61) and Myres Threepenny Journal."

TRAGEDY AT TIVERTON.—UpOR a constable being called into a house at Tiverton early on Wednesday he found the wife of a mason named Sanders covered with, blood, caused by a heavy blow cn the bead with a hammer. The husband was found in bed, bleeding from several stabs in the throat and head. Both husband and wife were removed to the in- firmary, where the former lies in a precarious condition. The Wife refuses to give any account ct how her injuries were caused.

DEsrnuertvz RanEs.—A fire occurred early on Wednes- day morning at Oa Temperance Hall, Londion-square,Stock- port. A good deal of damage was done to the building, and a valuable collection of books and specimens belonging to a botanical socioty which meets in one of the rooms was destroyed. On Wednesday evening a firs broke out at Messrs Poole's Deese Mill, Pike's-lane, Bolton,. and it waa not ex- tinguished till the premises had been devastated. The loss is estimated at 030,000.

THE WIGAN. TOWN. Conerom nr. .t.‘ Fix —Ora Wednes- day the Tory majority in the Wigan 'bowls Council refused —in opposition to the " opinion "or one of the counsel to the Treasury, and also against the urgent advice of the Town Clerk--to declare vacant one. of the seats for All Saints' Ward, the holder of which had Gust sent in his resig- nation in order that be might offer himself as a candidate for the town clerkship, and had aftenwards tendered a with- drawal of hia resignation. The Town Clerk warned the Councirthatthey were taking a curse which might lead to much trouble and expense.

BANvErTO LORD' RIPON.—The Marquis of Ripon, who was entertained at a banquet by the. Liverpool Reform Club on Tuesda:y night, said we should altogether reject the de- mand for a war of revenge in the SOULI47I, which had been put forward in some quarters. A policy of that nature had been repudiated by writers and speakers, he was happy to say, dur:ng the last few days,.and he was sure the British public mould also reject it. He hoped the Government would steadily adhere to the-refusal hitherto given by them 1 in favcar of annexation. Whllst in Egypt let us do our duty to defend and consolidate, it, but reject th 3 mischievous policy of annexing either Egypt or the Soudan. FtitiEnAL OF CARDINAZ 514103E.—0n Tuesday, the re- maias of the late Cardinal llPCabe were removed from the Cathedral, Marlborough-street, Dublin, where they had loin imstate since Monday, te Glasnevin Cemetery for interment. The funeral was of a public character, and was very largely attended by both cleagy and laity. The Lord-Lieutenant was represented, and among those present were the Lord Mayor of Dublin, the Roman Catholic Primate of Delaads the Archbishop of Armagh and Tuam, and almost all the members of the hierarchy. The students of the local Roman Catholic colleges and schools and the various city sodalities walked in procession, as did also a considerable number of the general public. INTERESTII*7O DISCOVERY AT CANTERBURY CA,TFIEDBAL.

—A discovery of much interest has just been tnaWe-by wol k- men engiged in excavations in the lobby of the French Huguenot church in the crypt of Canterbury Cathedral. A finely chiselled head and fragments of ston?, many of which are richly gilded, and in one of which a pearl remains, have been exhumed. They are undoubtedly portions of the shrine of St. Dunstan. It was at the time of the Re- formation that the shrine is believed to have been damaged, and it is supposed that the pieces were subsequently col- lected as rubbish and thrown into the Black Prince's Chan- try (the present site of ths. French church), where St. Dun- stan himself is said to have been interred.

MR. COWEN AT NEWCASTITE-.:-.Mr,TO;eph Cowen, M.P., addressed his constituents at Newcastle on Saturday, prin- cipally on questions of foreign policy. He said a myste- rious fatalism bad doomed her Ma;esty's Government to pick up the dropped links of tho policy of their profligate predecessors. Notwithstanding declarations to the contrary, the hon. ger.tletnan said our authority. if not our armies, would remain in, Egypt. He said the Government argued, from principles to facts, instead of from facts to principles, ' and this he regarded as evidence of "the vigour of help. lessness." The foreign policy of England should not be 1 that of a sordid conqueror, nor yet that of abnegation. A vote Of confidence was Pls°e4 in Mr, Cowen, and a SiMilar vote was Daased at an over-flow meeting.
