Eosin, FRIDAT.—A bottle-fill-ell:with gunpowder was ex- ploded last night by some persons unknown near t he Sen- ator? and Deputies' entrance. The explosion, however, caused no damage.

THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN. DEATH OF GENERAL STE.WART. The following despatches are from Teerd Woleeley FRIDAY, 9 30 &m.—General Stewart died at Gak- dui on the 16th inst from the wowed received in the battle at Abu Klea, near Metemtneh, on the Mb January. The news has cast a great gloom over the whole of the British troops here. The doctors had pronouneed that the nature of the General's wound was of such a character as to have ren- dered recovery hopeless. Despatches are published in Gzeette from General Lord Wolseley to Secretory of State for War:—.-." Camp, Korti, January 26th :—My Lord,—l forward herewith the copy of a defined] from Brigadier General Sir Herbeet Stewart, in which he describes the action he fought on the 17th inst. at Abu Klea. lam now waiting reports from him as to his further proceedings subsequent, to the battle, and I reserve comments upon his eperationsmotil I am in receipt of them.l At present I shall content meself with remarking that all he has done proves him to be n. real leader of men and an able general. All ranks under hie command have displayed that discipline and those high fighting qualities for which Her Majesty's army have always been renowned. I deeply de- plore our loss, which was. considerable in proportion to the numbers engaged, but this must generally be the case where we have to contend with a brava and determined enemy five or more times eler strength, and who invariably cornea to close quarters an band to hand fighting." The other deepatch gives general Stewart's account of the fighting at Abu Kisa. The Gazette also publishes the Royal Proclamation calling out the militia. It is followed by a War Office notice ordering the undermentioned brigades and battalions of militia to be embodied at their respective bead quarters on March Oth, vie. :-2nd brigade, Southern diviaion, Royal Artillery ; 3rd battalion Est Kent Regiment ; 3rd battalion Royal Fusiliers; 3.. d bettalion Royal Irish Regiment; 3rd battalion East Surrey: Regiment • 3rd battalion Durham 1 Light infantry; and sth battalion Rifle Brigade; West Kent; South Yorkshire. MORE FIGHTING AT ABU KLEA. General Buller telegraphs from Abu Klee that on the 16th inst. about 30 of the enemy's cavalry were scouting round the British force all day, and wore reinforced here before sunset by some 400 infantry, armed with rifles. The enemy kept up a well-aimed but desultory long-range fire all night, which had continued until eleven a.m. the 17th inst. There were 16 cesuelties, including Captain Walsh, Somer- set Light Infantry, wounded severely, and Captain Paget. 17th Hussars; Quarter-master Jamison, Reyal Irish, and Surgeon O'Neill wounded slightly. Lord Wolseley telegraphs that General Wood is sending from Gakdul a transport of camels to General Buller, who will then prnbably move to Gakdul. THE RESERVES AND THE MILITARY, QUEEN* PROCLANIATIQNS, The Gatette puiebos iin; Queen's proclamation euepend- ing transfers into the reserve for the following regiments : —Fifth Royal Irish Lancers, Sixth Inniskilling Dragoons Thirteenth Hussars, Nineteenth Hussars, Twentieth Hus- sars, Royal Artillery, Royal Engineers, Grenadier Guerds, Coldstream Guards, Scots Guards, Royal Scots (Lothian) Regiment, Etat Kent Ways' Fusiliers, Royal Irish, Princess of Wales Own, Yorkshire, the Cheshire, East Surrey, Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry, Royal Sussex, the Hampshire, South Staffordshire the Dorsetshire, South Lancashire, the Welsh, the Black Watch, Oxfordshire Light Infantry, the Essex, the North emptonshire, King's Shrop- shire Light Infantry, King's Royal Rifles' Durham Light Infantry, Gordon Highlanders, Cameron Highlanders, Ar- gyll and Sutherland Highlanders, Royal Dublin Fusiliers, e'eince Consort's Own Rifle Brigade, Commissariat and Tranepert Medicel Staff Corps' and Ordnance Store Corps. The proclanieien states that this step has been taken in consequence of the present eta le of public affairs in the Soudan, and the necessity In connection therewith of taking steps for the defence of Egypt and for the protection of the interests of the empire, which in Her Majesty's opinion constitute a state of great emergency within the meaning of the act. DEPARTURE OF THE GRENADIER GUARDS. The 3rl Battalian Grenadier Guards, which was inspec- ted by the Queen at Windsor Castle, left Windsor on Friday morning for London, en route for Suakim. Previous to their departure from Windsor the Prince of Wales, who bad stayed all night at the Royal Horse Guards Barracks, walked to the Victoria Barracks, end inspected the bat- talion, a ter which the men were drawn up in three-quarter square, and his Royal Highness addressed them, remarking that he well remembered that very day 31 years ago when that very battalion left for the Crimea. He remembered how well the Guards fought on that occasion, and he knew they would uphold the honour of their country. He wished them "God Speed " and a safe return. The train conveying the battalion tee Gravesend, where the men were to embark on the hired transport Australia, left Waterloo at 9-25, amid a renewed outburst of cheering, and arrived at Gravesend at a quarter-past ten. The 2nd marching rquadron of the 20th Hussars em- barked at Portsmouth on Friday morning, on board the transport Italy, which sailed in the afternoon for Egypt, in- stead of Saturday, THE PROPOSED RAILWAY. The shipment of materiel for the Suakim•Berber rail. way is being proceeded with rapidly. In addition to vessels already chartered, the Admiralty have taken up-the steamers Osprey and Lapwing, belonging to the General Steam Navi- gation Company, and it is hoped to despatch two steamers with railway plant each week. Each vessel will take out a complete set of material f3r laying down about twelve miles of railway, and for several weeks to come each will convey to Suakim one locomotive and 20 covered trucks. Altogether about 10 locomotives and a proportionate number' of trucks will be eventually landed at Suakim for use on the new railway.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

At a Nationalist meeting at Newry, on Monday night, a disturbance arose between rival parties, and culminated in a free fight. The Bishop of Liverpool has decided to sanction the prosecution of the rector of St. Margaret's Church, Prince's- road, Liverpool, for alleged unlawful ritualism. At Salisbury on Monday, it was decided that the city memorial to the late Right Hon H. Fawcett should take the form of a bronze statue by some eminent artist.. •
Madame Saintou-Dolby, tge popular vocalist, died at her London residence at an early hour on Wednesday morn- Madame Sainton-Delby was born on the 17th of Hay, 1821.
lliE CABINET.—A prolonged meeting of the Cabinet was held on Monday. It is understood that the matters chieP4 under consideration were those to be brought before Par. liament.
The body of a young farmer, named Timothy Murphy, was on Wednesday found at Cloobarrk Waterford, under circumstances which point to marder having been com- mitted.

A meeting of the electors of the city of London was held, on Monday afternoon, at which it was resolved to protest against reducing the Parliamentary representatives of the city below four. At the Kensington Petty Sessions, on Tuesday,. the Countess de la Torre was committed to prison for a month in default of paying a fine of £7, imposed upon her for keeping a large number of cats and dogs in her residence at Pembroke-square. Earl's-court.

The Duke of Buckingham and Chandos was married on Tuesday morning at St. Peter's Church, Eaton-suguare. London, to Miss Graham Montgomery, eldest daughter of Sir Graham Montgomery, of Stobo Castle, Peebles. A brutal murder took plac3 on Saturday asight, near Moats, county Westmeath. A farmer, named Peter Kelley, was waylaid and fatally beaten, his head being corn. pletely battered in. The crime is attributed to an agrarian dispute. .

, An explosion of gis took place on Saturday evening in the vestry of the Wesleyan Chapel, Rodley. Mrs. Wilson, the caretaker, and her 801 l were injured, and soino damage was done to the property. There had been a leakage of gas, which was ignited by a lighted candle. Anazsr OF A RUNAWAY COUPLE.—On Monday, at the North-wall, Dublin, two detectives arrested a young couple who had eloped from Galway and were on their way to America. The young lady is only 16, and her companion a year older. The former had £4O upon her. Her father charges them with robbery.—Both were locked up. • THE BOOTLE FRALTDS.—At the Assizes, on Saturday, the test case, which was to decide whether the Corporation of Bootle was responsible for the fraudulent bonds on which the late Town Clerk of that borough raised money, was settled privately, end it is said that the Corporation has agreed to pay one-half of the sums fraudulently bor- rowed. Suocama RAILWAY ACCIDENT—About ten o'clock On Tuesday night a lamentable accident occurred on the Lon- don and North-Western Railway at Whaley Bridge. The engine of a goods train appears to have left the line at some ' ',icing points, and it fell from a bridge into the roadway ten I yards beneath, The driver of the train and also tho guard, who happened to be on the engine, were killed. A HORRIBLE DISCOVERY.—For some time theze has been seen floating in a mill reservoir at Farnworth, near Bolton, and near a number of cottages, what appealed to be a dead du, which was frequently being driven Ly the wind to the cottage doors. On Sunday afternoon, on being pushed away from one of the doors, the people, were horrify...el to see a woman's face, The body seems to have been in the water three weeks. 1

div.head: Wettero to tht editor.
div.p: Wettero to tht editor.
TEETOTALISM IN EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—! am sure it must be quite evideat te your readers that our friend " Moderator ' has grown weary of the dis- cussion on the above subject, and would be glad to get out of it. fie set out to prove that Christ was not an abstainer, and he has certainly made a miserable failure of it; so far, ha has not even shown that Christ partook of wine at all. I did think, when I made the admission in my last that our Siviour partook of wine at the last Supper, that I was help- ing him on a little, and I fully expected the point would have been taken up; but not having done so, only confirms the opinion that he has really had enough of it. He might at least have acted a little more reasonably. How he can expect me to deal with authorities out of my reach alto- gether, as I la.,ve stated plain enough, I cannot understand. He has given us the quotation from the Rev. F. A. Wale- son, MA., and I have promised to deal with it when the point is introduced. But " Moderator" declines to act on the same principle by quoting—as I requested him—Dr. Giekie's facts, Dean Stanley's arguments, and Dr. Blackie's reasons, which every intelligent writer or debater would have done in the first instance. I can only sty I am prepared to carry out the promise I made in my last letter on "Moderator" fulfilling his part. We should have got on much better if •‘ Moderator" had not had such a bad habit of misconstruction. Instead of replying to argument and reasoning ha plays upon words and phrases that do not really beat on the question at Issue. Why I cannot accept the opinions expressed by the Rev. E. Day I stated fully in my last letter; bat I should like to know what "Moderator" means by saying he con- futed my erroneous conclusions in his last. What sort of con- futing is this? " Moderator " asks my views of the " new wine in new wine bar," and adds his own opinion. I give him a full eplanation, showing that the new wine—grape I juice—was put into tit* bags to keep it from fermenting; When " Moderator " replies in a very confused style, giving a quotation from an authority whose words refer to the wine in the cup at Easter, and not to the neW wine in ntw skins at all. The custom of carrying wine in skin bottles Was not confined to one period of the year. " Moderator" has been anything but straightforward throughout this discussion. He has all along evaded per- tinent points, neglecting the wheat to deal with chaff ; and lam astonished at his simplicity in even hinting that the two paints I put before him are anything but pattinent to the question at issue; in fact, he cannot prove his posi- tion without taking them up, and I cannot understand i" Moderator " to mean " serious business " until he deals I with them to the exclusion of other irrelevant matter he I has introduced, if, instead of taking the course he has, " Moderator" had intr9dpc,4 the question of the wine at the last supper, of eyed the creation of wine by our Saviour at the marriage of Cana. he would have been more serious in his arguments, and his foundation might, haVe appeared more like what he styled it—impregnable—for though there Is no record that Christ drank the wine at the marriage feast, in my bumble opinion there is as much argument in the fact of Christ making the wine as there would have been in his drinking it. The habits of the Jews don't prove Christ either an abstainer or otherwise. In conclusion,l beg to say that your space and my time are far too valuable to be wasted any longer in quibbling about the question •, and if " Moderator "is not prepared to take up in earnesqthe task beset out to accomplish—that it is an " historical fact" that Christ was not an abstainer, and which from the way it has been introduced, one would have thought would have been as easy as proving the " his- torical fact "that Oliver Cromwell was Lord Protector of England, I shall certainly decline to carry on the discus- sion; but will, with your permission, Mr. Editor, for the benefit of your readers, give my views on the two or tbree points I have myself raised in one or two letters more, and then quietly retire.—Yours respectfully, TEE TEE. Earlestown, 18th February, 1885.

div.head: "SMASH THE MAHDI."
div.p: "SMASH THE MAHDI."

Sir,—The mighty " Thusderer " has spoken ; the word has gone forth, and now we know the work set out for us, "We must smash the Mandi." The words have been re- echoed in Warrington. The paper that upon such unim- portant subjects as politics and religion deems it wise (Ore- main neutral, upon this exhibits no hesitation whatever, but at once bids us to support the Government in its efforts to " Smash the Mandi." Well, this may be our duty; as a patriotic people no doubt we ought to smash everybody and everything that dares to interfere with our efforts in civilising the world; but I cannot help thinking it is wrong. We talk of putting down the rebels; so we talked of putting down Arabi, yet, what is the fact? It is acknow- ledged on all hands that the Egyptian rule has been one of base and grinding tyranny; that the wasteful expenditure of English money in Constantinople, grinding of the poor Turkish labourers, is an example only too keenly followed in Cairo, by those who sit in high places. Is it to put down patriots by bombarding cities ? to lay waste the cities of the plain, and to smash up nomadic races that we English support standing armies? Truly, our ways are ways of pleasantness, and our paths are paths of peace. Sir, what are we doing in the Soudan now ? How many can give an explicit answer to this? Especially, how many of those now under orders for Egypt could answer this? Oh, the answer is, "We go to relieve Gordon, and If he has been killed, wby, then we go for revenge." Truly this is a most charitable errand. r 4 Vengeance is mine, saith the Lord ; I will repay." " Ah," say the British Jingoes, "that is all very well in theory, but in practise, you know, we keep our powder dry." There used to be a Peace S miety, but I think its duties became nil when the Liberals came into power. The Manchester Examiner. speaking of this unhappy Egyptian business, says :—" It is absurd to talk of putting down a revolt, or of chastising the rebels. These men, in our eyes, are not rebels, and are engaged in no re- volt." No doubt this is most unpatriotic talk, and will re- ceive little or no support, but I hope it may cause some, at least, to think a little. M. de Lessens tale's praise to him- self that he kept out of the business, for, says he," Such an enterprise is tantamount to sending soldiers to he butchered." "To reach Khartoum," says M. de Lessens," whatever road may be taken, an army must traverse deserts in which water is absolutely wanting. The invading army, whether going or returning, will always be an easy prey to the warlike population of Nubia, who can throw on the enemy a hun- dred thousand combatants, to whom death is a matter of indifference," I think these are words that ought to be listened to. In the language of John Morley, "After war- taxation has increased the burdens on industry, after we have flung mountains of treasure and armies of brave men into its (the Soudan) gulf, from which nothing good and nothing useful could ever be given back to us, then the awakening and reckoning will come."

Suppose, even, we take-Khartou.n, what are we going to do with it ? To keep it, means to annex the Soudan, a territory in the interior of Africa as large as our Indian Empire. Well, certainly in these days of annexation and federation this may seem to seine a small matter ;to me the whole thing seems the biggest piece of folly the nation could be guilty of. Yet the Government has but just given the nation a guarantee that our policy shall at last be a vigorous one. A member of the Rothschild family, Lord Rosebery, has been appointed a cabinet minister, and now, surely the bond-holders will be satisfied that even Alexan- dria was not bombarded in vain. When will the people open their eyes, wake up, and shake themselves clear of this huge nightmare whose grip seems so tenacious? Was ever Europe in such a state? Germany making a cut and dried course for dame natnre to walk in. Seeking an out- let for her teeming and dissatisfied population, she vet seeks to tie them to fatherland ; England with her surplus popu- lation seeking to keep them tied to her apron strings, as if her own sons were too puny to be cast adrift; Russia, iznor- log Lord Salisbury's "big map," and with seven league boots striding away to Herat on his supposed way to grip the brightest jewel in the British crown" ; and above all this is lobe seen the man who works the puppets, Prince Bistnarck. According to some of our political prophets we are with- in measurable distance of seeing the " resources orciviliza- tion " thrown to the winds, and all the world will soon be- hold the moat gigantic European war ever knswn. And all for what? So that each nation may have better opportu- nities for carrying out its trade purposes ? " Well, we always bad war, and we always shall have " ; so reassn the people, and we seem to be a long way off the time when they will refuse to don a red coat -as a more conspicuous target at which some equally submissive tool may take aim. I cannot see why the various peoples of the civilized world should consent to be ordered about to shoot one another ; why Herr Krupp should now be making gnus without num- ber, so that the Russians may more effectually slaughter the British soldiers ; why Sir W. Armstrong should bring out a forty ton gun so that some milb else may have the opportunity of bringior out a thicker armour plate. Surely kuropean "civilization "is a mystery._
CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: ' ST. BARNABAS' TEA PARTY.
div.p: ' ST. BARNABAS' TEA PARTY.

_ . . On Tuesday evening the first tea party in connection with St. amebas' Church took place in the Public Hell, and was numerically a great success. At six o'clock tea was partaken of, about 500 persons sitting down to a substantial repast. The room had been decorated for the occazion, and wore a bright appearance. The following Ladies and gentle- men gave trays .--Lady Greenell, Mesdames Beamonr, W. Jones, Charlton Parr, Quekett, Allton, Harrison (Mayoress), Wilkinson, Morris, Reid, Milling, Mackie, Dyson, Owen, Pendlebury, Monks, J. Houghton, Denham, Proud, Yeo- mans, Gilroy, Woods, Smith, Gorse, Townsend, Pollitt, I Carter, F. Monks, H. Houghton, Taylor, Rose, KenteCald- well, Roscoe ; Mr. J. G. McMionies, M.P., Councillor J. Pierpoint, Rev. J. Ward, Messrs. R. Davies, T. Seaton, P. Leigh, G. Cropper, G. Tot t, Leeson, Robinson, Beans, Milnere Howson, Japer, Patchett, Hollingsworth, Smith, Bellian,,Taylor. After tea a concert was given, pre- sided over by the Vicar, the Rey. G. Allton, and amongst those present were the Mayor end Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Herrison), the Revs. S. Wilkinson and J. Ward,Coun- cillor J. Pierpeint, Mr. and Mrs. T. Morris, Messrs, T. Sut- ton, Stnetherst, Gilroy, Pilkington, Cropper, &c.,&.—The CneeemAxe„ in opening the proceedings, said that he thought the-largo attendance at their first tea party augured well for the future of tee parish. There were persons of all denominations present, which showed that amcngst their working population there was as much commett feeling, union, and he hoped as much Christian sympathy as was ' to be foeedamongst their more wealthy brethren. (Applause.) That, and: the hearty reception that had been accorded him on other occasions, was very cheering to him. Trays had been given with great willingness, an abundance of food had: been provided, and in asking contrilautious from their wealthier friends he had not bad one reSusal. They had tried, to make their party as cheerful as possible, for he tkought that when working-men and their wives had been at the trouble of putting on their best attire they expected to find something more cheering and bright than they could atta'n in their own homes. lie thought the working people richly deserved something, more cheerful than they could provide for themsdves, for he believed them to be liberal minded and liberal givers, in St. 13ernabae parish he had always found it. 31).. He was sure that it was only the present depression in trade that caused them to be in such low water respecting! their church of St. B arnabas. He was glad to see that amongst the working- men of the parish there was a growing feeling of religion. Although they could not say that their old machinery was all in good working order—being a new parish, they could say they were providing new machinery which, all hoped, would work well amongst the 6,000 working population. As they were aware he had no Sunday sohool in the parish for tha children logo to, and he appealed to all present to speak to their friends and neighbours of the great necessity of providing a school or building of some kind for the work- men's children of St. Ba Reims. He was thankful to the Sunday school teachers who bad stuck by him under great difficulties, and were deserving of more praise than were teachers in schools were the ease was different. In their case they had to teach in the church under great difficulty. Having referred to the excellency of the voluntary choir and the generosity of the org tnist in dispensing with pecaniary reward for the present, Mr. Allton described some of the dire distress prevalent in the parish, reminded his hearers that the church was unendowned, and, remarking with concluding reference to the school, said it was foreign to him to wish to ask for such a thing as any school to be built by compulsory means ; what he wanted to do was to raise, by degrees, volunta, y schools by voluntary effort, whereby they would be in the bands of a body of gentlemen, and could be con- ducted upon the best and broadest principles compatable with sound education, both religious and moral. (Lep. plause.)—A miscellaneous programme was then gone I through by the following :—Mise Davies; Illssrs Ware- ham, Massey, Short, Kent, Baxter, and Bellian, assisted by the choir.—Subsequently Mr, Gilroy delivered a short a]- = concerning the work of St. Barnabas Mr. Allton, he I said, took charge of a parish without endowment or peen. Diary recompense, and in it an amount of distress that many would have no idea of. The distress in the parish was not as Some thought, highly exaggerated, hut in P 9119 Ca-Ps it was indeed appalling. Mr. Anton laboured in a zealous and hearty manner, and the very fact of so many people being then present and using their endeavours for the success of the tea party, was proof of the goodwill borne to Mr. Allton and their appreciation of his work.—A vote of thanks was passed to the tray givers and the ladies who had given their services were heartily thanked on the motion of Councillor Pierpoint, seconded by the Mayor.—The singing of the national anthem concluded the entertainment, and for some time afterwards dancine was indulged in, but the room was too crowded for the pleasant exercise to b 3 fully en- joyed.

div.head: BRITISH AND FOREIGN- BIBLE
div.p: THE BRITISH AND FOREIGN- BIBLE
SOCIETY.

Oil Tuesday evening the annual meeting of the Warring- ton Auxiliary of the above society was held in the Co- operative Hall, Warrington. The chair was occupied by the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), and there were also on the platform the Rev J Yonge, the Rev J McTurk, the Rev C C Harrison, the Rev F Wainwright, vicar of St John's, Altrin- cham ; the Rev W H Williams, Niigata ; Mr E J Guest, hon. sec.; and Mr W Owen, hon. treasurer. There was a thin attendance. Mr E J Guest read the report of the local committee, as follows :—" The work done during the past year by the Warrington Auxiliary and its association at Penketh, Moore, and Padgate does not call for much remark. Whilst you committee would gladly render more efficient snvice to the parent society, they are thankful for the steady and persistent help of their friends In Warrington and the villages adj want. - They regard this as the more en- couraging avhen they consider ths increasing number of claims the Christian public have on their means, their time, and their energy. It is their endeavour, however, not to allow these other and important claims to eclipse those of the British and Foreign Bible Society, which they consider to be of primary importance both to the Churches and to the world. That these claims may be clearly understood and felt, your committee secure from year to year, for the annual meeting, the services of some of the ablest advocates to be found in the Anglican and Nonconformist Churches. This advocacy, in addition to that of our esteemed district secretary, the Rev Jelinger E Symons; has done mach to clear away the ignorance and prejudice that existed concerning the mission of this society Your committee would again invite the co-operatien of such of the local clergy and wealthy men who held aloof from this auxiliary; indeed they claim the helo of all who desire that the Word of the Lord may have free course and be glorifi:d.' During the year Mr John Crosfield' found it necessary to resign his position as treasurer-of this auxiliary. Your committee reluctantly accepted the resignation. They feel indebted to Mr William Owen for so willingly and ably filling up the vacancy. You have doubtless noticed with regret the absence of our district secretary from this our annual meeting. Mr Symons is always welcomed' amongst us from the catholicity W his-spirit and the earnestness of his advocacy. But this year it falls to his lot to do work for the society on the continent of Europe. The Rev F Wainwright, M.A., vicar ot St. Jirtin'e, Altrincbam, comes before us to-night in a two-fold capacity—first, as Mr fiymon's substitute, and secondly as the invited speaker of the evening to represent the Church Of England. Tour committee feel under obligation to him for thus adding this to the many duties be has to discharge in the care of a large church." The report also contained extracts from the report of the committee of the parent society. —Mr W Owen read the treasurer's report. which showed as follows :—Receipts Balance in hand,. 19 Ida Id; received for Bibles, £l7; Os 104; collected by Mr Guest, £l6; Warrington collection, £4 10i 2d; Moore pri- vate collection, £8 193 Ocl-; ditto public collection, £2; collected by Mr. Richardson, £1 4 13,1 ; bank interest, 9s id; Penketh collection, £2'l7s 4d; collected by Mr Guest, MO; interest, 93 7d; by Mr Guest, Zfa Os fid ; by Mr Garnett, £l3 13e; sales by Mr Powleon, £l3 Is 8d ; total, £134 4a 10d. Amongst the payments was one of 170-to the parent society, leaving a net balance in hand of £43; us Bd.—The Mayor said he extremely regretted-that there was so small an attendance that night, but he did not for a moment believe that it was owing to any lukewarmnese on the part of the public towards that excellent society, but rather owing to the inclemency of the weather, and the fact that there were three or four other meetings in Warrington that night —The Rev. F. Wainwright then gave an address on the work of the Bible Society, in the course of which he gave some interesting information as to, the way in which the bible had been translated into various tongues. He concluded by proposing the adoption of the report.—The Rev J McTurk, in seconding this proposal, said he should like to see a little additional report on local effort, and, referring to-bible canyassenhe had been engaged in in other towns, he said be had no doubt that a canvass of that kind would result in a very great number of copies of the Word of God being disseminated in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He also suggested that a, stall for the sale of bibloo might be erected in the mar Net, and he hae no doubt that on some Saturdays there would be a considerable number of bibles distributed. ( Hear. hear.) The report was then-adopted. —The Rev C C Harrison moved the appointment of the following officers,„ viz :—President, Lord Winmarleigh ; vice-presidents, Messrs Peter Stubbs. Peter Rylands, MP, J G McMinnies, M P, W Bearcont, George Crosfield, J P; John Crosfield, Ji P: treasurer, Mr William Owen ; secre- taries, the Revs it C E Carleton and John Yonge, and Mr E J Guest; committee' Messrs Cr Poulson, ;;;Smith, MB. J P, William Barlow,M Bowden. E J Guest, It Garnett, Z Armitage, J P, Lewis Reyno:ds, R A Naylor, S Chandley, J P, J Faircicugh, J P, J R Buckton, J S Garland, and J Hall ; district secretary, Rev Jelinger E Symons.—Mr Councillor Dixon secon.dad this proposal which was car- ried.—The Rey J Yonge moved, and tho Rev 3 rilcTurk seconded a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding, and his Worship having responded the meet'..ng concluded.
